sections.heading: 09 — Source Catalog
sections.intro:
Every source ingested into this knowledge package, with the Main subjects, Anatomy, Management options, and Important concepts each one covers.

**Video sources from:** Dupuytren Foundation — https://www.youtube.com/@DupuytrenFoundation  
**Sources catalogued:** 122

Entries are alphabetical by title. Use the source ID to trace any claim in the other files back to its source.

---

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `AEtlrIjvGDM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AEtlrIjvGDM
- **Upload date:** 2015-12-12
- **Duration:** 05:25
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/AEtlrIjvGDM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** whether repeating needle fasciotomy on successive recurrences remains worthwhile, a retrospective UMCG cohort tracking patients through their 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th PNF treatments, how much each successive PNF treatment postponed more aggressive surgery, a joint-specific trend (MCP outperforming PIP) too small to confirm statistically
- **Anatomy:** MCP joint, PIP joint
- **Management options:** repeated percutaneous needle fasciotomy (PNF), across successive recurrences on the same ray, limited fasciectomy, as the alternative chosen at each recurrence decision point
- **Important concepts:** primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary recurrence as successive treatment decision points, total passive extension deficit (TPED) reduction tracked separately at each successive treatment, retrospective medical-record study design and its data-quality limitations
subsections.heading: 1. "Percutaneous Needle Fasciotomy" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `wSZhfP1r1OY`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wSZhfP1r1OY
- **Upload date:** 2016-05-18
- **Duration:** 09:26
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/wSZhfP1r1OY.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why open surgery's own biology works against Dupuytren's disease control, a risk-tolerance explanation for why patients avoid surgery but accept needle release, specific technical keys — needle gauge, anesthesia depth, and the "do no harm" checks, a full case walkthrough, from anesthesia to final manipulation
- **Anatomy:** pretendinous, natatory, and spiral cords, digital nerve, MCP and PIP joints
- **Management options:** needle fasciotomy (needle aponeurotomy), Eaton's modified technique
- **Important concepts:** flap elevation and wound tension as drivers of post-surgical inflammation, prospect theory — modest risk outweighing modest gain in patient decision-making, real-time patient feedback (sensation, tendon excursion) as the intraoperative safety check
subsections.heading: 2. 2010 IFSSH Needle Aponeurotomy presentation

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `2Dq1u73_LZU`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Dq1u73_LZU
- **Upload date:** 2018-05-12
- **Duration:** 04:35
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/2Dq1u73_LZU.txt`
- **Main subjects:** reframing Dupuytren's as a systemic disease, not just a hand contracture, what's well understood about the disease (end-stage nodule/cord biology) versus poorly understood (earlier stages), a proposed shift from a "wait and cut" model to a chronic-disease, biomarker-guided model, the International Dupuytren Data Bank, and a direct appeal for more patient enrollment
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** Dupuytren's disease as probably not a single disease with a single gene, a biomarker-driven treatment algorithm modeled on rheumatoid arthritis and gout, most existing knowledge deriving from surgical/end-stage tissue rather than earlier disease
subsections.heading: 3. 2018Germany

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `X-LhucSUXgQ`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X-LhucSUXgQ
- **Upload date:** 2026-02-10
- **Duration:** 07:11
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/X-LhucSUXgQ.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why finger-angle measurement can only show damage already done, not predict it, the rheumatoid arthritis/TNF precedent for how a blood biomarker enables prevention, a preliminary Dupuytren biomarker panel the Dupuytren Research Group says it has developed
- **Anatomy:** fingers, palm
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** diagnostic versus predictive biomarker tests, biomarker-driven research as more fundable than clinical-measurement-only research, damage control versus disease control as models of care
subsections.heading: 4. Advancing Dupuytren disease diagnosis and treatment

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `kq4hr06tOtY`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kq4hr06tOtY
- **Upload date:** 2010-09-11
- **Duration:** 12:24
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/kq4hr06tOtY.txt`
- **Main subjects:** reframing the bent Dupuytren's finger as tissue retention rather than active contraction, why the disease is proposed to occur specifically in the finger's mobile, flexed-position tissue, reinterpreting Luck's histogenic classification and the myofibroblast's role, a modified subcutaneous fasciotomy technique following from this theory
- **Anatomy:** subcutaneous fibro-fatty tissue of the finger, Cleland's ligament, the palmar aponeurosis
- **Management options:** Meinel's modified, exclusively subcutaneous release technique, called digital fasciotomy, static extension splinting, proposed to prevent tissue/finger retention
- **Important concepts:** tissue retention versus active tissue contraction as competing explanatory models, fingers spending most of the day and night in a flexed position as a precondition for the disease, stress adaptation/remodeling of connective tissue as the proposed mechanism, rather than active shortening
subsections.heading: 5. Albrecht Meinel MD, "The palmar fibromatosis the..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium Presentation

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `iD3mYMmfN-Q`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iD3mYMmfN-Q
- **Upload date:** 2017-09-06
- **Duration:** 14:22
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/iD3mYMmfN-Q.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the palmar fascia as a multi-layer, quilted scaffold, not a single structure, the four main finger cord types and how they differ clinically, why MCP and PIP joints have very different cord patterns, why a finger can lose correction after apparently successful surgery
- **Anatomy:** palmar fascia, natatory ligament, Grayson's ligament, Cleland's ligament, pretendinous bands, spiral bands, central and lateral cords, MCP and PIP joints, accessory collateral ligament, palmar plate, extensor mechanism
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** central, retrovascular, lateral, and spiral cords as distinct clinical entities, residual contracting force without a palpable cord, incomplete correction versus early loss of correction as separate failure modes
subsections.heading: 6. Anatomy Cords

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `ZFj6QIZfHq8`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFj6QIZfHq8
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-23
- **Duration:** 11:05
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/ZFj6QIZfHq8.txt`
- **Main subjects:** what bioengineered skin graft actually is and why it was tried as an alternative to autologous skin, a prior off-label precedent in epidermolysis bullosa hand surgery, zero recurrences in a small, long-followed subgroup, alongside a slower healing time, the study's own honest "this is a focus group, not a trial" framing
- **Anatomy:** palmar skin, dermal matrix
- **Management options:** bioengineered (tissue-engineered) skin graft applied over open-palm (McCash) fasciectomy wounds
- **Important concepts:** bioengineered skin as living cell therapy, not just a physical barrier, the McCash open-palm technique as the baseline being modified, donor-site pain reduction with bioengineered coverage
subsections.heading: 7. Anne Ouellette MD MBA, "Outcomes of Apligraf use in... " 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `oRdE0UKeJF0`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oRdE0UKeJF0
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-22
- **Duration:** 11:41
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/oRdE0UKeJF0.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the first randomized trial directly comparing needle fasciotomy to limited fasciectomy, the actual 5-year recurrence rates for each technique, and how much sooner PNF recurs, a striking age effect — younger patients recur regardless of technique chosen, why patient satisfaction stayed high even in the higher-recurrence group
- **Anatomy:** PIP, DIP, and MCP joints
- **Management options:** percutaneous needle fasciotomy (PNF), limited fasciectomy (LF)
- **Important concepts:** recurrence defined as a 30-degree TPD worsening from the 6-week post-operative measurement, worst-case and best-case sensitivity analysis for patients lost to follow-up, age as a predictor of recurrence independent of technique
subsections.heading: 8. Annet Van Rijssen MD, "5-year results of first-ever randomised..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `g40N2M2C6qM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g40N2M2C6qM
- **Upload date:** 2011-03-13
- **Duration:** 22:45
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/g40N2M2C6qM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** what evidence base is needed to call Dupuytren's a genetic disease, the practical difficulty of choosing tissue and controls for genetic studies, linkage, candidate-gene, and copy-number-variant studies, and their limited replication, genetic testing as a proposed (not current) tool for personalized treatment selection
- **Anatomy:** palmar fascia, nodules and cords
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** sibling recurrence risk ratio as genetic evidence, LOD score as a linkage-study significance threshold, copy number variation (CNV), gene expression comparison across nodule, cord, and control tissue, personalized medicine / pharmacogenomics applied to treatment selection
subsections.heading: 9. Ardeshir Bayat MD PhD "Genetics of Dupuytren's Disease" 2010 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `r5L_NKVFdQw`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r5L_NKVFdQw
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-21
- **Duration:** 11:14
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/r5L_NKVFdQw.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a joint-severity-specific flap algorithm for skin closure after PIP joint release, a modified homodigital/heterodigital transposition flap technique, and why it replaced an earlier design, a five-year, 50-patient outcome series stratified by preoperative contracture severity, complications, including vascularity problems and two revision procedures
- **Anatomy:** MCP joint, PIP joint, proximal and middle phalanx, neurovascular bundle
- **Management options:** Z-plasty (for PIP contracture under 30 degrees), dorsolateral/homodigital and heterodigital transposition flaps with full-thickness skin grafting (for PIP contracture over 30 degrees), open arthrolysis, combinable with open palm technique
- **Important concepts:** Tubiana staging (0 through IV) as the severity framework guiding technique choice, tension-free wound closure as essential after open arthrolysis, recurrence versus loss of intraoperatively achieved correction, tracked separately over time
subsections.heading: 10. Bernhard Lukas Dr med, "Treatment of severe Dupuytren contracture..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `-32nd2vQexQ`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-32nd2vQexQ
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-22
- **Duration:** 08:55
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/-32nd2vQexQ.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a personal reversal — publicly opposing needle aponeurotomy, then adopting it after a mentor's death, a prospective 62-finger series and how its results compare to prior literature, why the technique worked best at the MCP joint specifically, one flexor tendon laceration complication, and what Gan took from it
- **Anatomy:** MCP joint, PIP joint, flexor tendon (zone I/II border)
- **Management options:** needle aponeurotomy (a slicing, radial-to-ulnar technique variant)
- **Important concepts:** total digital extension deficit as the outcome measure, cord proximity to the neurovascular bundle as the rationale for joint-specific technique preference, Gan's own stated lesson from reversing a public position, that never is not very long
subsections.heading: 11. Bing Siang Gan MD PhD, "Needle aponeurotomy for..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `Eqpst2Of7ow`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eqpst2Of7ow
- **Upload date:** 2021-09-24
- **Duration:** 19:19
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/Eqpst2Of7ow.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why finger-angle measurements are geometrically unreliable, not just imprecise, why age of diagnosis is biased by family history and shouldn't be read as disease onset, amputation as a real, quantified outcome of failed Dupuytren's treatment, IDDB's 2021 enrollment numbers and treatment-burden statistics, the biomarker panel design (why whole exome sequencing is deprioritized)
- **Anatomy:** PIP joint, MCP joint, CMC joint, lateral versus central cords
- **Management options:** repeat/revision fasciectomy after dermofasciectomy, with a stated amputation rate
- **Important concepts:** cord-to-joint-axis geometry determining angular contracture, Dupuytren's diathesis as an "educated guess," not a measurement, age of diagnosis versus age of onset, blood biomarkers as the emerging standard across fibrotic diseases generally
subsections.heading: 12. Biomarkers and the IDDB: 2021Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `fvmRS3OiWic`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fvmRS3OiWic
- **Upload date:** 2010-09-08
- **Duration:** 17:36
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/fvmRS3OiWic.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the myofibroblast as a functional phenotype, not a fixed cell type, two separable contraction pathways and what each one actually does, a rubber-band model reconciling brief calcium-driven contractions with sustained Rho-kinase tension, the diseases and processes myofibroblasts drive beyond Dupuytren's
- **Anatomy:** myofibroblasts, extracellular matrix / collagen
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** myofibroblast as phenotype rather than cell type (Gabbiani's functional definition), the calcium/calmodulin/myosin light chain kinase pathway, the Rho-kinase pathway, periodic versus isometric contraction, matrix remodeling via cyclical slack creation and take-up
subsections.heading: 13. Boris Hinz PhD, "Fundamental aspects of..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium Presentation

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `-jLfWXX3YUM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-jLfWXX3YUM
- **Upload date:** 2020-04-06
- **Duration:** 21:20
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/-jLfWXX3YUM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** what specialist to see, and how to vet a hand surgeon before committing to treatment, the evidence quality behind preventive versus corrective treatments, why a biomarker's absence blocks testing preventive treatments at all, diathesis factors and how they should change the treatment plan, natural history odds after a first nodule appears
- **Anatomy:** PIP joint, MCP (MP) joint, palmar fascia
- **Management options:** minimally invasive procedures (collagenase, needle fasciotomy) versus open procedures (fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy), tamoxifen and repeated cortisone injection as post-procedure recurrence-slowing trials, hand therapy, splinting, radiotherapy, massage, and supplements, each rated by evidence quality
- **Important concepts:** Dupuytren's diathesis, the biomarker gap and why it blocks preventive-treatment research, the 20–40 degree PIP treatment window, minimizing lifetime permanent complications as the actual treatment goal
subsections.heading: 14. British Dupuytren Society Seven Questions

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `MKJlNbyux0o`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKJlNbyux0o
- **Upload date:** 2015-11-30
- **Duration:** 06:20
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/MKJlNbyux0o.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why there is currently no agreed definition of "early" Dupuytren's disease, a systematic review finding only 15 usable studies out of 618 screened abstracts, what the evidence shows for steroid injection, vitamin E, splinting, and radiotherapy — and how weak that evidence is, the review's own recommendations for improving future early-disease research
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** intralesional steroid (triamcinolone) injection, vitamin E, hyperbaric oxygen, splinting, ultrasound, and stretching, radiotherapy
- **Important concepts:** the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine grading scale as applied to this literature, PECOS framework (Population, Exposure, Comparison, Outcome, Study design) for structuring a systematic review, most included studies mixing early-disease patients into broader, more-advanced-disease cohorts
subsections.heading: 15. Catherine Ball "Systematic Review Of Non-Surgical Treatments" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `2Yi43NqnvfM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Yi43NqnvfM
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-24
- **Duration:** 13:11
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/2Yi43NqnvfM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** relaxin's mechanism as a selective anti-fibrotic hormone, not a general anti-collagen agent, how relaxin blocks TGF-beta signaling specifically through SMAD2 and nitric oxide, its track record across essentially every fibrotic disease model tested so far, genetic knockout evidence for relaxin as an endogenous anti-fibrotic regulator
- **Anatomy:** myofibroblasts, collagen
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** relaxin (H2 relaxin) and its receptor RXFP1, SMAD signaling (SMAD2/3/4 pro-fibrotic, SMAD7 anti-fibrotic), disease-selective anti-fibrotic action (no effect on basal matrix turnover), relaxin knockout mice as causal evidence of its regulatory role
subsections.heading: 16. Chrishan Samuel PhD, "Relaxin: an emerging therapy for..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `8Kp5Fz7ZKl0`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8Kp5Fz7ZKl0
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-17
- **Duration:** 09:52
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/8Kp5Fz7ZKl0.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why IGFBP6 is downregulated in diseased tissue, and TGF-beta makes it worse, a dose-response experiment showing IGFBP6 suppresses contraction while IGF2 induces it, IGFBP6 proposed as a potential non-surgical therapeutic target
- **Anatomy:** myofibroblasts
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** IGFBP6 as a negative regulator of IGF2 bioavailability, TGF-beta repressing IGFBP6 as a proposed disease mechanism, dose-response fibroblast-populated collagen lattice (FPCL) testing
subsections.heading: 17. Christina Raykha MSc Candidate, "Insulin-like Growth Factor..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `XMQEyF-Gtv0`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XMQEyF-Gtv0
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-17
- **Duration:** 13:42
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/XMQEyF-Gtv0.txt`
- **Main subjects:** testing whether disease spreads by nodule cells migrating, or by conditioning the matrix, a 3D migration assay comparing Dupuytren's disease cells to matched normal fascia cells, a conditioned-collagen experiment showing normal cells "catch" disease markers from DD-cell secretions
- **Anatomy:** palmar fascia, nodules and cords, extracellular matrix
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** the extracellular matrix as an active mediator of disease, not a passive scaffold, the cell migration hypothesis versus the ECM-mediated disease hypothesis, beta-catenin and periostin as matricellular/signaling markers, patient-matched genetically identical controls (disease-affected versus phenotypically normal fascia, same patient)
subsections.heading: 18. David O'Gorman PhD, "Primary Dupuytren's Disease cell..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `e_14ZbU3pFM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e_14ZbU3pFM
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-24
- **Duration:** 09:48
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/e_14ZbU3pFM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** testing four novel compounds for selective antiproliferative activity on diseased cells specifically, why compound 4 stood out — specific to diseased cells, low toxicity to healthy ones, a practical tissue-collection lesson for advanced-stage cases, proposed future drug targets named at the close
- **Anatomy:** myofibroblasts
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** selective versus non-specific antiproliferative activity, IC50/LC50 testing for differential drug effect, topoisomerase inhibition and tubulin interference as a drug mechanism
subsections.heading: 19. Davor Jurisic Phd MD, "Screening of potential prodrugs on cells..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `KjV8R8x4OwE`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KjV8R8x4OwE
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-23
- **Duration:** 10:14
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/KjV8R8x4OwE.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a multi-center RCT design comparing night splinting to no splinting after fasciectomy, three different analyses of the same data, and why they gave three different answers, the striking finding that splinting looked worse than no splinting once confounding was removed, the study's own honest limitations, including questioning its own primary outcome measure
- **Anatomy:** MCP joint, PIP joint
- **Management options:** static thermoplastic night splinting, six months, after fasciectomy or dermofasciectomy
- **Important concepts:** pragmatic trial design, intention-to-treat versus per-protocol versus explanatory analysis, the minimally clinically important difference (MCID) used for sample size calculation, a "wait and see" splinting policy as a study conclusion
subsections.heading: 20. Debbie Larson BScOT, "Splinting after contracture..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `t8kzlpSJLj0`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8kzlpSJLj0
- **Upload date:** 2015-10-25
- **Duration:** 05:19
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/t8kzlpSJLj0.txt`
- **Main subjects:** using propensity score matching to compare collagenase and limited fasciectomy in real-world practice, joint-specific results — similar at the MP joint, LF favored at the PIP joint, collagenase patients reporting larger functional and satisfaction gains despite the PIP correction gap, all serious adverse events occurring in the surgical group, none in the collagenase group
- **Anatomy:** MCP (MP) joint, PIP joint, DIP joint
- **Management options:** collagenase injection (manufacturer-standard dosing), limited fasciectomy (LF)
- **Important concepts:** propensity score matching as an alternative to randomization when a randomized trial is impractical, contracture correction versus patient-reported functional outcome as separate, sometimes diverging, measures, comparing objective outcome differences against comparative complication severity
subsections.heading: 21. Dr Chao Zhou "Collagenase Injection versus Limited Fasciectomy" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `dp45M2IEW3k`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dp45M2IEW3k
- **Upload date:** 2015-11-20
- **Duration:** 05:56
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/dp45M2IEW3k.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a laboratory rationale for why splinting tension might not help fibroblast biology, the single available paper on non-operative splinting, and its real limitations, three randomized trials of post-surgical night splinting, presented in sequence, why the debate concludes routine post-op night splinting isn't supported by the evidence
- **Anatomy:** MCP joint, PIP joint
- **Management options:** post-surgical night splinting, tested against hand therapy alone across three randomized trials
- **Important concepts:** fibroblast/myofibroblast response to tensile stress in laboratory culture, intention-to-treat analysis with a built-in, ethically necessary crossover allowance, distinguishing patient satisfaction from statistically measured functional outcome
subsections.heading: 22. Dr. Adrian Chojnowski "Debate: Splinting confers no benefit" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `pE5YRmrXIGY`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pE5YRmrXIGY
- **Upload date:** 2015-11-21
- **Duration:** 07:28
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/pE5YRmrXIGY.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a retrospective comparison of a dynamic external distraction device against fasciectomy with check-rein release, why acute soft-tissue release risks digital artery spasm and skin loss, a detailed case walkthrough, including a secondary complication that emerged mid-treatment, where this device fits relative to needle aponeurotomy and collagenase by contracture severity
- **Anatomy:** PIP joint, check-rein ligaments, digital arteries
- **Management options:** the "digit widget" — a dynamic external soft-tissue distraction device, fasciectomy with check-rein ligament release
- **Important concepts:** gradual soft-tissue lengthening as an alternative to acute surgical release, severity-stratified treatment selection across three modalities, retrospective cohort comparison design
subsections.heading: 23. Dr. Atanu Biswas "Soft Tissue Distraction versus Fasciectomy" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `3PcPMAWaUDM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3PcPMAWaUDM
- **Upload date:** 2015-10-25
- **Duration:** 06:17
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/3PcPMAWaUDM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a national survey of German hand surgeons' preferred treatment by disease stage, why limited fasciectomy, not needle fasciotomy, dominates German practice overall, a stark national contrast — collagenase is effectively unavailable in Germany for reimbursement reasons, how surgeon patient volume relates to treatment choice and care setting
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** limited fasciectomy (LF), percutaneous needle fasciotomy (PNF/PMF)
- **Important concepts:** a health-authority policy decision (Germany's GBA) shaping national treatment availability, low complication risk versus best possible outcome as competing decision criteria by disease stage, survey response-rate methodology and a volume-weighted sensitivity analysis
subsections.heading: 24. Dr. Bert Reichert "Favorite Options of German Hand Surgeons" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `L3kjpUIwHIQ`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L3kjpUIwHIQ
- **Upload date:** 2015-10-25
- **Duration:** 17:15
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/L3kjpUIwHIQ.txt`
- **Main subjects:** defining "severe" PIP contracture and the specific problems it creates (skin, fascia, joint), why skin grafting protects specifically against recurrence, with her own outcome data, why chasing complete PIP extension can cost more in flexion than it's worth, comparative recurrence data across needle, collagenase, fasciectomy, and dermofasciectomy
- **Anatomy:** PIP joint, central, lateral, spiral, and double-spiral cords, flexor sheath and pulleys, extensor mechanism (central slip)
- **Management options:** local flaps (V-Y) for isolated contracture under 90 degrees, skin grafting/dermofasciectomy for high-diathesis or recurrent contracture, two-stage palmar fasciotomy before definitive PIP surgery in very severe cases, external fixators for extreme contracture, PIP joint shortening arthrodesis (removing the middle phalanx) as a salvage option
- **Important concepts:** the 90-degree threshold for defining severe contracture, dermofasciectomy's protective effect specifically under the grafted skin, the extension-versus-flexion tradeoff in aggressive joint release, the Tubiana disease test for extensor slackening
subsections.heading: 25. Dr. Caroline Leclercq "Severe PIPj contractures" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `SZEmawrCaK8`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SZEmawrCaK8
- **Upload date:** 2015-10-25
- **Duration:** 05:30
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/SZEmawrCaK8.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the preoperative hand-appearance score as the single strongest predictor of postoperative satisfaction, a striking gender gap in satisfaction, left unresolved, separating preoperative predictors from postoperative outcome confounders, why hand appearance matters functionally, not just cosmetically, to patients
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** limited fasciectomy (primary and recurrent cases)
- **Important concepts:** patient satisfaction as a distinct, increasingly used quality-of-care outcome measure, the Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire (MHQ) hand-appearance subscore as a predictive variable, unexplained variance in satisfaction remaining even after accounting for known predictors
subsections.heading: 26. Dr. Chao Zhou "Hand function following fasciectomy" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `wsqTB5LAGYo`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wsqTB5LAGYo
- **Upload date:** 2015-10-25
- **Duration:** 05:12
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/wsqTB5LAGYo.txt`
- **Main subjects:** three clinical observations Eaton argues rule out an active-contraction model, why contracture is site-specific to the palm despite identical histology at other sites, periodic versus isometric myofibroblast contraction as the mechanistic basis of the passive model
- **Anatomy:** palm, dorsum of the fingers, plantar fascia, myofibroblasts
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** passive versus active contraction models, tissue laxity versus tissue tension as the determinant of where contracture develops, periodic contraction (calcium-regulated) versus isometric contraction (Rho-kinase pathway)
subsections.heading: 27. Dr. Charles Eaton "Debate: Passive More than Active Contraction" 2015 Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `AbY1KVhTVAo`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AbY1KVhTVAo
- **Upload date:** 2015-07-01
- **Duration:** 19:00
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/AbY1KVhTVAo.txt`
- **Main subjects:** why chronic-disease research methods, not surgical-research methods, fit Dupuytren's, Eaton's own 3,400-patient intake data on what predicts hand interference, the genetic/systemic versus exposure/epigenetic disease-subset hypothesis, the International Dupuytren Data Bank's design and recruitment plan
- **Anatomy:** palm, fingers, myofibroblasts

- **Anatomy:** MCP (MP) joint, PIP joint
- **Management options:** concurrent double-dose collagenase (CCH) injection, two joints treated 24-72 hours apart in the same hand

- **Anatomy:** tunica albuginea (the "plaque"), dorsal penile nerve, neurovascular bundle of the penis
- **Management options:** Nesbit plication procedure and its variations, plaque incision or excision with grafting (bovine/porcine pericardium), penile prosthesis implantation, collagenase injection into the plaque

- **Important concepts:** lipophilic fluorescent cell tracing for in vivo cell-fate tracking, nude rat forepaw injection as an animal model platform, the absence of a good animal model as a stated impediment to new treatments
subsections.heading: 112. Sandeep Kathju MD PhD, "Establishing an animal model of..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `dsPwSUDrz1Y`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dsPwSUDrz1Y
- **Upload date:** 2010-09-11
- **Duration:** 28:26
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/dsPwSUDrz1Y.txt`
- **Main subjects:** where myofibroblasts come from (lineage-tracing evidence, not Dupuytren-specific), TGF-beta as the driver of both differentiation and myofibroblast survival, the Fizz1/Jagged1/Notch pathway, with one stated point of Dupuytren relevance, epigenetic repression (DNA methylation, NKX2.5) as a second control layer
- **Anatomy:** myofibroblasts, fascia, perivascular adventitial fibroblasts
- **Management options:** none — basic-science mechanism talk, no treatment discussed
- **Important concepts:** myofibroblast differentiation, TGF-beta/SMAD signaling and SMAD binding elements, Notch/Jagged signaling, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (evidence against, in vivo), DNA methylation and histone modification as differentiation gatekeepers
subsections.heading: 113. Sem Phan PhD MD, "Mechanisms of Myofibroblast..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium Presentation

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `Fj5WfRonTOg`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fj5WfRonTOg
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-16
- **Duration:** 19:05
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/Fj5WfRonTOg.txt`
- **Main subjects:** what makes a protein a collagen, and which collagen types matter in Dupuytren's cords, how collagen is synthesized, cross-linked, and degraded, step by step, two competing framings of collagen's role in disease — imbalance versus signal transduction, the "tug of war" model explaining how myofibroblasts and collagen reinforce each other
- **Anatomy:** collagen types I, III, IV, and V, myofibroblasts, extracellular matrix / collagen fibrils
- **Management options:** collagenase as a drug, explained mechanistically via what "collagenase" activity actually requires
- **Important concepts:** the triple helix and Gly-X-Y motif defining collagen, fibripositor-mediated collagen secretion and fibrillogenesis, the three-step requirement (bind, unwind, cleave) for true collagenase activity, collagen as a signal transducer under mechanical tension
subsections.heading: 114. Susan Emeigh Hart VMD PhD, "A primer of collagen biology..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `MO1w1Ed-Yqc`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MO1w1Ed-Yqc
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-23
- **Duration:** 16:59
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/MO1w1Ed-Yqc.txt`
- **Main subjects:** pre-operative splinting/traction devices and whether they help before surgery, the evidence for post-operative dynamic splinting (Gelberman's compliance data), Roz Evans's "no tension" dorsal block splinting rationale, continuous passive motion (CPM) — a modality with mixed evidence, {'practical post-operative therapy': 'scar, edema, and exercise management'}
- **Anatomy:** PIP joint, MCP joint, DIP joint, central slip and oblique retinacular ligament
- **Management options:** pre-operative splinting and continuous elongation devices, post-operative dynamic and static splinting protocols, continuous passive motion (CPM), scar and edema management techniques
- **Important concepts:** the "no tension" splinting hypothesis (mechanical stress, hypoxia, and hypertrophic scar), splint compliance as an outcome predictor, boutonnière-pattern central slip attenuation after release
subsections.heading: 115. Terri Skirven OTR/L CHT, "Hand therapy for Dupuytren's..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `5fqC-xS8WhM`

- **Upload date:** 2010-10-24
- **Duration:** 16:20
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/5fqC-xS8WhM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** how cryosurgery works mechanically, and why it spares motor function, the procedure itself, freeze-thaw protocol and all, success-rate data compared to traditional plantar fibroma surgery's poor track record, a podiatrist's own admission that he'd never thought to check patients' hands before this conference
- **Anatomy:** plantar fascia (Ledderhose disease), peripheral nerve (myelin sheath, perineurium, epineurium)
- **Management options:** cryosurgery (cryoprobe freezing) for plantar fibromas
- **Important concepts:** the Joule-Thomson effect as the physical basis of the ice ball, Wallerian degeneration with preserved myelin sheath, perineurium, and epineurium, ruling out sarcoma before treating an arch lesion as a simple fibroma
subsections.heading: 116. Terry Spilken DPM, "Cryotherapy for Plantar Fibromas" 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `future-intervention-risk-cohort-2026`
- **URL:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42274446/
- **Author:** El Bachaoui R(1), Cossu E(2), Zhang D(2), Earp BE(2), Blazar PE(3).
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/future-intervention-risk-cohort-2026.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the odds of needing more treatment somewhere else after an initial procedure, how those odds split between the same digit, another digit, and the other hand, which patient factors predict spreading to a new location versus recurring in place
- **Anatomy:** same digit as initially treated, other digits of the same hand, contralateral hand
- **Management options:** collagenase treatment, surgical fasciectomy
- **Important concepts:** future intervention as a single umbrella outcome spanning three different locations, retrospective cohort design at a single institution
subsections.heading: 117. The Likelihood of Future Dupuytren Disease Intervention After Initial Treatment in the Same Digit, Another Digit, and Contralateral Hand.

- **URL:** https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31232804/
- **Author:** Sayadi LR(1), Alhunayan D(1), Sarantopoulos N(1), Kong C(1), Condamoor S(1), Sayadi J(2), Banyard DA(1), Shaterian A(1), Leis A(1), Evans GRD(1), Widgerow AD(1).
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/sayadi-2019-molecular-pathogenesis-review.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a systematic review of the basic-science literature on Dupuytren's, organized into three categories, how many studies were screened versus actually included
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** future biologic treatments aimed at the disease process itself, not yet named specifically
- **Important concepts:** the proliferative, involutional, and residual disease stages, three organizing categories -- molecular alterations, structural alterations, genetic predisposition, PRISMA-guided systematic review methodology applied to basic science literature
subsections.heading: 118. The Molecular Pathogenesis of Dupuytren Disease: Review of the Literature and Suggested New Approaches to Treatment.

- **Upload date:** 2010-09-12
- **Duration:** 09:56
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/doc6HW0c3RE.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a tissue-engineered skin model used to study cell-cell interaction in fibrosis, hypertrophic-scar keratinocytes driving a thicker dermis via a secreted factor, a newly found role for myofibroblasts in promoting capillary network formation, why this matters for pathological tissue formation generally
- **Anatomy:** none recorded
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** self-assembly tissue engineering as an in-vitro model that behaves like in vivo tissue, keratinocyte-to-dermis signaling as a driver of fibrotic thickening, myofibroblasts as active participants in angiogenesis, not just matrix contraction
subsections.heading: 119. Veronique Moulin PhD, "Tissue engineering and the myofibroblasts." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

- **Upload date:** 2010-10-16
- **Duration:** 11:00
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/W_Tbwi613Qw.txt`
- **Main subjects:** a street-survey epidemiological study of Dupuytren's prevalence in Bosnia, the strong, quantified association between diabetes and disease prevalence, an ethnic/religious prevalence difference that may or may not be real, why prevalence and treatment need are very different numbers
- **Anatomy:** right versus left hand asymmetry
- **Management options:** none recorded
- **Important concepts:** prevalence versus need for treatment, a three-stage severity classification (palmar changes only, under 90 degrees, over 90 degrees), DASH score comparison against other hand conditions
subsections.heading: 120. Vilhjalmur Finsen Phd, "The epidemiology of Dupuytren's..." 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

subsections.body:
- **Source ID:** `nLR3nKuAufs`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nLR3nKuAufs
- **Upload date:** 2010-10-23
- **Duration:** 14:08
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/nLR3nKuAufs.txt`
- **Main subjects:** Peyronie's disease prevalence, and how much higher it is than long assumed, the specific overlap rate between Peyronie's and Dupuytren's contracture, the psychological burden of the disease and why patients stay silent, non-surgical treatment options, rated individually by evidence quality
- **Anatomy:** tunica albuginea, penis, dorsal plaque
- **Management options:** interlesional injection therapies (steroids, verapamil, interferon, collagenase), surgical reconstruction as the eventual gold standard for established disease
- **Important concepts:** Peyronie's disease as a heterogeneous, not uniform, wound-healing disorder, the early/active phase versus stable phase distinction, and why surgery waits, modeling (mechanical straightening after injection) as an outcome modifier
subsections.heading: 121. Wayne Hellstrom MD, "Medical Management of Peyronie's Disease" 2010 Miami Dupuytren Symposium

symptoms.raw: **Loss of active finger flexion appearing three days post-procedure**, the presenting sign that led to discovering the flexor tendon laceration `[06:14]`.
**A palpable cord near the web space with 45–50 degrees of contracture**, shown as a specific preoperative/postoperative case example `[04:09]`.
**Contracture recurrence risk stratified by the Abe score** — Degreef states a roughly 38% recurrence risk with zero risk factors present, rising sharply as more risk factors accumulate `[05:16]`.
**Fifth-finger PIP joint contracture specifically flagged as the hardest to treat**, used as the reference joint when multiple digits were affected `[06:16]`.
**Nodule regrowth within weeks of stopping tamoxifen in a treatment-responsive patient**, and shrinkage again on restarting `[13:26]`.

**Placebo-arm side effects (carpal tunnel syndrome, reported impotence, sleeplessness, weight gain)** — presented as a caution about symptom reporting under expectation, not as evidence against tamoxifen's real effects `[11:23]`.
**Patient-rated pain, on a visual-analog scale from "non-existent" to "unbearable,"** one of the eleven attribute items composing the PEM score `[01:00]`.

**Patients ending up subjectively worse than their pretreatment baseline** — quantified separately for operated (~1 in 5) and non-operated (~1 in 3) groups, rather than assumed to be a negligible outcome `[05:09]`.
**A new palm nodule, and the specific odds of it regressing, progressing, or staying stable over 10 years** `[18:30]`.
**Contracture recurrence after any corrective procedure, framed as a prevention problem rather than a treatment-failure problem** `[07:12]`.
**PIP contracture in the 20–40 degree range as the window where a corrective procedure is worth the risk** `[17:29]`.
**Knuckle pads and concurrent Ledderhose disease as diathesis markers predicting faster recurrence** `[16:28]`.
**Post-procedure loss of circulation in the finger, named directly as a question to ask a prospective surgeon about in advance** `[03:06]`.
**Contracture recurrence timing concentrated in years 2–3**, with a specific, quantified drop-off pattern afterward `[05:10]`.
**Swelling as a formally counted adverse event** under FDA reporting criteria, distinct from more clinically significant complications `[06:11]`.
**A possible measurement artifact (decreased circumference) mistaken for a genuine physical change** — flagged as worth reconsidering rather than accepted at face value `[06:11]`.

**Skin laceration as the characteristic PNF complication, versus ecchymosis and hematoma for CCH** — the two treatments' complication profiles explicitly distinguished by type, not just rate `[04:09]`.
**A flexor tendon rupture following CCH**, cited as a factor that shifted the clinic's later treatment mix toward more PNF `[05:12]`.
**Skin tears during manipulation**, quantified at 14% (his practice) to 22% (multi-center data) `[05:07]`.
**An active extension lag at the PIP joint after release**, flagged as a likely sign of central slip stretching requiring dynamic splinting `[09:12]`.
**A hidden/retracted cord preventing full PIP release** despite apparently complete treatment of the visible cords `[08:12]`.
**An unexplained axillary lump after collagenase**, cited as a real but easily-alarming side effect if not pre-disclosed `[02:04]`.
**A positive Hueston tabletop test as her operational definition of recurrence** `[04:14]`.
**Patient-perceived recurrence versus surgeon-perceived success** — explicitly framed as potentially divergent, with patient perception treated as the outcome that actually matters `[04:14]`.
**A hand feeling stiffer throughout the day, not just briefly after splint removal**, cited as Wach's own reason for eventually discontinuing his splint despite it maintaining correction `[01:01]`.
**Recurrence returning a joint to roughly its pre-treatment state within months of stopping a splint**, reported across multiple individual patient cases `[01:01]`, `[02:02]`.
**PIP joint fixed in flexion, resistant to passive straightening** `[00:00]`.
**MP joint hyperextension developing secondary to a long-standing PIP contracture**, and progression toward a claw-hand posture `[07:11]`.
**Skin blistering, ulceration, or pain under splint/cast pressure**, particularly in a neuropathic hand where pain wouldn't otherwise signal the injury `[11:14]`.
**Loss of active extension after a technically successful release**, attributed to the lateral band failing to migrate back dorsal to the joint axis `[06:09]`.
**Simultaneous bilateral hand and foot disease presentation**, contrasted directly with a single isolated palm lump as an example of the disease's poorly understood clinical variability `[01:04]`.
**Rapid appearance of multiple new nodules across both hands shortly after a technically successful fasciectomy** — described as Wach's own post-surgical experience `[02:11]`.
**A new fibrotic nodule triggered by localized mechanical irritation from a night splint**, absent any actual wound `[04:16]`.
**Male:female presentation age gap**, with the apparent sex ratio narrowing sharply by advanced age `[05:17]`.
**Pain from plantar fibromas significant enough to affect walking and daily activity**, framed as the primary treatment target `[02:06]`.
**Temporary sensory numbness from arch to second toe after cryosurgery**, typically resolving within weeks to a few months `[06:14]`.
**Nodule softening and size reduction after cryosurgery**, presented as a secondary sign alongside the primary pain-relief outcome `[14:26]`.
**The need to actively examine feet in Dupuytren's patients and hands in Ledderhose patients**, given clinicians in either specialty commonly don't check the other `[09:18]`.

**Skin splitting during collagenase manipulation, typically healing within ten days**, contrasted directly with a comparably timed but categorically different surgical wound-healing complication `[05:05]`.
**Anaphylactic shock as a rare but serious collagenase complication**, referenced as an example of a severity tier that resists direct comparison to more common, milder complications `[04:03]`.
**Loss of passive MCP joint hyperextension**, named directly by one surgeon as their personal trigger point for starting treatment `[01:08]`.
**Difficulty putting on gloves**, cited by more than one surgeon as the practical, functional threshold that would prompt them to seek treatment `[00:06]`, `[04:10]`.
**Cord palpable well enough to bowstring on finger extension, used as the injection landmark** `[19:22]`.
**Skin tearing during the manipulation/extension step, minimized by gentle technique** `[29:35]`.
**Recurrence after any treatment modality — surgery, needle aponeurotomy, or collagenase** `[29:35]`.
**Residual PIP contracture from joint stiffness even after successful cord rupture** `[25:28]`.

**Hand interference correlating with early age of onset, family history, concurrent Ledderhose disease, pain, and itching** — proposed markers of a more aggressive, systemic disease subset `[06:08]`–`[09:13]`.
**Pain in Dupuytren's disease, reported by 20–35% of patients presenting for treatment** `[08:11]`.
**Itching in nodular Dupuytren's disease** — linked to immune-cell activity alongside myofibroblasts `[08:11]`.
**Disability specifically from finger flexion contracture**, the narrow domain URAM's nine questions are built around `[00:00]`.
**Pain, general function, and overall hand dysfunction** — explicitly named as dimensions URAM does *not* capture, a gap Dias treats as its central limitation `[04:03]`.

**Fingers feeling "not one's own" — strange, stiff, numb, or tender — after multiple minimally invasive procedures, described as a real and worsening outcome, not merely subjective dissatisfaction** `[00:01]`.
**Loss of finger circulation during a redo procedure, severe enough to require amputation** `[00:01]`.
**Peau d'orange-like dermal ridging over long-standing palm nodules**, compared explicitly to the skin changes of inflammatory breast cancer `[08:10]`.
**Unconscious CMC joint flexion masking the true severity of a more distal contracture** `[05:08]`.
**Nodules and cords in the palm, described as the defining clinical and pathologic findings of the disease** `[00:04]`.
**Plantar nodules/cords (Ledderhose disease) as an ectopic presentation** `[00:04]`.
**Penile curvature (Peyronie's disease) as an ectopic presentation**, described as a related but distinct condition with its own, non-surgical treatment approach `[01:05]`, `[06:15]`.
**Palmar bruising following distal radius fracture, associated with later Dupuytren's-like changes** `[05:13]`.
**Finger stiffness and cold sensitivity**, the specific complaints among the minority of patients not rating their outcome good or excellent `[05:08]`.
**Joint contracture and extrinsic tendon imbalance from surgical complication**, explicitly distinguished from true disease recurrence `[03:05]`.
**Contracture increase after fasciectomy, quantified with explicit trigger thresholds (15° PIP / 20° MCP) for adding a rescue splint** `[02:06]`.
**Patient satisfaction and DASH-measured disability**, tracked as primary/secondary outcomes independent of raw range-of-motion numbers `[03:07]`.
**PIP joint stiffness after surgery, explicitly distinguished from true contracture recurrence** — shown in a case with a good functional result that some might misread as recurrence `[02:05]`.
**Extensor mechanism slackening in long-standing severe contracture**, assessable intraoperatively and easily missed if attention stays only on the flexor-side cords `[09:18]`.
**Vascular compromise risk specific to the second and fifth fingers during dissection near the vascular pedicle** `[08:17]`.

**Persistent patient dissatisfaction in high-function patients (e.g., competitive golfers) even after a technically successful release**, described as an unresolved problem in her own long-term follow-up `[10:20]`.
**Frozen shoulder and knuckle pads**, named as commonly co-occurring conditions among Dupuytren's survey respondents `[04:05]`.
**Onset shifting several years earlier among smokers**, specifically after a roughly ten-year smoking history threshold `[06:10]`.
**Nodule consistency**, the primary outcome most consistently tracked (albeit subjectively) across the steroid and radiotherapy studies reviewed `[03:04]`.
**Grip strength**, specifically noted as improved following ultrasound and stretching in the physical therapy literature, despite small sample sizes `[04:05]`.
**Recurrence of contracture once a pre-operative elongation device is removed** — described as consistent across studies, even when the device produced real interim straightening `[00:03]`.
**Active extension lag despite full passive extension**, specifically in boutonnière-pattern presentations after release, from central slip attenuation `[11:17]`.
**Post-operative flare, hypertrophic scarring, and prolonged inflammation**, linked to mechanical tension on healing tissue and to overly aggressive exercise `[06:11]`, `[12:18]`.
**New-onset carpal tunnel syndrome or trigger finger symptoms provoked by over-repetitive gripping exercises during recovery** `[16:21]`.
**Patient expectation mismatch about return to activity** — Skirven notes patients commonly assume they can resume activities like golf within days of surgery `[16:21]`.
**MP versus PIP joint contracture responding very differently to the same drug and dose**, with PIP joints — especially more severe ones — responding meaningfully less well `[08:19]`.
**Tendon rupture and complex regional pain syndrome**, named as the specific serious complications observed in the trial, rare but real `[11:22]`.
**Immediate, audible cord rupture on manipulation the day after injection**, described as the clinical event defining treatment success `[05:15]`.

**Progressive joint contracture as an active, ongoing cellular process rather than a fixed scar** — reframes why contracture can continue to worsen rather than stabilizing once tissue matures `[04:06]`.
**Rebound contracture appearing within 12 weeks of segmental fasciectomy**, quantified and directly compared between implant and non-implant groups `[07:15]`.

**Dimpled skin overlying a contracture**, described as a sign surgeons associate with a more stubborn, skin-involved case — connected here to direct histological evidence of myofibroblasts retracting the skin itself `[03:08]`.
**Post-operative tissue softness**, described as a real but currently unmeasurable clinical observation `[07:15]`.
**Glans numbness from dorsal nerve injury**, specifically flagged as an underappreciated consequence of the original Nesbit technique `[01:02]`.
**Ventral penile curvature**, quantified as affecting roughly half of Peyronie's patients over time `[05:11]`.
**Painful sharp edges from an ossified "towbar" plaque**, given as the specific indication for plaque removal in that presentation `[04:06]`.

**Feeling hampered in hand use, or feeling depressed, specifically due to hand appearance** — the exact MHQ subscore items found to predict overall satisfaction, linking cosmetic perception to functional and emotional impact `[04:03]`.
**Residual contracture and postoperative complications**, confirmed as outcome-level factors influencing satisfaction alongside the identified preoperative predictor `[02:02]`.
**Bruising extending well beyond the injection site — up the arm, into the armpit, or the chest** — noted as an unexpectedly wide-reaching side effect `[05:05]`.
**Declining patient satisfaction and declining willingness to repeat treatment over a four-year period**, tracked as recurrence set in `[04:04]`.
**Tissue described as "gummy and gooey" during surgery performed after a prior failed collagenase treatment** `[07:09]`.

**Flexor tendon bowstringing at the MP level after combined fasciotomy and trigger-finger release**, described as a severe, sometimes unfixable complication of over-aggressive sheath release `[07:12]`.
**Finger rotation at the MP joint not explained by visible palmar cords**, flagged as the specific sign of a missed sagittal band rupture rather than pure Dupuytren's contracture `[08:12]`.
**Rapid recurrence after a prior procedure**, used as a specific signal to escalate rather than repeat the same treatment approach `[08:12]`.
**A palm lump prompting cancer-related fear**, distinct from a functionally motivated presentation, and resolving once reassurance is given `[04:11]`.
**A finger catching on pockets or during handshakes**, cited repeatedly as a specific, concrete functional trigger for seeking treatment `[04:11]`.
**Pain as a signal of a separate, coexisting condition (commonly base-of-thumb arthritis)** rather than Dupuytren's itself, since the disease is typically painless on its own `[06:12]`.
**Full straightening producing a loss of full flexion**, an under-anticipated trade-off patients need to understand before choosing aggressive correction `[03:08]`.
**A four-fold right-versus-left hand asymmetry in men, with no such asymmetry in women** `[04:01]`.
**Diabetes strongly co-occurring with Dupuytren's**, with prevalence reaching 60–70% in a proven-diabetic clinic population `[07:03]`.

**Low measured disability (DASH ~10–12) among patients actually on a surgical waiting list**, well below several other common hand conditions, contextualizing how mild most treated disease actually is `[09:04]`.
**Bent fingers and tight palms interfering with keyboard use, fine dexterity, and daily activity** — described as a burden that's "often hard to describe" `[01:01]`.
**Social anxiety about appearance, and anxiety about an unpredictable disease future**, named explicitly as part of the disease's personal impact `[01:01]`.

**Recurrence as the most common reason patients choose finger amputation**, and as the point where patient goals shift ("from 'I want my finger straight again' to... 'I want this finger gone'") `[02:02]`.
**Children of affected parents sometimes presenting with more severe disease than the parent had** — cited as evidence of the disease's unpredictable course `[02:02]`.
**Recurrence and progressive worsening after surgery, in a minority of patients not captured by standard outcome reporting** `[05:10]`.
**Regret and reluctance to pursue further surgery after a bad surgical outcome** `[05:10]`.
**Contracture severe enough, after repeated operations, that a surgeon tells the patient nothing more can be done** `[06:12]`.
**Post-operative wound pain**, reported as reduced with bioengineered skin coverage compared to standard open-wound or donor-site care `[08:19]`.
**Delayed wound closure time (average 40 vs. 27 days)** as an observed tradeoff against the pain benefit `[07:17]`.
**Recurrence versus disease progression at long-term follow-up**, acknowledged as sometimes genuinely hard to distinguish on exam `[08:19]`.
**Restricted active and passive shoulder range of motion**, quantified separately across three specific motion planes (forward flexion, abduction, internal rotation) `[08:06]`, `[09:06]`.
**Shoulder pain and functional limitation**, tracked via a validated orthopedic questionnaire alongside range-of-motion measures, not just range of motion in isolation `[09:06]`.
**Cords visibly shrinking and receding when the finger is mechanically straightened**, offered as observational support for the reactive-tissue hypothesis `[05:08]`.
**Firm lumps or nodules in the palm, stuck to the skin** `[p.1]`.
**Thickened, puckered palm skin** ("speed bump" / "pothole" pattern) `[p.1]`.
**A cord running from the palm into a finger, pulling it toward the palm** `[p.1]`.
**Inability to lay the hand flat on a table, or open it fully** `[p.2]`.
**Difficulty washing hands, wearing gloves, holding large objects, using pockets, or shaking hands** `[p.2]`.
**Lumps on the soles of the feet, or thickening on the knuckles, alongside hand symptoms** `[p.2]`.
**A PIP joint that fails to fully extend despite apparently complete fasciectomy**, worked through via the staged algorithm rather than treated as a single undifferentiated problem `[05:10]`.
**A "snapping" finger** — instability flicking between flexion and extension rather than holding mid-range position — as the specific sign of a tight accessory collateral ligament `[06:13]`.
**A digit that passively straightens but persistently "lies in flexion"** — the specific sign of central slip attenuation, distinguished from other causes of incomplete correction `[07:14]`.
**DIP joint hyperextension with tight conjoined lateral bands**, limiting full DIP flexion `[09:18]`.

**Skin laceration during finger manipulation**, specifically identified as elevated (22%) relative to single-dose historical safety data — the one clear safety trade-off of the concurrent approach `[06:18]`.
**Patient-perceived hand functionality**, tracked separately from the strict clinical-success contracture threshold, per FDA-required patient-reported outcome surveying `[04:12]`.
**Increase in contracture angle over time**, defined as the trial's specific progression measure, tracked separately in treated versus untreated fingers `[¶5]`.
**Retreatment need**, tracked as a downstream consequence of progression `[¶6]`.
**Dermal thickening driven by a keratinocyte-secreted factor**, demonstrated to be reproducible by adding that single factor (TIMP1) alone `[05:14]`.
**Capillary/angiogenic network formation** as a previously unrecognized function of myofibroblasts, quantified via an angiogenic index `[08:17]`.
**Recontracture following surgery, in roughly 10–17% of patients across trials**, explicitly named as an unresolved problem regardless of the splinting conclusion `[05:06]`.
**Reflex sympathetic dystrophy after surgery**, reported in 11 of 123 followed patients, fully resolving with conservative management (analgesics, ~3 months physical therapy) `[08:22]`.
**Compromised digital blood supply after recurrence surgery**, in some cases severe enough to require amputation `[08:22]`.

**Psychological distress from viewing an open, healing surgical wound** in the weeks after Jacobsen flap surgery, named explicitly as a real disadvantage of the technique, not just a physical one `[09:22]`.
**Skin necrosis at incision flap tips**, graded systematically (0–3) rather than described impressionistically, at three specific follow-up points `[08:16]`.
**Delayed wound healing requiring prolonged, repeated dressing changes**, named as a specific source of patient burden with standard flap techniques `[02:10]`.
**Small hematomas as the only complications observed**, all self-resolving `[11:17]`.
**Pain specifically at the moment of collagenase injection**, quantified and distinguished from manipulation-related pain and from pain experienced at home in the days between visits `[04:03]`.
**Residual finger contracture at the MP and PIP joints after percutaneous or open treatment**, with specific improvement figures reported `[10:12]`.
**Palpable hard nodules softening ("melting") after mechanical disruption**, described as visible during the procedure itself `[12:14]`.
**Post-procedure erythema (redness) as an early warning sign of fat graft failure**, in his one flagged complication case `[13:16]`.
**Recurrence after fat grafting**, in at least one documented case, attributed by Khouri to insufficient graft volume in that area rather than a technique failure generally `[13:16]`.
**Recurrence of contracture in the originally treated digit** `[¶6]`.
**New Dupuytren's intervention needed in a digit that was not initially treated**, whether in the same hand or the opposite one `[¶6]`.
**Pre-existing, untreated contracture in a digit other than the one initially addressed**, named repeatedly as a risk factor for further treatment regardless of location `[¶6]`.
**Nerve injury as a recognized surgical complication**, with a specific cited rate range (1.4–7.8%) from the existing literature `[00:03]`.
**Risk of mistaking a chevron-pair branch for the proper digital nerve itself**, specifically flagged as more likely once the anatomy is distorted by a spiral cord `[03:07]`.
**Pressure, tension, and pain while walking or at rest, plus itching sensation and walking difficulty**, the primary patient-reported complaints in plantar fibroma disease `[06:12]`.
**Deep, harder-to-palpate nodules compared to Dupuytren's**, requiring imaging support (MRI/ultrasound) in unclear cases `[07:13]`.
**Foot arch shape distortion from nodule bulk**, described as improving as nodules shrink under treatment `[12:21]`.
**Worse acute skin reaction in previously operated (recurrent) sites** than in untreated primary disease `[10:16]`.
**Firm nodules fixed to the skin or deep fascia, with skin thickening or pitting in the palm** `[p.1]`.
**Fibrous, tendon-like cords, and flexion deformity at the MCPJ and IPJ** `[p.1]`.
**Reduced span between thumb and index finger webspace; inability to lay the palm flat on a table** `[p.1]`.
**Ectopic nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles of the feet, or penile tissue** `[p.1]`.
**Persistent painful nodules**, distinguished in the pathway from nodules that are simply present but not painful `[p.1]`.
**Dupuytren's occurring in a patient with no other affected family members**, used here as the prompt for questioning a purely hereditary explanation in that specific case `[09:20]`.
**Prominent fat pads between fingers mistaken by patients for new nodules or fluid collections**, actually normal anatomy made more visible by adjacent tissue retraction `[04:09]`.
**Residual contracting force in a finger with no palpable cord**, potentially explained by a retrovascular cord lying too deep to feel `[09:15]`.
**A finger that straightens during surgery but drifts back over the following months**, distinguished explicitly from a finger that never fully straightens in the first place `[12:17]`.
**Progressive bending of the ring and little fingers into the palm, historically documented as early as the 17th century** `[02:05]`–`[03:07]` (Felix Platter of Basel, 1614).

**PIP joint contracture specifically flagged by Cooper as a marker of poor surgical candidacy** — "when the joint is contracted, nothing should be attempted... no operation... will succeed" `[06:11]`, an early clinical observation resonant with later, quantified treatment-window findings elsewhere in this library.
**The specific contracture thresholds (composite >90°, MCP >50°, PIP >40°) marking a sharp drop in correction likelihood** `[06:05]`.

**A young female patient with no family history developing apparent early Dupuytren's after hand trauma or in the context of diabetes** — flagged as possibly pseudo-Dupuytren rather than the genuine disease `[05:05]`.
**PIP contracture over 60 degrees as a marker of likely extensor mechanism incompetence**, predicting early loss of correction specifically `[07:06]`.
**Recurrence beneath a graft versus extension of disease at the graft's margin**, explicitly distinguished as two different failure modes requiring different technical fixes `[01:05]`.
**Graft loss from premature dressing removal**, tied to a specific healing-time mechanism (capillary ingrowth maturity) rather than treated as a generic complication `[04:11]`.
**Decreased sensibility in grafted skin**, noted as a real but not clinically bothersome finding for patients `[12:27]`.
**A bent finger understood as fixed/retained tissue rather than actively shortening tissue** — Meinel's central reframing of the disease's basic mechanical presentation `[09:36]`.
**A spiral cord displacing the neurovascular bundle near the web space**, shown as a case example and attributed to a hypertrophic, fixed Cleland's ligament `[08:34]`.
**Knuckle pads and plantar (Ledderhose) involvement**, quantified at 6% and 5% respectively in this cohort `[04:11]`.

**No elevated diabetes-style association with rheumatoid arthritis, smoking, or alcohol use** — presented as reassuring negative findings against commonly assumed risk factors, checked against real national baseline rates rather than assumed `[04:11]`–`[05:11]`.
**Penile angulation, painful erections, and erectile dysfunction**, with specific co-occurrence rates given `[02:05]`.
**Loss of penile length**, named specifically as an under-recognized driver of patient distress `[05:09]`.
**Dorsal plaque formation**, the most common presentation pattern `[06:10]`.
**Concurrent Dupuytren's contracture, in up to 20% of Peyronie's patients** `[01:03]`.
**Full fist achieved within fifteen minutes of PALF**, shown on film as the marker of early functional recovery `[02:04]`.
**Transient versus non-transient complex regional pain syndrome**, distinguished explicitly by which arm of the trial the patient was in `[06:11]`.
**Median days to resume activities of daily living**, quantified and compared directly between treatments `[06:11]`.
**Difficulty extending the fingers, from a fibrous cord in the palm or finger** `[¶2]`.
**Recurrence of contracture after treatment** — described as expected in roughly half of patients within 3 to 5 years, not a sign the procedure failed outright `[¶2]`.
**Regression, stabilisation, or progression of existing nodules and cords, tracked as the three primary outcome categories across every cohort in this guidance** `[¶6]`, `[¶10]`.
**New nodules, new cords, or increased flexion deformity as markers of on-treatment progression** — 6%, 4%, and 6% of hands respectively in the RCT `[¶6]`.
**Post-treatment skin symptoms**: tenderness, dryness, thickening, reduced sweating, altered sensation, or weakness at the treated site `[¶24]`–`[¶49]`.
**Recurrence of contracture after initial successful treatment**, defined explicitly per study rather than left to inconsistent wording `[¶5]`.
**Need for a repeat procedure (reintervention)** as a distinct, trackable consequence of recurrence `[¶6]`.
**Digital nerve injury, tendon injury, skin tears, swelling, pain, and bleeding** as the complications reported across the pooled studies `[¶6]`.
**Recurrence quantified as a specific 30-degree TPD threshold from the 6-week post-operative baseline**, not a vaguer clinical impression `[04:08]`.
**Faster recurrence after PNF (mean 2.1 years) versus LF (mean 3.8 years)**, a concrete timing difference patients can be counseled on directly `[06:10]`.
**Near-universal recurrence in younger patients regardless of technique chosen**, versus much lower recurrence risk in patients over 75 `[07:10]`.
**Itching, tension sensation, pressure sensation, and pain in plantar (Ledderhose) nodules**, with specific symptomatic relief rates from radiotherapy `[14:23]`.
**Difficulty walking normally due to plantar pain**, reported as reversible with treatment in a majority of cases `[14:23]`.
**Progressive nodule and cord formation as the proliferative signal indicating radiotherapy candidacy**, distinguished sharply from established, already-scarred contracture `[02:08]`.
**Dry skin as the primary chronic side effect of radiotherapy**, consistent across both hand and foot treatment `[10:18]`, `[13:22]`.
**Digital artery spasm and possible ischemia from acute neurovascular bundle stretching**, the specific vascular risk motivating a gradual-distraction approach `[01:00]`.
**A secondary boutonnière deformity developing mid-treatment**, shown as an evolving complication requiring its own management rather than a fixed starting condition `[03:02]`.
**MP joint hyperextension**, identified as a device-specific complication that led to a protocol change (adding a flexion strap) `[05:04]`.
**New Dupuytren's tissue with contracture worse than the immediate postoperative result**, the specific operational definition used for recurrence in this study `[03:06]`.
**Minor wound complications resolving with local wound care alone**, reported identically in both study arms, indicating no added surgical risk from the graft material `[04:07]`.
**Splint-related pain**, specifically flagged as the tension splint's disadvantage and the reason two patients dropped out of that arm `[03:05]`.
**Difficulty achieving full, consistent skin contact**, flagged as the compression splint's specific limitation `[05:08]`.

**Flap-related sensibility deficit and cold sensitivity**, tracked from early postoperative period through gradual improvement at two years, and explicitly described as an expected part of recovery rather than a complication `[06:13]`.
**Vascular compromise during intraoperative extension in Tubiana stage IV disease**, requiring surgeons to deliberately accept less correction to preserve blood supply `[07:15]`.

**Nodule/cord area and total passive extension deficit fluctuating over a two-year period in some patients** — confirmed to exceed measurement error, describing genuine, non-monotonic disease-course variation `[04:09]`.
**Recurrence of contracture after surgery or injection treatment**, described by multiple commenters as the dominant experience rather than the exception `[¶4]`.
**A finger that no longer straightens due to scar tissue from treatment**, distinguished by one commenter from a genuinely returned contracture `[¶4]`.
**Residual contracture angle after treatment**, tracked separately from whether the contracture later returns `[¶4]`.
**Recurrence of contracture** as its own outcome, distinct from initial correction `[¶4]`.
**Pain, hand function, and global satisfaction** named as outcomes the review tracked, though the specific figures for these were not given in the excerpt available here `[¶4]`.
**Frozen shoulder and knuckle pads**, reported as commonly co-occurring conditions among Ledderhose survey respondents, paralleling the same associations found for Dupuytren's disease `[01:01]`.
**Tenosynovitis requiring intervention and nerve injury**, the specific serious adverse events found exclusively in the surgical group `[04:06]`.

**Work performance and activities-of-daily-living satisfaction**, patient-reported domains found significantly more favorable after collagenase despite similar or lesser objective contracture correction `[03:04]`.

**Visual resemblance between a thumb Dupuytren's contracture and a burn scar contracture**, raised as an open question about shared scarring predisposition rather than an established finding `[06:14]`.

**Depth-dependent tissue response to injury** (superficial versus deep fibroblasts behaving differently), a general wound-healing principle with a plausible but unconfirmed parallel to Dupuytren's `[10:19]`.
**Minor skin lesions from the hyperextension "cracking" maneuver**, specifically occurring where the cord remained adherent to the skin `[05:11]`.
**A pricking sensation reported by the patient during the anesthesia-free cutting step**, used directly as an intraoperative nerve-safety signal `[04:10]`.
**A roughly 2.5-year average delay between a patient's first noticing a sign of Dupuytren's and seeking care**, meaning true disease onset is typically well before diagnosis `[02:12]`.

**Early subjective symptoms** referenced from a 1956 published account (not further detailed in this transcript): stiffness/swelling sensation, localized discomfort at the base of the ring finger, and a sense that something had changed in the palm — offered as illustrative of what pre-nodular disease can feel like to a patient.
**Fingertip numbness, needle-provoked paresthesia, or active flexion catching the needle** — the three specific real-time signals Eaton names as his intraoperative "do no harm" check `[02:06]`.
**Skin bunching, curved skin creases, and absence of blanching** — visual/tactile signs used to identify where fascial tension is greatest and portal placement will be most effective `[04:06]`.
**Loss of functional grip (e.g., inability to hold a golf club) despite a straighter finger** — used to argue that angular correction alone is an incomplete outcome measure `[01:03]`.
**Recurrent contracture presenting as "almost the same cord" reappearing after collagenase**, illustrated directly with a before/after/recurrence case sequence `[06:11]`.
**Bruising, swelling, and hematoma as expected but manageable side effects of injection**, shown in one case as more pronounced than typical `[08:17]`.

**Combined multi-joint (MP/PIP/DIP) contracture presenting together**, framed as the norm rather than the exception in real patients: **"patients don't present often with isolated PIP joints... you have to treat what comes"** `[04:08]`.
**Contracture occurring only in the palm, not the finger dorsum or sole, despite nodules appearing in all three sites** `[00:00]`–`[01:02]`.
**Slow, gradual progression from nodule to bent finger, typically over years rather than the roughly one-year timeline active contraction would predict** `[01:02]`.

**Fingertips digging fully into the palm — flagged as a sign of an additional process** (undiagnosed spasticity, prior scarring, or boutonnière-related cortical reorganization) **rather than Dupuytren's contracture alone** `[02:02]`.
**Increasing nodule count, cord count, itching, and sensitivity changes as tracked progression signals** that inform the decision to treat `[08:09]`.
**Loss of fine hand function in high-stakes users (musicians, performers)** cited as a reason to intervene earlier rather than wait for surgical-threshold contracture `[08:09]`.
**Dry skin as the most common persistent side effect of radiotherapy, at about 15%**, manageable with topical creams `[13:17]`.

**Whitish skin areas, altered skin folding, and V- or U-shaped nodule patterns** described as visible clinical signs a patient photograph alone can reveal, sufficient to suggest radiotherapy candidacy `[11:14]`.
**Pain, disputed as present or absent** — several commenters directly contradicted the framing that Dupuytren's is typically painless `[¶4]`.
**Recurrence after surgery, and reduced or absent response to a repeat collagenase injection** `[¶2]`, `[¶3]`.
**Reduced range of motion and nodule size**, reported by one commenter as improving with regular manual stretching — a single, unverified account `[¶6]`.
