heritability versus genetic variation explained
the Wnt signaling pathway as a candidate mechanism

sections.body:
**Dupuytren's is genuinely one of genetics' rare success stories for a complex trait — a small sample
identified an unusually large number of disease loci — but the variants found so far explain only a small
fraction of the disease's overall heritability, and the rest remains genuinely unaccounted for.** Ophoff
states this gap directly: **"if I look at all the SNP variants... it explains roughly 14% of the
heritability... but we know [total] heritability is roughly 80%"** `[12:14]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[06:09]`–`[07:09]` — A **Danish twin study**, population-based (which Ophoff flags as important
specifically because it avoids selection bias), found **heritability of roughly 80%**, with a **population
incidence of 0.6%.** A separate study found disease severity correlating with family history. Together with
a 2005 Swedish family linkage study (a single locus with sufficient evidence in one large pedigree, though
the causal mutation itself was never identified), Ophoff treats these as firmly establishing that genetic
factors are involved — **"Dupuytren's in general can be considered a heritable trait — there's no doubt
[about that]"** `[16:18]`.
sections.heading: How heritable Dupuytren's actually is

sections.body:
`[07:09]` — The genome-wide association study Ophoff references identified **nine distinct genomic loci**
from **fewer than 1,000 cases** — a sample size he calls **"unheard of for any other complex trait,"**
contrasting it directly with schizophrenia, where a comparable finding would have required roughly **20,000
cases.** He attributes this efficiency to Dupuytren's genetics being unusually tractable relative to most
complex diseases, not to any special feature of the study design.
sections.heading: Why the GWAS result is a genuine outlier

sections.body:
`[08:10]`–`[12:14]` — Ophoff frames genetic variants along two axes: **allele frequency** (common versus
rare) and **effect size** (small versus large). Using a 2012 study sequencing ~200 drug-related genes across
14,000 people as an illustration, he notes **common variants are visibly few relative to the much larger
number of rare, often family-unique variants — "an iceberg [where] only the top... we can see... are common
ones, and the rare ones are underwater."** Most genetic studies, including the Dupuytren's GWAS, have only
been able to detect **common variants of modest effect**, because rare-variant, large-effect cases require
multi-generation pedigrees that are hard to find and hard to prove causal — what he calls **"the unlucky
corner"** for a researcher. The quantified gap: the **statistically significant GWAS loci alone explain only
about 1% of heritability**; **all common SNP variation together explains roughly 14–16%**; against an
**overall heritability of ~80%**, this leaves the large majority of Dupuytren's heritability **unexplained
by anything found so far** — implying rare variants likely carry real, currently invisible weight.
sections.heading: The common-versus-rare-variant framework, and the missing heritability

sections.body:
`[13:16]`–`[16:18]` — Ophoff's own group's rare-variant search, using **six Dutch pedigrees, 32 affected
individuals**: a **linkage study found no evidence of a major shared locus across or within any of the
families** — "no major gene explaining Dupuytren's" in this dataset, despite disease clustering within
families. A follow-up **exome sequencing** approach (sequencing all coding regions in 2–3 affected
individuals per family, searching specifically for previously unreported, predicted-deleterious variants)
found **four candidate rare variants across two families** — one family alone contained three different
variants, in different genome locations, all co-segregating with disease in that pedigree (making it
impossible to distinguish which, if any, is truly causal). **One of the four overlapped with a gene already
implicated by the GWAS** — flagged as worth pursuing further, not yet confirmed.
sections.heading: The Dutch pedigree study: linkage finds nothing, sequencing finds a little

sections.body: None directly — this is a genetics-methodology talk, not a discussion of clinical presentation.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)** — a common single-base genetic variant, explained here as
  occurring roughly once per 1,000 nucleotides but numbering in the millions across a genome `[08:10]`.
- **Missing heritability** — Ophoff's own framing (not necessarily his coined term, but his explicit focus)
  for the large gap between total estimated heritability (~80%) and the much smaller share (~14–16%)
  explained by identified common variants `[12:14]`.
- **Exome sequencing** — sequencing all protein-coding regions of the genome at once, used here to search
  for rare causal variants within affected families `[14:16]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **The iceberg** — common genetic variants as the small visible tip, with a much larger population of rare,
  family-unique variants hidden "underwater" `[09:10]`.
- **"The unlucky corner"** — a researcher's position when studying a rare variant of small effect: hard to
  find, and hard to prove causal even once found `[11:13]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Unusually rigorous and self-limiting throughout — Ophoff repeatedly quantifies exactly how much of
heritability current findings explain (1% from significant loci, ~14–16% from all common variants) rather
than letting the GWAS "success story" imply more than it shows. The rare-variant pedigree findings are
explicitly labeled as **not yet distinguishable from one another causally** ("we cannot distinguish one from
another") and the shared-gene overlap with the GWAS is called something "we need to pursue further," not a
confirmed link. He also flags a general risk in pedigree-based rare-variant research from his own
schizophrenia genetics experience: families initially thought to fit a clean Mendelian inheritance pattern
"may not be Mendelian after all."
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**The "9-locus GWAS" referenced here is very likely the same study shown mid-analysis in `-3a_yiOu_3I`**
(Dolmans's 2010 talk) — that note shows the first two loci (chromosome 7 and 22) emerging from the same
Dutch multicenter cohort this talk cites five years later as an established finding. **Directly updates and
refines `g40N2M2C6qM`** (Bayat's 2010 genetics talk) — both cover Dupuytren's
genetics broadly, but this 2015 talk gives cleaner, more current figures (80% heritability from a
population-based Danish twin study, a specific 9-locus GWAS, and a quantified 14–16% common-variant
explained-heritability figure) than the more transcript-degraded 2010 talk was able to convey. Both agree
genetic association findings so far have not converged on a single confirmed causal pathway, though this
talk specifically flags the **Wnt signaling pathway** as one promising GWAS-implicated candidate worth
further study — a lead not clearly recoverable from the 2010 talk's degraded transcript. **Consistent with
`AbY1KVhTVAo`** (Eaton's IDDB talk) — Eaton's proposed genetic/systemic versus exposure/benign disease
subsets remain, per this talk, still unconfirmed at the single-gene level, consistent with Eaton's own
framing of that split as hypothesis rather than established fact.

management: needle aponeurotomy (a slicing, radial-to-ulnar technique variant)

sections.body:
**Gan had publicly and repeatedly stated he would never perform needle aponeurotomy, calling it unsafe — then
adopted the technique after his mentor Bob McFarlane, a lifelong opponent of the procedure, died in 2006, and
found in his own prospective series that MCP contracture improved from a mean 46 degrees to 14 degrees,
maintained at six weeks, with results consistent with prior published literature.** His closing, self-directed
lesson: **"my real lesson for this test was actually that never is not very long, and I think that applies to
Dupuytren's contracture"** `[08:15]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:05]`–`[03:08]` — Gan trained under **Bob McFarlane**, founder of London, Ontario's Hand and Upper Limb
Centre and, separately from his medical career, a celebrated Canadian university football athlete (four Yates
Cup championships, the 1951 Lou Marsh Trophy for Canada's top athlete — a trophy later won by figures
including Bobby Orr and Wayne Gretzky). McFarlane was **adamantly opposed to needle aponeurotomy**, published
against it before the technique's more recent popularization (by Lermusiaux) in the early 1990s, and argued
instead for fasciectomy and radical fasciectomy, becoming well known for detailed anatomical descriptions of
the disease. Gan states plainly: **"one of the other legacies of Dr. McFarlane was that he was adamantly
against needle aponeurotomy... he died in 2006, and shortly after that I started doing this needle
aponeurotomy — the master was gone, I was allowed to do it"** `[02:06]`.

A 2002 newspaper article is shown directly on screen: a patient publicly complained he'd had to travel to
Europe for a needle aponeurotomy procedure unavailable in Canada, and had raised the issue with federal
health officials. Gan is quoted twice in that article stating **"I would never do that procedure because I
think it's an unsafe procedure"** — a position he shows himself now having fully reversed `[07:14]`.
sections.heading: The reversal

sections.body:
`[03:08]`–`[04:09]` — Gan's variant: minimal local anesthesia (roughly 0.3–0.5cc, just enough to anesthetize
the skin), then the needle is moved **radial to ulnar to slice the cord rather than repeatedly puncture it**.
He describes it as a safe procedure in the palm given good direct contact with a palpable cord, typically
requiring two to four needle-stick sites, taking roughly three minutes per procedure.
sections.heading: Technique

sections.body:
`[04:09]`–`[06:14]` — Prospective series of patients enrolled from **September 2009**, inclusion focused on
**MCP contractures**, excluding recurrences; most patients presented with a **palpable pretendinous cord**.
MCP, PIP, and DIP contracture were diagrammed preoperatively and tracked as total digital extension deficit,
followed at 6–8 weeks. **62 fingers**, predominantly ring, small, and long fingers, matching the
demographic pattern reported elsewhere in the literature. Results: **total extension deficit fell from 46
degrees preoperatively to 14 degrees**, maintained at six weeks — **most correction occurred at the MCP
joint**, with meaningfully less improvement at the PIP joint. **No neurovascular injuries** occurred, but
**one flexor tendon laceration** was identified when a patient stopped flexing his fingers three days
post-procedure and did not return until the six-week follow-up; the laceration was at the zone I/zone II
border and was successfully repaired primarily.
sections.heading: Study design and results

sections.body:
`[06:14]` — Gan explains his joint preference directly: at the MCP joint, the relevant cord is usually a
**pretendinous cord relatively far from the neurovascular bundle**, whereas closer to the neurovascular
bundle he remains cautious — a stated rationale for restricting the technique's use rather than a limitation
of the needle method itself.
sections.heading: Why MCP specifically

sections.body:
- **Loss of active finger flexion appearing three days post-procedure**, the presenting sign that led to
  discovering the flexor tendon laceration `[06:14]`.
- **A palpable cord near the web space with 45–50 degrees of contracture**, shown as a specific
  preoperative/postoperative case example `[04:09]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body: None beyond standard terms already established elsewhere in this library (total digital extension deficit).
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"Never is not very long"** — Gan's own phrase summarizing the lesson of publicly opposing a procedure and
  later adopting it `[08:15]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Gan discloses no financial relationships and is unusually candid about the limitations of his own study: a
**small series, very short-term follow-up (six to eight weeks only)**, and he frames his conclusion modestly
— the technique "may be beneficial for a select group of patients," possibly useful as an adjunct before open
fasciectomy in more severe cases, rather than a broad endorsement. He reports his one serious complication
(flexor tendon laceration) openly rather than omitting it, and explicitly walks through his own prior public
opposition to the technique before explaining his change of position.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `1BURdqs3a4U`** (Pess's technique talk) and other needle-aponeurotomy notes in this
library — Gan's joint-specific outcome pattern (strong MCP correction, weaker PIP correction) and his
radial-to-ulnar slicing variant add a second technique description and outcome dataset to compare against.
**Relevant to `nUVjZI2XCg0`** (Hovius's PALF trial) — both report needle-based release techniques correcting
MCP contracture more reliably than PIP contracture, a consistent joint-specific pattern across different
needle-based series in this library. **Relevant to `gMD3XNuUFFM`** (Choa's nerve anatomy talk) — Gan's stated
caution about staying away from the neurovascular bundle, and his one tendon-injury complication, are a
concrete illustration of exactly the anatomical risk that talk formally characterizes.

concepts: genome-wide association study (GWAS) methodology
linkage disequilibrium (correlated markers)
odds ratio as a measure of a genetic marker's disease-risk effect
single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
the Manhattan plot and QQ plot as GWAS result visualizations

sections.body:
**This talk presents what appears to be the original, preliminary results of the genome-wide association
study later cited elsewhere in this library as identifying nine Dupuytren's susceptibility loci** — here,
still in progress, with **two highly significant chromosomal regions already identified: chromosome 7 and
chromosome 22.** Dolmans states the top chromosome 7 marker's significance directly: **a P-value of "10 to
the power of minus 15"** and **an odds ratio of "1.8, 1.9"** — meaning **"if you have this marker, you have
90% more chance of developing the disease"** `[11:20]`–`[12:23]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:02]`–`[02:04]` — Dolmans distinguishes two research approaches by what kind of disease they're suited
to: **Mendelian disease** running in families, driven by **rare, high-effect mutations**, studied via
linkage analysis; versus **sporadic, non-familial disease**, potentially driven by **common genetic
variants** that everyone carries some combination of, studied via **genome-wide association studies (GWAS)**
— the approach chosen here specifically to study **non-familial (sporadic) Dupuytren's cases.**
sections.heading: Why GWAS, not family linkage studies

sections.body:
`[02:04]`–`[07:13]` — Explained step by step: a **SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)** is a single-base-
pair variant at a specific genome location; genotyping hundreds of thousands of these across an individual
produces a genetic "fingerprint." A **case-control design** compares allele frequencies at each marker
between affected and unaffected people — a marker allele that's meaningfully more common in cases than
controls suggests a disease gene lies near that location. Results are visualized across all chromosomes to
find the markers with the strongest association signal. Two technical points Dolmans is careful to explain:

- **Multiple testing**: testing hundreds of thousands of markers across thousands of people means chance
  alone can produce a seemingly striking result (he gives the example of a P-value of 10⁻⁵ arising by chance)
  — so **the genome-wide significance threshold used is far stricter, at P < 10⁻⁸**, and any finding still
  requires **replication in an independent cohort** before being trusted.
- **Linkage disequilibrium**: you don't need to directly test all ~3 billion base pairs, because nearby
  markers are statistically correlated — testing ~300,000 well-chosen markers captures information about
  many more untested ones nearby. This also means a *significant* marker on the chip may not itself be the
  causal variant — it may simply be correlated with a nearby causal variant that isn't directly on the chip,
  requiring the whole surrounding region to be studied further.
sections.heading: How a GWAS actually works

sections.body:
`[07:13]`–`[09:19]` — A **multicenter study across six major hospitals in the Netherlands**, recruiting every
Dupuytren's patient presenting to participating clinics, collecting blood, DNA, and questionnaires. At the
time of the talk: **864 cases analyzed, with 960 in progress.** The control group came from a **large,
same-region biobank** already tracking thousands of individuals prospectively for roughly 30 years for
unrelated epidemiological research — chosen specifically because these controls were genotyped **"with
exactly the same chip, in exactly the same lab"** as the cases, and drawn from the same geographic
population (northern Netherlands), minimizing population-structure confounds. Standard quality-control
steps are named: correcting genotyping errors, checking for ethnic outliers, and checking for undisclosed
relatives among participants, all before the case-control statistical comparison (a chi-squared test of
allele frequencies).
sections.heading: The study design

sections.body:
`[09:19]`–`[12:23]` — A **QQ plot** is used to show the observed association signal diverges meaningfully
from what chance alone would produce, before the **Manhattan plot** (his aside: "you could also call it the
Miami plot," a joke given the conference location) shows two regions clearing the strict genome-wide
significance threshold: **chromosome 7** and **chromosome 22**, each represented by multiple correlated
markers clustering at the same genomic position. The top chromosome 7 SNP reaches **P = 10⁻¹⁵** with an
**odds ratio around 1.8–1.9**; additional markers on both chromosomes showed somewhat lower but still
significant effect sizes (one example given at 1.6).
sections.heading: The results

sections.body: None directly — this is a genetics-methodology and results talk, not a discussion of clinical presentation.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism)** — a single-base-pair genetic variant, the marker type used
  throughout GWAS genotyping `[02:04]`.
- **Genome-wide significance threshold (P < 10⁻⁸)** — the strict statistical cutoff required to call a GWAS
  finding significant, given the multiple-testing burden of scanning hundreds of thousands of markers
  `[05:12]`.
- **Linkage disequilibrium** — the statistical correlation between nearby genetic markers that lets a
  limited chip capture information about a much larger number of untested variants `[06:13]`.
- **Manhattan plot / QQ plot** — the two standard visualizations used to display and validate GWAS
  association results `[09:19]`–`[10:20]`.
- **Odds ratio (as a GWAS effect-size measure)** — here, roughly 1.8–1.9 for the strongest chromosome 7
  marker, interpreted directly as "90% more chance of developing the disease" per copy of the risk allele
  `[12:23]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Genetic "fingerprint"** — hundreds of thousands of genotyped markers combining into an individual
  signature usable for case-control comparison `[03:08]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Unusually careful and pedagogical about what a GWAS finding does and doesn't establish: Dolmans explains the
multiple-testing problem before presenting any result, explicitly states that a significant marker may not
itself be the causal variant, and closes by stating plainly that **replication in an independent cohort is
still needed** before these preliminary findings can be trusted — **"the thing we have to do now is
replicate."** He frames the talk's title modestly too, opening by noting **"it says the first genome-wide
association study, but maybe we're not the first."**
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Is very likely the primary, earlier-stage presentation of the same GWAS finding `-0JtjUrrU4o`** (Ophoff's
2015 genetics talk) cites as already-published, describing **"nine different loci... from fewer than 1,000
cases."** This talk shows that same study mid-analysis (864–960 cases) with its first two significant loci
(chromosome 7 and 22) identified — the two chromosome 7/22 findings here are plausibly among the nine loci
Ophoff references five years later as an established, if still only ~14–16%-heritability-explaining, result.
**Extends `g40N2M2C6qM`** (Bayat's 2010 genetics talk, delivered the same symposium) — that talk's
badly-degraded transcript could not confidently convey specific GWAS numbers; this talk supplies exactly the
methodology and preliminary results that talk was gesturing toward. **Relevant to `AbY1KVhTVAo`** (Eaton's
IDDB talk) — Eaton's proposed genetic/systemic versus exposure/benign disease-subset hypothesis remains
consistent with, but not yet directly confirmed by, the specific loci identified here. **`hRJZEQzxy4U`**
(Werker and Aartsen's 2015 introductory remarks) supplies the human backstory behind this collaboration —
Werker's own account of meeting Ophoff and the 2010 Miami symposium becoming the moment this work turned
international.

concepts: Dupuytren's framed explicitly as a lifelong disease surgery treats but doesn't cure
neoadjuvant dosing (before and after surgery, not instead of it)
the Abe risk score for recurrence
management: high-dose neoadjuvant tamoxifen combined with segmental fasciectomy

sections.body:
**Surgery treats Dupuytren's contracture, not Dupuytren's disease — "surgeons don't cure a disease, they
just treat it" — and Degreef's trial tests whether adding tamoxifen around surgery can address the disease
process itself, at least in the highest-recurrence-risk patients** `[00:03]`. Her framing of the disease
itself: **"you have the disease, and you will have it the rest of your life. You may become symptom-free
for a while"** — comparing it explicitly to rheumatoid arthritis, and crediting a colleague's line that
**"disease symptoms will occur as long as the patient lives long enough."**
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:08]`–`[04:14]` — The idea came from **desmoid tumors** (also fibroblast-driven), already treated with
high-dose tamoxifen in some cases, combined with lab evidence that **tamoxifen specifically inhibits
myofibroblast proliferation and contractility in Dupuytren's tissue.** Degreef deliberately selected
**high-recurrence-risk patients (using the Abe risk score)** rather than a general population, reasoning
that a real effect would be easiest to detect where recurrence risk — and therefore statistical power — was
highest. The trial: **randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled**, tamoxifen given **neoadjuvantly** —
starting **six weeks before surgery and continuing twelve weeks after** — combined with standard segmental
fasciectomy and standard splinting. Fertile women and cancer patients were excluded (tamoxifen is an
estrogen-pathway drug); embolism-risk patients were excluded given the drug's clotting risk, which Degreef
states she disclosed to every patient directly: **"there is a risk to medication — you could die from it. I
always say that to the patient."**
sections.heading: Why tamoxifen, and why this patient group

sections.body:
`[07:18]`–`[09:21]` — Degreef reports specific difficulty recruiting men to a trial of **"female hormone"**
at first, improving only with practice explaining it. Notable dropouts: one patient developed pulmonary
emphysema and became inoperable; one patient, convinced the drug worked from his own symptom improvement,
**left the trial, obtained needle aponeurotomy elsewhere instead, and took the remaining study medication
with him** — lost to follow-up; one patient's medication was interrupted by an unrelated severe appendicitis
but the surgical outcome was still good. She also tested whether a **biopsy-based marker** could identify
high-risk patients directly (rather than via risk-factor scoring) and found **no meaningful biopsy
difference** between recurrent and non-recurrent disease, consistent, she notes, with other published
findings.
sections.heading: Recruiting and running the trial: real friction, honestly reported

sections.body:
`[09:21]`–`[12:24]` — Assessed via blinded digital photography and anonymized satisfaction scoring. Before
formal unblinding, Degreef could already see **two visually distinct outcome groups**: one group nearly all
achieved complete correction, the other included the two patients with insufficient correction. This
pattern held across **visual analog satisfaction scores, total joint correction, and PIP-joint-specific
correction** — described explicitly as preliminary and not yet statistically analyzed. A striking, honestly
reported false alarm: **three patients developed carpal tunnel syndrome**, which Degreef initially assumed
must be the tamoxifen arm (given the drug's hormonal mechanism) — **"I was relieved" to later learn, on
unblinding, that these were placebo-arm side effects**, alongside other placebo-arm complaints (reported
impotence, sleeplessness, weight gain). Her point: **"if we give placebo to patients, apparently we have to
warn them for the side effects [too]"** — patients report symptoms consistent with what they were told to
expect, regardless of which arm they're in. On unblinding, **one genuine tamoxifen-arm complication** was
identified: a serious wound-healing problem requiring tenolysis and pulley reconstruction, limiting final
flexion despite full extension being achieved.
sections.heading: Preliminary one-year results

sections.body:
`[13:26]`–`[14:26]` — Outside the formal trial, Degreef describes offering tamoxifen to a patient with
**severe, treatment-resistant recurrent disease** after a fifth-finger PIP arthrodesis — the patient's
disease **"completely disappeared,"** symptom-free, while adherent to the medication. When the patient chose
to stop on her own, **a recurrent nodule appeared within four weeks**; restarting tamoxifen, the nodule had
**shrunk to half its size within a couple of weeks.** Degreef is careful to label this **"preliminary,"**
not trial-level evidence, but treats it as consistent with the randomized data.
sections.heading: A later case report: stopping and restarting

sections.body:
- **Contracture recurrence risk stratified by the Abe score** — Degreef states a roughly 38% recurrence
  risk with zero risk factors present, rising sharply as more risk factors accumulate `[05:16]`.
- **Fifth-finger PIP joint contracture specifically flagged as the hardest to treat**, used as the
  reference joint when multiple digits were affected `[06:16]`.
- **Nodule regrowth within weeks of stopping tamoxifen in a treatment-responsive patient**, and shrinkage
  again on restarting `[13:26]`.
- **Placebo-arm side effects (carpal tunnel syndrome, reported impotence, sleeplessness, weight gain)** —
  presented as a caution about symptom reporting under expectation, not as evidence against tamoxifen's
  real effects `[11:23]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Neoadjuvant** — medication given both before and after the definitive surgical procedure, rather
  than as a substitute for surgery `[03:11]`.
- **Abe (risk) score** — the clinical risk-factor scoring system used to select high-recurrence-risk trial
  candidates; family history is noted as not directly included but statistically correlated with score
  components `[06:16]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Dupuytren's compared directly to rheumatoid arthritis** — a disease surgery/medicine manage but do not
  cure, with symptom-free periods properly understood as remission, not resolution `[00:03]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Unusually candid throughout: results are repeatedly labeled **"preliminary," "not a 100% sure," "I haven't
had any statistics [yet]"** `[10:23]`; the biopsy-marker negative finding is reported plainly rather than
omitted; the placebo-arm side-effect scare is told against her own initial assumption, undercutting rather
than protecting her hypothesis; and the closing case report is explicitly flagged as anecdotal ("I might be
optimistic... we have to look at the outcome later on") rather than presented as confirmed.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Is the primary source behind `-jLfWXX3YUM`'s (British Dupuytren Society Seven Questions) secondhand
summary** — that later video states tamoxifen "reduced the risk of early recurrence compared to placebo...
the first proof that medicine could slow down recurrence," attributing the finding to "Dr. Ilse Degreef;"
this talk is Degreef's own original presentation of that same trial, ten years earlier, with substantially
more methodological detail (patient selection via Abe score, the neoadjuvant dosing window, the placebo
side-effect confound, and the specific tenolysis complication) that the later secondhand summary doesn't
include. **Directly relevant to `AbY1KVhTVAo`** (Eaton's IDDB talk) — Degreef's biopsy-marker negative
finding here (no clear histologic difference between recurrent and non-recurrent disease) is a concrete data
point bearing on the same biomarker gap Eaton's IDDB talk identifies as the field's central obstacle.
**The mechanism behind this trial's clinical result is shown directly in `dMW6VVm4FhU`** (Robson's lab
models talk) — tamoxifen inhibiting Dupuytren's fibroblast contraction and lowering TGF-beta 1/2 levels in
an FPCL model, a plausible molecular explanation for the recurrence reduction reported here.

concepts: a transition question used to anchor score change against the patient's own sense of "better" or "worse"
minimum clinically important difference (MCID) as distinct from statistical significance
receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis used to derive a numeric MCID threshold
management: the Patient Evaluation Measure (PEM), a UK hand-specific patient-rated outcome measure

sections.body:
**Dias derives a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 3 points for the Patient Evaluation
Measure using ROC analysis anchored to patients' own sense of being better or worse — and finds that while the
average score improvement across a 1,200-patient cohort was surprisingly small, surgery still produced three
times the improvement seen with no treatment at all.** He states the core distinction driving the whole talk:
**"you can get a statistical significance if you're testing two groups... but the statistically significant
difference may not be clinically relevant. The smallest change in a score that the patient can appreciate...
is the minimum [clinically] important difference"** `[00:00]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[02:03]` — The **PEM** is a UK patient-administered outcome measure, similar in spirit to the DASH
but specific to the hand rather than the whole upper limb. It has three sections; Dias focuses on the second,
an **11-question attribute section** using visual-analog-scale items (e.g., pain rated from "non-existent" to
"unbearable"), combined into a total score from **0 (normal) to 100 (severely abnormal).**
sections.heading: The Patient Evaluation Measure

sections.body:
`[02:03]`–`[02:03]` — **1,200 consecutive Dupuytren's contracture patients** were reviewed; 125 had died.
**878 patients** had PEM scores available at both baseline and final review; **526** additionally completed a
transition question (described below). Mean follow-up exceeded **two years** — Dias notes most recurrence and
change typically occurs within the first year. **Two-thirds of the cohort were operated on, one-third were
not.**
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[02:03]`–`[03:05]` — Mean PEM score: **40 at baseline, 32 at 27 months** — a mean improvement of only **8
points**, which Dias calls **"quite shocking,"** noting it should give pause to assuming that improving
clinical measures necessarily tracks with a correspondingly large improvement in what patients themselves
perceive.
sections.heading: A surprisingly small average change

sections.body:
`[03:05]`–`[04:07]` — Patients were separately asked a **transition question**: how they considered themselves
now compared to before treatment, on a scale from "cured" to "terrible." This let Dias split patients into two
groups — **improved** versus **no better/worse** — and compare each group's actual PEM score change. Patients
who rated themselves "cured" showed a large mean PEM improvement; the "no change" group showed essentially
none. Using **receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis** (sensitivity and specificity) to find the PEM
score change that best distinguished the "better" group from the "worse" group produced the study's headline
result: **a minimum clinically important difference of 3 points.**
sections.heading: Deriving the MCID from a transition question

sections.body:
`[04:07]`–`[05:09]` — Comparing groups: patients who were **not operated on still improved, by roughly the
MCID (3 points), over the same follow-up period** — a natural-history effect. Patients who **were operated on
improved roughly three times as much.** Dias's summary: **patients' perceived wellbeing improves somewhat
regardless of surgery, but surgery adds meaningfully more benefit than natural history alone** — while noting
the absolute improvement from surgery, in this outcome measure, is still fairly modest in scale.
Additionally: **about one in three non-operated patients worsened over time**, versus **roughly one in five
operated patients** who ended up worse than their baseline. Dias states he does not yet have comparable
data for collagenase specifically, though some relevant data exists for percutaneous needle fasciotomy.
sections.heading: Operated versus non-operated, against natural history

sections.body:
- **Patient-rated pain, on a visual-analog scale from "non-existent" to "unbearable,"** one of the eleven
  attribute items composing the PEM score `[01:00]`.
- **Patients ending up subjectively worse than their pretreatment baseline** — quantified separately for
  operated (~1 in 5) and non-operated (~1 in 3) groups, rather than assumed to be a negligible outcome
  `[05:09]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Patient Evaluation Measure (PEM)** — a UK hand-specific patient-rated outcome measure, structurally
  similar to the DASH but scoped to the hand alone `[00:00]`.
- **Minimum clinically important difference (MCID)** — the smallest score change a patient can perceive as a
  real improvement or worsening, distinct from a statistically significant difference `[00:00]`.
- **Transition question** — a direct patient self-rating (cured to terrible) used to validate and calibrate
  the MCID against the patient's own sense of change `[03:05]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None stated — the talk presents outcome-measure methodology and results directly.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Dias opens with a self-deprecating joke about the previous night's alcohol, then presents the methodology and
results directly and without noticeable hedging on the numeric findings — describing the small mean
improvement candidly as "quite shocking" rather than minimizing it. He explicitly flags a gap in the current
evidence base: comparable MCID-anchored data for collagenase specifically does not yet exist, distinguishing
what is and isn't yet known rather than extrapolating the surgical findings to other treatments.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly extended by `EAU0emyHHOg`** (Dias's companion talk on URAM as a PROM, same cohort and methodology)
— that talk uses this talk's transition-question technique to derive a 2.6-point MCID for URAM, then shows
head-to-head that URAM underperforms the PEM as an outcome measure, with a clear ceiling effect traced to
URAM's lack of a complications domain. **Directly relevant to `R4WPhcOpAMo`** (Selles's consensus recurrence definition talk) and `EAU0emyHHOg` (Dias's
own URAM-as-PROM talk) — all three address the broader problem of standardizing outcome measurement in
Dupuytren's disease; this talk supplies a patient-perception-anchored MCID specifically for the PEM, a distinct
methodological contribution from a purely clinician-defined threshold like a fixed-degree recurrence
definition. **Relevant to `93IWNYYqCjs`** (Warwick's "what we may never know" talk) — Warwick's objection that
no validated, agreed outcome measure exists for comparing Dupuytren's treatments is directly answered, in part,
by this talk's rigorous, patient-anchored derivation of a specific MCID threshold for one such measure.
**Relevant to `mUFigJz8r-U`** (Badalamente's clinical research talk) — Dias's finding that a statistically
detectable difference is not automatically clinically meaningful is a concrete illustration of exactly the
kind of underpowered-study concern that talk raises about small trials that report "a trend but no statistical
significance."

concepts: Dupuytren's diathesis
minimizing lifetime permanent complications as the actual treatment goal
the 20–40 degree PIP treatment window
the biomarker gap and why it blocks preventive-treatment research
management: hand therapy, splinting, radiotherapy, massage, and supplements, each rated by evidence quality
minimally invasive procedures (collagenase, needle fasciotomy) versus open procedures (fasciectomy, dermofasciectomy)
tamoxifen and repeated cortisone injection as post-procedure recurrence-slowing trials

sections.body:
**Almost nothing about Dupuytren's treatment is evidence-based except the choice between minimally
invasive and open corrective procedures — everything upstream of that (prevention) and much alongside it
(hand therapy, massage, supplements) rests on theory or anecdote, and Eaton is explicit that this is a
structural problem, not a knowledge gap that better studies alone would fix: "we don't have Dupuytren's
biomarkers yet... [without one] we can't predict which patients might benefit and which won't"**
`[00:00]`, `[09:15]`. He opens by naming this directly: **"we're still in an age of profound ignorance about
the basic nature of Dupuytren's disease... we have to resist our natural tendencies to oversimplify and to
see patterns where there are none"** `[00:00]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[03:06]` — **A hand surgery specialist, before contracture is even present**, for two reasons:
ruling out look-alike diagnoses (**tendinitis, flexor tendon sheath cysts, flexor tendon bowstringing,
diabetic stiff hand syndrome, atypical mycobacterial infections, reflex sympathetic dystrophy, giant cell
tumors, sarcomas**, and others — noting tendinitis can coexist with Dupuytren's in the same finger and
change treatment) and speed to diagnosis (**"the average Dupuytren's patient will see two or three doctors
over the course of sometimes several years before getting the right diagnosis"**). Any surgeon who operates
on hands can call themselves a hand surgeon, but **hand surgery specialists have additional post-residency
fellowship training** specifically relevant to handling **complications and recurrence** — which Eaton
calls the real differentiator, not routine outcomes. His concrete advice for vetting a surgeon: **ask where
they trained, what they'd do if the finger loses circulation mid-procedure, and what happens if the
contracture returns worse than before** — and treat vague answers ("don't worry," "nothing can be done,"
deflection to a colleague) as a reason to look elsewhere.
sections.heading: Who to see, and how to vet them

sections.body:
`[04:06]`–`[07:12]` — Eaton states plainly there are **no evidence-based preventive treatments**, and
explains why testing one is so hard without a biomarker: **"you'd need to study at least a thousand people
with early disease, treat half with a preventive treatment and half with a placebo, and then see how bent
their fingers are five years later... that hasn't been done anywhere on this scale, with any treatment,
including radiotherapy."** A partial workaround, credited to Dr. Ilse Degreef: since recurrence after
surgery in high-risk patients is fast and predictable, her trials substitute **post-surgical recurrence**
for **early-disease progression** as the measured outcome, cutting the needed timeline to about a year.
Two results from this approach, both real but both time-limited:

- **Tamoxifen** (an estrogen-blocking breast cancer drug), tested against placebo after surgery in
  high-recurrence-risk patients, **reduced early recurrence** — replicated after percutaneous needle
  fasciotomy too. Eaton calls this **"the first proof that medicine could slow down recurrence"** — but
  flags tamoxifen's side-effect profile as too risky for long-term use, and the benefit **stopped once the
  drug stopped**.
- **Cortisone injections every three months for a year** after percutaneous needle fasciotomy (Dr. Paul
  Binhammer), showed the same pattern: **slower recurrence only while injections continued.**
sections.heading: Preventive treatment: blocked by the missing biomarker

sections.body:
`[07:12]`–`[08:13]` — Two families of corrective procedure. **Minimally invasive** (collagenase, needle
fasciotomy) versus **open** (fasciotomy, dermofasciectomy). Short-term straightening is roughly comparable
between the two, with open surgery somewhat better for severe contractures — but the real differences are
elsewhere: **"fasciotomy lasts over twice as long as minimally invasive procedures"** before recurrence,
open surgery recovery takes **months versus days-to-weeks**, and **"the risk of permanent complications
after fasciotomy is almost 10 times higher than minimally invasive procedures"** — which Eaton states as
the direct rationale for starting with a minimally invasive procedure as first-line treatment. Splinting has
**two studies** showing improvement with several months of around-the-clock use, but Eaton is skeptical the
gains persist once splinting stops. (The "over twice as long" figure is broadly consistent with, though less
severe than, the specific 5-year randomized trial data in `oRdE0UKeJF0` — see that note's Conflicts section
for the discrepancy worth flagging.)
sections.heading: Corrective treatment: the actual evidence base

sections.body:
`[09:15]`–`[14:26]` — Eaton's own opinions, explicitly labeled as such ("remember, I'm not your doctor"):

| Treatment | What the evidence shows |
|---|---|
| **Hand therapy / splinting** | "A half a dozen well-conducted randomized, prospective, controlled" studies across different countries showed **no long-term benefit** after open surgery; one showed **aggressive splinting performed worse than gentle splinting**. Eaton still believes it helps some patients subjectively, but a biomarker would be needed to predict who. |
| **Radiotherapy** | Kills the living cells in nodules (helps roughly half the time), but **cords are collagen with few cells and don't respond** — so radiotherapy is only a theoretical option *before* cords/contracture form, and its preventive effectiveness is untestable for the same biomarker reasons as above. Complications are "rare but not zero." |
| **Cortisone shots** | Similar profile to radiotherapy — can help nodules, but contracture can still develop; **avoid once contracture is present unless paired with a straightening procedure.** |
| **Massage** | No long-term study either way; theoretically, *aggressive* massage could aggravate the disease by the same mechanical-stress logic that applies to heavy manual work. Gentle massage: "can't hurt, might help, no evidence." |
| **Avoiding heavy manual/strenuous hand use** | Grounded in real data that heavy manual work or sports **"slightly increase the chance of Dupuytren's"** — protective avoidance is theoretical, not tested. |
| **Supplements** (NAC, rutin, sulforaphane, caffeine) | Plausible from anti-fibrotic biology, **no human studies exist** for any of them. |
| **Topical verapamil** | Marketed for Peyronie's and sold for Ledderhose, but **no evidence it works for either**, and Eaton doubts it penetrates palm skin thickness regardless. |
sections.heading: What's not evidence-based, rated one by one

sections.body:
`[14:26]`–`[18:30]` — Citing Degreef again, Eaton frames the actual treatment goal as **"minimize the number
of permanent complications from Dupuytren's disease and from its treatment over the lifetime of the
patient,"** not maximize any single procedure's result — because repeat procedures carry higher complication
risk and lower success than the first one. **Diathesis factors** — **onset before age 50, close family
history, knuckle pads, Ledderhose disease, three or more digits involved** — predict faster, more
treatment-resistant recurrence, which is the stated rationale for choosing **dermofasciectomy over
fasciotomy as the first open procedure** in diathesis-positive patients, even though dermofasciectomy is the
more invasive option. Diathesis does **not**, however, predict how fast disease progresses before any
treatment starts — that remains unknown without a biomarker.
sections.heading: Diathesis and the decision pathway

sections.body:
`[17:29]`–`[18:30]` — Separate from diathesis, **how bent the joint already is changes the odds of a good
outcome.** For the PIP joint: **the effective treatment window is roughly 20–40 degrees of contracture** —
below 20 degrees, the improvement doesn't justify procedural risk; above 40 degrees, tendon damage risk
rises and can prevent a good result. The MCP joint tolerates waiting longer, with **50 degrees** described
as a common (not absolute) threshold to stop waiting.
sections.heading: Degree of joint bend as its own independent factor

sections.body:
`[18:30]`–`[19:32]` — Eaton gives specific 10-year odds after a first nodule appears: **roughly 1 in 10
nodules regress spontaneously without treatment; about 2 in 10 (1 in 5) progress to needing a corrective
procedure; the remaining ~7 in 10 either don't change or don't progress enough to need treatment.** His own
first nodule, he notes, has shown "little change" over six years of his own watching.
sections.heading: The reassurance: natural history after a first nodule

sections.body:
- **A new palm nodule, and the specific odds of it regressing, progressing, or staying stable over 10
  years** `[18:30]`.
- **Contracture recurrence after any corrective procedure, framed as a prevention problem rather than a
  treatment-failure problem** `[07:12]`.
- **PIP contracture in the 20–40 degree range as the window where a corrective procedure is worth the
  risk** `[17:29]`.
- **Knuckle pads and concurrent Ledderhose disease as diathesis markers predicting faster recurrence**
  `[16:28]`.
- **Post-procedure loss of circulation in the finger, named directly as a question to ask a prospective
  surgeon about in advance** `[03:06]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Dupuytren's diathesis** — a cluster of risk factors (early onset, family history, knuckle pads,
  Ledderhose disease, multi-digit involvement) predicting faster, more treatment-resistant recurrence
  `[16:28]`.
- **Biomarker gap** — Eaton's own recurring term for the absence of any objective, non-clinical-exam way to
  diagnose or stage Dupuytren's, which he treats as the field's central obstacle `[04:06]`.

sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Exceptionally well-hedged throughout — Eaton distinguishes evidence-based claims (the minimally invasive
versus open procedure comparison, the tamoxifen and cortisone recurrence trials) from stated personal
opinion (hand therapy, massage, heavy-activity avoidance, supplements), repeatedly flagging the latter
category explicitly ("that's my opinion," "remember, I'm not your doctor"). He states directly where no
evidence exists at all (massage, supplements, topical verapamil for Ledderhose) rather than implying support
where none exists.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly extends `AbY1KVhTVAo`** (Eaton's own IDDB talk) — the biomarker gap named here as the central
obstacle is the same problem the IDDB was built to solve, and this video ends with the same call to enroll
at dupestudy.com. **The tamoxifen finding cited here secondhand is presented firsthand, with far more
methodological detail, in `-OKFB6sX_64`** (Degreef's own 2010 trial presentation) — that note is the primary
source for this video's summary claim. **Consistent with `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`**, whose ~50%-at-3–5-years recurrence
figure for needle fasciotomy is compatible with this video's framing of minimally invasive procedures as
shorter-lasting but lower-complication-risk than open surgery. **Relevant to `9LY5fyLw618`** (Hurst's
collagenase talk) — Hurst's practice pattern (443 of 955 patients treated with collagenase, prior surgery in
31% of them) is consistent with this video's stated rationale for starting minimally invasive. **The
radiotherapy summary here is expanded with full trial data and a specific mechanism in `x_vecaIme58`**
(Seegenschmiedt's dedicated radiotherapy talk) — this talk's cells-versus-collagen distinction (why radiation
works on nodules but not cords) is consistent with, and less detailed than, that note's TGF-beta-based
mechanism and 612-patient outcome data. **The "half a dozen well-conducted" splinting studies referenced
here are very likely to include `KjV8R8x4OwE`** (Larson's UK multi-center RCT) — that trial's own strictest
analysis found splinting performed significantly *worse* than no splinting, matching this video's claim that
"one [study] even showed worse results with aggressive splinting compared to gentle splinting."

sections.body:
**Across a 950-patient, five-year prospective follow-up of collagenase-treated joints, 84% of successfully
treated joints needed no additional treatment at all — and no serious long-term safety risks emerged, even
though recurrence by strict criteria still affected nearly half of joints treated.** Peimer's closing
summary states both facts plainly, without softening either: **"eighty-four percent of successfully treated
joints had no additional treatment, which is encouraging"** alongside recurrence figures of **47% (20-degree
criteria) or 32% (30-degree criteria)** `[08:15]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[02:04]` — **CORDLESS** is a prospective five-year follow-up of patients drawn from **five prior
collagenase trials** (CORD I, CORD II, Joint I, Joint II, and a CORD I extension study), covering anyone who
received one or more collagenase injections and at least one post-treatment assessment in those studies,
with **annual reevaluation starting two years after treatment.** Peimer notes the general literature's
recurrence figures vary enormously (roughly 12–100% depending on the technique and combination of
procedures compared) — attributed to **inconsistent follow-up periods and inconsistent recurrence
definitions across studies**, which is exactly why this study adopts strict, explicit criteria:

- **Successfully treated joint**: 0–5 degrees of contracture within 30 days.
- **Measurably improved joint**: at least 20 degrees of contracture reduction.
- **Recurrence (after successful correction)**: a contracture increase of 20 degrees or more, *plus* either
  a palpable cord or any secondary medical/surgical intervention.
- **Non-durable response**: the same recurrence pattern, but specifically in joints that only achieved
  partial (not full 0–5-degree) correction to begin with.
- A **post-hoc 30-degree threshold** was also calculated, specifically to allow comparison against the more
  commonly reported figure in older published literature.
sections.heading: What CORDLESS is, and why the definitions matter

sections.body:
`[03:07]`–`[04:08]` — **950 eligible patients, over 1,000 joints**, each receiving three or fewer
injections; **156 joints (about 12%) were not effectively treated** at baseline. Five-year recurrence in
successfully treated joints, by joint and by threshold:

| Joint | 20° recurrence | 30° recurrence |
|---|---|---|
| **All joints** | 47% | 32% |
| **MP (MCP)** | 40% | 26% |
| **PIP** | 66% | 46% |
sections.heading: The cohort and five-year recurrence figures

sections.body:
`[04:08]` — Looking at pretreatment contracture severity: **at the PIP joint, more severe cases had higher
recurrence, as expected.** But **at the MP joint, the pattern reversed — higher-severity joints appeared to
do *better* (lower recurrence) than lower-severity joints.** Peimer doesn't try to explain this away,
stating plainly: **"the MP joints are counterintuitive... maybe we need an even larger study"** — treating it
as an open finding rather than forcing a narrative onto it.
sections.heading: A counterintuitive severity finding, flagged honestly

sections.body:
`[05:10]` — The time course, not just the endpoint, is informative: recurrence risk **rises most sharply in
years 2–3 (about a 15% increase)**, then **drops to about 7% the following year**, and continues flattening
toward year 5 — the same general pattern held for both MP and PIP joints. Practical implication: **most
patients who are going to recur do so within the second and third year**, not steadily throughout follow-up.
sections.heading: When recurrence actually happens

sections.body:
`[06:11]`–`[07:14]` — **365 patients (57%) had an adverse event** of some kind — Peimer notes this figure is
inflated in part because the **FDA counts swelling itself as a reportable adverse event.** One specific,
almost amusing observation: a **decrease in measured circumference** was recorded as an adverse event in
some cases, which Peimer flags may actually reflect a **measurement artifact** (a change in how skin-to-skin
distance was measured) rather than a genuine physical change, referencing a colleague's separate presentation
on thumb web-space outcomes. **181 serious adverse events occurred, but none were judged treatment-related**
— they included unrelated incidents like car accidents and broken bones, reported per protocol regardless of
cause. **No allergic reactions occurred in this specific series**, though Peimer notes the general
possibility of an allergic reaction to any drug should still be anticipated, with resuscitation equipment
kept available. **Tendon rupture: 1 case in this series, 3 across the full clinical trial program, and 26
reported worldwide** out of roughly **50,000 total treated cases** at the time of the analysis — plus one
pulley injury and one ligament injury. These tendon-related events were **"late"** — occurring within the
first 30 days post-injection, but not at the time of manipulation itself.
sections.heading: Safety data

sections.body:
- **Contracture recurrence timing concentrated in years 2–3**, with a specific, quantified drop-off pattern
  afterward `[05:10]`.
- **Swelling as a formally counted adverse event** under FDA reporting criteria, distinct from more clinically
  significant complications `[06:11]`.
- **A possible measurement artifact (decreased circumference) mistaken for a genuine physical change** —
  flagged as worth reconsidering rather than accepted at face value `[06:11]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **CORDLESS** — the five-year prospective follow-up study pooling patients across the original CORD/Joint
  collagenase trial cohorts `[01:01]`.
- **Non-durable response** — recurrence-pattern deterioration specifically in joints that never achieved
  full initial correction, distinguished from recurrence after a genuinely successful correction `[02:04]`.

sections.body:
Peimer states upfront that this talk is **"data-driven and on-label,"** distinguishing it from a separate,
explicitly off-label talk he was giving the following day — a clear, stated boundary around what evidence
supports what claim. He reports the counterintuitive MP-joint severity finding without forcing an
explanation, and is direct that the elevated overall adverse-event percentage partly reflects a broad FDA
reporting definition (counting swelling) rather than necessarily reflecting clinically significant harm.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly extends `OwSS6grbMAc`** (Badalamente's CORD I trial talk) — that talk reports the original
30-day primary endpoint results (64% full correction, 85% ≥50% reduction) from the same underlying trial
population; this talk reports what happened to those same patients **over the following five years**,
completing the picture from initial success through longer-term recurrence. **Directly relevant to
`oRdE0UKeJF0`** (Van Rijssen's randomized PNF-vs-fasciectomy trial) — this collagenase cohort's PIP-joint
five-year recurrence (66% at the 20-degree threshold) sits between that trial's reported LF (26%) and PNF
(85%) recurrence rates, broadly consistent with collagenase's usual positioning as intermediate between
open surgery and needle fasciotomy in durability. **Corroborates `-jLfWXX3YUM`** (Seven Questions) — the
84%-no-further-treatment figure here is a concrete number behind that video's general framing of
minimally invasive treatment as offering meaningfully durable benefit for most patients despite documented
recurrence risk.

patient choice as an unavoidable source of selection bias in comparative studies
management: collagenase (CCH) injection, at the standard 0.58mg dose
percutaneous needle fasciotomy (PNF), a fan-shaped vertical/horizontal technique

sections.body:
**In a non-randomized prospective comparison, collagenase (CCH) and needle fasciotomy (PNF) produced closely
matched extension-deficit outcomes at three weeks and comparable, lower-than-expected recurrence rates at 24
months — with the choice between them driven in practice by patient preference and practical factors like
cost, procedure count, and typical complication profile, rather than a clear efficacy advantage for either.**
Baur states the closeness of the result directly, comparing the two groups' extension deficit at the PIP
joint: **"it's really very narrow together — it's 16 and 23 degrees, so it's not so big [a] difference"**
`[03:07]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[01:04]` — Baur explains the study proposes all available treatments (needle fasciotomy, surgery,
radiotherapy, and collagenase) to each patient, with the final treatment decision made jointly between
physician and patient — a design choice made explicitly because many patients arrive already asking for a
specific treatment (collagenase), making formal randomization impractical in this clinical setting. Enrollment
began **November 2011**. Of 93 candidate patients, **48 remained in the study**: 23 in the PNF group, 25 in
the CCH group. The clinic sees roughly 180 Dupuytren's patients a year overall (a mix of information-only
visits, PNF, and surgery).
sections.heading: Why the study isn't randomized

sections.body:
`[01:04]`–`[02:05]` — Follow-up occurred at 3 weeks, 6 weeks, 6 months, 12 months, and 24 months, with
complications tracked at one week and three weeks. Outcome measures: **range of motion / extension deficit**
of the treated fingers, and the **QuickDASH** questionnaire. Baur's PNF technique uses local skin
anesthesia followed by a **vertical/horizontal needle fasciotomy in a fan-shaped pattern**; the CCH group
received the standard **0.58mg dose**. A case example is shown maintaining correction from 3 to 24 months.
Post-CCH manipulation, Baur notes patients are advised to wear a splint, though she is candid that **it's
unclear whether continuous splint-wear is actually necessary**, and some patients instead adapt a soft
bandage's tension themselves.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[02:05]`–`[04:09]` — The PNF group had somewhat more severe baseline cases and more multi-digit involvement,
yielding **58 treated fingers in PNF versus 32 in CCH**. At the 3-week post-treatment baseline: extension
deficit was closely matched between groups, including at the PIP joint (16° PNF vs. 23° CCH — "not so big a
difference"). **Clinical success** was defined as a straight finger post-treatment (under 10% persisting
extension deficit); **recurrence** was defined as more than 20 degrees of deficit increase from the 3-week
post-op baseline. Reported recurrence: **25% or 16%** (the two figures given without full disambiguation in
the transcript) — Baur notes she was surprised recurrence was *lower* after two years than she expected, more
so at the PIP joint, broadly consistent with rates reported elsewhere in the literature. QuickDASH scores were
nearly identical between groups. **No major complications occurred in either group**; typical complications
differed by type — **skin laceration for PNF**, versus **ecchymosis and hematoma for CCH** — and one flexor
tendon rupture is noted in a CCH-treated digit.
sections.heading: Results

sections.body:
`[04:09]`–`[05:12]` — Baur offers several possible, unconfirmed explanations for why results improved over the
study period: possibly more severe cases entering later, possibly a **learning curve effect**, and she notes
this candidly as an open question requiring longer follow-up. She also flags a specific selection bias: the
treatment ratio shifted from roughly 60% CCH / 40% PNF at the study's start toward more PNF later, which she
attributes partly to a colleague's report elsewhere of a flexor tendon rupture following CCH.
sections.heading: Candid uncertainty about the improving results

sections.body:
`[05:12]`–`[07:15]` — In favor of PNF: **lower cost, ability to treat multiple digits and joints in one
session**, patients returning to work or hobbies within days with no restriction, and generally softer/less
painful skin than after collagenase injection — though Baur notes PNF becomes personally "a little bit
boring" for the surgeon after 15–20 minutes on a difficult case. She also flags that **surgery performed after
a failed PNF is sometimes more difficult (more scarring) than surgery after failed collagenase.** One
practical caution she offers, contrasting with another speaker's guidance the previous day: she avoids doing
**severe-case PNF in wintertime**, because bandaging (not splinting) is harder to manage well on a cold hand,
citing one case with a poor outcome from this specific timing issue.
sections.heading: Practical trade-offs

sections.body:
- **Skin laceration as the characteristic PNF complication, versus ecchymosis and hematoma for CCH** — the
  two treatments' complication profiles explicitly distinguished by type, not just rate `[04:09]`.
- **A flexor tendon rupture following CCH**, cited as a factor that shifted the clinic's later treatment mix
  toward more PNF `[05:12]`.

sections.body:
Baur discloses no conflicts of interest and is explicit and repeated about this study's limitations: it is
**prospective but not randomized**, specifically because patient preference for a named treatment made
randomization impractical in her clinical setting; she is candid that she does not have a full explanation for
why recurrence was lower than expected at 24 months, and flags the shifting CCH/PNF treatment ratio over the
study period as a real source of bias rather than omitting it.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `93IWNYYqCjs`** (Warwick's "what we may never know" talk) — Baur's own study is a live
example of exactly the equipoise problem Warwick describes: patients arriving with a treatment preference made
true randomization impractical, precisely the obstacle his talk argues makes valid comparative trials
essentially undoable. **Directly comparable to `oRdE0UKeJF0`** (Van Rijssen's randomized PNF-vs-fasciectomy
trial) and `0MBhLab1KUI` (Peimer's CORDLESS collagenase data) — Baur's 24-month PNF and CCH recurrence figures
sit in the same general range as those other studies' reported rates, though methodology and follow-up length
differ enough that direct numeric comparison should be made cautiously. **Relevant to `R4WPhcOpAMo`**
(Selles's consensus recurrence definition talk) — Baur's own recurrence definition (20+ degrees increase from
a 3-week post-op baseline) is close to but not identical to that consensus definition's 20-degree,
6-week-baseline standard.

management: collagenase injection (technique detail)
percutaneous needle fasciotomy (technique detail)
splinting (static and dynamic) after either procedure

sections.body:
**There is no cure for Dupuytren's contracture, so Pess's stated priority is not a perfect finger but fast,
low-risk functional improvement — which argues for treating early, aggressively, and with minimally invasive
technique rather than waiting.** His opening philosophy: **"achieving perfection is not necessary, though
it's always our goal. Patients appreciate rapid recovery [and] improvement of function... even if the finger
is not perfectly straight"** `[00:00]`. He explicitly rejects the older wait-and-see convention: **"I do not
believe the old paradigm of [waiting until] 30 degrees, and then come back — patients should be treated
early and aggressively,"** ideally **before 45 degrees** of PIP contracture, which he associates with
**higher efficacy, lower recurrence, and less PIP joint scarring.**
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[02:04]` — Confirm a **palpable cord actually causing the contracture** (as opposed to scar or
flexor tendon insufficiency allowing tendon bowstringing to mimic contracture); set **realistic patient
expectations**, using educational materials/videos so patients understand risks regardless of which
technique they choose; and **map every cord with a marker** before injecting, including natatory,
commissural, and ADM cords — all of which sit **superficially, only 2–4mm beneath the skin.** He emphasizes
listing every possible side effect up front: **"if you list them all to the patients, then when they only
get one or two, they're a lot happier"** than surprised by an unmentioned one (his specific example: a
collagenase-related axillary nodule prompting a 3am call).
sections.heading: Shared principles before either procedure

sections.body:
`[02:04]`–`[05:07]` — Confirm the drug is actually in the syringe (visually distinguishing a small air
bubble from an air-filled syringe — "air does not release a cord"). Use adequate local anesthesia (wrist,
palmar, digital, dorsal, or PIP blocks as needed). **Maintain constant tension on the cord** to maximize
bowstringing, and inject at the **point of maximum bowstringing**, angled away from the flexor tendon
sheath. His **pinch-and-poke technique**: pinch the cord between two fingers, palpate it, and inject directly
between them. For wide cords, inject **transversely in a T-shape** rather than the usually-taught
longitudinal approach; for Y-shaped cords, inject at the base and up both limbs to release both fingers with
one dose. The stated **safe zone: 4mm from the proximal digital crease, 2–3mm in depth** — he notes deeper
injection is possible with experience but this is the conservative baseline. Critical safety point: **watch
the distance between the needle hub and skin continuously**, since needles tend to creep deeper during
injection — **if you penetrate dorsally, do not pull back and reinject; withdraw fully and reposition**, to
avoid driving the drug toward the flexor tendon.
sections.heading: Injection technique and the safe zone

sections.body:
`[05:07]`–`[06:10]` — Manipulation is done **24 hours after collagenase injection**, not sooner, since
delay reduces swelling, bruising, and tenderness at the time of manipulation. Skin tears are common —
**averaging 14% in his own experience, up to 22% in multi-center studies** — managed simply, without
sutures. Manipulation should move the finger through **extension, abduction, adduction, pronation, and
supination**, not extension alone, and should include the **adjacent unaffected fingers**, which he says
increases overall release.
sections.heading: Manipulation, 24 hours later

sections.body:
`[06:10]`–`[09:12]` — Using a **20–25 gauge, 5/8-inch needle**, changed frequently — **15–25 needles per
finger** is normal, since dulling needles don't cut well and "you're not looking to save a dollar or two."
Distinguish the anesthesia used for numbing (intradermal, not a nerve block) from procedural blocks, and
maintain constant verbal check-in with the patient ("do you feel an electric shock?") to detect
neurovascular proximity. The needle bevel is kept **perpendicular to the cord** for cutting action; flexing
and extending the finger periodically confirms the needle isn't caught in the flexor tendon. Three named
techniques: **"clear, perforate, and slice."** Narrow lateral and natatory cords in particular respond well
to needling followed by **massage** — "you can feel the crackling and the release" even without a sense of
total mechanical release. After finishing, **reassess the palm proximal to distal** for residual cords
regardless of technique used, and check specifically for a **hidden or retracted cord** if a joint isn't
releasing as expected — Pess describes a recent case where an unsuspected retracted cord was the actual
block to full PIP release.
sections.heading: Needle fasciotomy technique specifics

sections.body:
`[09:12]`–`[10:12]` — Pess states his own splinting practice directly, without claiming it's evidence-based:
**"I'm a splinter. I have no evidence. I splint for three to four months. I admit it, I'm ashamed, even
though I'm in a minority."** Static night splinting is his default; dynamic splinting (per what he calls "the
Philadelphia technique") is added specifically when there's an active extension lag at the PIP suggesting a
stretched central slip. For skin tears/lacerations from either technique, his approach is simple: **no
suture, no graft, no flap — local wound care, can get wet in the shower**, healing within two to five weeks
if kept moist. His memorable rule for an exposed flexor tendon: **"if you don't let it dry, it won't die"**
— keep it moist and it will not be damaged by exposure alone.

Notably candid about the limits of his own evidence: he explicitly labels his 3–4 month splinting practice
as unsupported by evidence ("I have no evidence... I admit it, I'm ashamed"), distinguishing it clearly from
the technique-safety points he presents as learned, reproducible experience. He also states his overall
conclusion modestly: **"there's a couple of bad collagenase cases, [a] couple of bad needle cases — no
matter which technique you use, if you get good at it, you can get phenomenal results,"** avoiding a claim
that either technique is categorically superior.

anatomically. **Complements `MO1w1Ed-Yqc`** (Skirven's hand therapy talk) — Pess's candidly unevidenced

compliance data, Evans's no-tension protocol), a useful contrast between personal practice and published
evidence on the same question. **Consistent with `-jLfWXX3YUM`** (Seven Questions) — Pess's "treat early,
minimally invasive first" philosophy matches Eaton's own stated rationale for starting with minimally
invasive procedures given their lower lifetime complication risk.

patient-perceived recurrence as the outcome measure that actually matters to patients
the Abe risk score used to test for and adjust away that bias
