loss of imprinting as a disease mechanism
oxygen tension as an overlooked culture variable
the need for tissue engineering, computational biology, and epigenetics expertise

sections.body:
**No laboratory in the world currently has a model that reproduces Dupuytren's disease developing over
time — only static snapshots — and O'Gorman argues building one, done properly, requires expertise the
field doesn't yet have enough of: tissue engineering, computational biology, and epigenetics.** He states the
gap candidly, citing a rejected grant review: **"a reviewer... told me, 'Dr. O'Gorman, it's a lovely grant,
you've got all kinds of great data, but all you have are windows in time — you have not shown us that you
have a model in your laboratory that actually shows the development of disease over time.' And they were
right, and I don't think anybody else does either"** `[03:03]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[03:03]`–`[04:04]` — Human cells with **pre-characterized genetics**, grown on **physiologically relevant
extracellular matrices** (his own point from a companion talk), subjected to realistic **biomechanical
stress and biochemical stimuli**, and — flagged as a likely-overlooked variable — **correct oxygen tension**:
**"I find it very, very unlikely that Dupuytren's cords grow at 21% oxygen, [because] very fibrotic tissues...
[are hypoxic] — yet we do all of our analyses at 21% oxygen."** Current tools (he cites a Flex Cell system
his own lab uses) can impose mechanical stress and support 3D culture, and are being adapted toward lower-
oxygen conditions, but still lack a **flowing vascular supply**, sufficient cell density, and adequately
dense collagen to be truly physiological.
sections.heading: What a proper model would require

sections.body:
`[02:01]`–`[06:05]` — **Tissue engineers**, to build reproducible cord models; **computational biologists**,
to handle the scale of modern genomic data (both large population studies like GWAS and deep individual-
patient sequencing); and **epigenetics specialists**, a discipline O'Gorman notes **wasn't discussed at all
at the conference that year**. To illustrate the scale problem concretely: a chromatin immunoprecipitation
sequencing (ChIP-seq) project on just **6 patients, 9 samples**, generated **~2×10⁷ sequence reads per
person**, amounting to **300 gigabytes of raw data — processing to 2 terabytes.** His point: that's the data
burden for six people; scaling to a hundred or a thousand patients isn't currently feasible, but the field
needs to be building toward that capacity.
sections.heading: Three kinds of expertise the field needs

sections.body:
`[08:06]`–`[10:10]` — O'Gorman gives a detailed, concrete example of what epigenetic research can reveal that
genome sequencing alone cannot. Background: most genes are expressed equally from both inherited alleles, but
**about 1% of human genes show "imprinting"** — parent-of-origin-specific expression. At the **IGF2/H19
locus**: on the paternally inherited allele, a methylated insulator region blocks a protein (CTCF) from
binding, allowing **IGF2 to be transcribed**; on the maternally inherited allele, the same region is
unmethylated, **CTCF binds and blocks IGF2 transcription**, so **H19** (a non-coding RNA) is transcribed
instead. Net normal result: **IGF2 is expressed only from the paternal allele.** Screening roughly a dozen
Dupuytren's-diseased cell samples against matched normal palmar fascia from the same patients, O'Gorman's
group found: **9 out of 10 (roughly) diseased samples showed loss of this imprinting** — **IGF2 being
transcribed from *both* alleles** instead of just one, attributed to **abnormal DNA methylation** at the
control region. This is explicitly an **epigenetic event, invisible to standard genome sequencing** — it can
only be detected through dedicated epigenetic assays, not GWAS or exome sequencing.
sections.heading: A striking epigenetic finding: loss of IGF2 imprinting

sections.body:
`[10:10]`–`[11:11]` — O'Gorman closes by naming the interdependence directly: his lab lacks expertise that
colleagues (named as "Rude" [likely Ruud Bank] and Dominic Furniss) have and vice versa; **none of this is
possible without clinical colleagues supplying tissue samples**, funding support, and — explicitly —
**patient community engagement** to help raise both money and awareness for the field.
sections.heading: Why this can't happen without collaboration

sections.body:
None directly — this is a research-infrastructure and epigenetics talk, not a discussion of clinical
presentation.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Genomic imprinting** — parent-of-origin-specific gene expression, affecting roughly 1% of human genes,
  typically involving growth-regulatory genes `[08:06]`.
- **Loss of imprinting** — the specific disease-associated finding here: a normally monoallelically expressed
  gene (IGF2) becoming biallelically expressed due to abnormal DNA methylation `[09:08]`.
- **ChIP-seq (chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing)** — the genome-wide technique used to map protein-DNA
  interactions (here, beta-catenin binding sites) across patient samples `[06:05]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"Windows in time" versus a true developmental model** — O'Gorman's own phrase (via the grant reviewer
  who challenged him) for the gap between current snapshot-based research and what the field actually needs
  `[03:03]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
O'Gorman is unusually candid about a personal setback (a rejected grant, quoted directly rather than
paraphrased favorably) and frames his research priorities explicitly as **his own opinion**, not a
consensus: **"I don't expect this to be representative of every research lab — Dominic will probably have
different thoughts, and Rude will probably have different thoughts."** The IGF2 imprinting finding is
presented with a specific, if modest, sample size (about a dozen matched pairs), appropriately scaled
confidence for a preliminary finding rather than a large validated result.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly extends `6aG_CIYTX8A`** (O'Gorman's own ECM talk, same symposium) — both talks argue current
laboratory methods (plastic culture substrates there, standard oxygen tension here) may be producing
non-physiological, potentially misleading data, and both call for more rigorous, physiologically matched
experimental conditions going forward. **Directly relevant to `-3a_yiOu_3I` and `-0JtjUrrU4o`** (the GWAS
talks) — this talk's emphasis on epigenetics as a layer invisible to standard genome sequencing supplies a
concrete reason why GWAS findings alone (explaining only ~14–16% of heritability per Ophoff's own figures)
would be expected to leave much of Dupuytren's biology unaccounted for. **Directly complements `8Kp5Fz7ZKl0`**
(Raykha's IGF talk, from O'Gorman's own lab, five years earlier) — that talk shows IGFBP6 downregulation
increasing IGF2 bioavailability post-translationally; this talk's imprinting-loss finding increases IGF2
*production* itself, epigenetically — two independent mechanisms converging on the same outcome.

sections.body:
**Dupuytren's contracture is fascia in the palm turning into thickened, static cord tissue that can pull the
fingers into a bent position — it is not curable, and every current treatment removes or breaks the cord
without preventing it from coming back.** `[p.1]`, `[p.2]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

**Fascia is the fibrous tissue that normally covers nerves, blood vessels, muscles, and tendons in the hand,
and stabilizes the skin.** In Dupuytren's disease, "this fascia can become abnormal. It becomes thicker,
forming cords." The source is explicit about what distinguishes a cord from a tendon: "Unlike a tendon that
is moved by a muscle that shortens and lengthens, cord tissue is not connected to a muscle. Cord tissue is
static and does not move."

**There may be one cord or several, separate or connected**, and most people also develop **nodules or
bumps** in the hand. Course is unpredictable: "these nodules and cords may not change for a long time. They
can also have a slow or fast change."
sections.heading: What it is

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

The source states the cause plainly as unresolved: **"The exact cause of Dupuytren's contracture is unknown
and very complex."** What is stated as known:

- **It is a hereditary disease** — "family history and ancestry play a role."
- **More common** in men, people over age 40, and people of Northern European descent.
- **Less common** in African and Middle Eastern descent.
- **Related**: smoking, diabetes, alcohol, lower body mass index, and aging.
- **Not related**: "There is no evidence that hand injuries or specific jobs lead to a higher risk of
  developing Dupuytren's contracture." A mild relationship to trauma is allowed only for someone already at
  risk, and occasionally "after a distal radius (wrist) fracture, a patient may develop a single nodule in
  the palm" that "often does not progress to result in a bent finger joint."
sections.heading: Who is affected

sections.body:
`[p.1]`–`[p.2]`

Symptoms are **"lumps, nodules, and bands or cords on the palmar side of the hands,"** firm and stuck to the
skin, with the skin itself often thicker and puckered. The source's own analogy for this: **"Think of the
Dupuytren's palm skin like a road. Some areas are swollen and puffy like a speed bump. In other areas the
skin is puckered and pulled down like a pothole."**

**The ring finger and little finger are most commonly involved**, either hand can be affected, and each hand
can progress on its own pattern and timeline. **It is usually not painful**, though lumps can be uncomfortable
in some people. It's often first noticed as **difficulty placing the hand flat on a surface** (the tabletop
test, Figure 3) or opening the hand fully — with downstream effects on washing hands, wearing gloves, holding
large objects, using pockets, and (if the right hand is involved) shaking hands.

**Severity is hard to predict**, but the source names concrete risk markers: earlier age of onset predicts
more severe disease; men develop more severe symptoms than women; more affected relatives predicts higher
risk; and involvement elsewhere in the body — **"called Dupuytren's diathesis"** — also predicts higher risk.
That elsewhere-involvement can appear as **plantar fibromatosis** (soles of the feet), **Peyronie's disease**
(the genital location, in men), or a **knuckle pad (or Garrod's pad)** on top of the knuckles.
sections.heading: How it's noticed and how severe it gets

sections.body:
`[p.2]`

**Not every palm lump is Dupuytren's**, so the source recommends a hand surgeon examination. "Sometimes a
history and examination is all that is needed," and imaging (x-ray, ultrasound, or MRI) is used at other
times. Factors weighed: **size, "feel," location, presence of pain, movement of the mass or skin around it,
family history, and other medical conditions.**
sections.heading: Evaluation

sections.body:
`[p.2]`–`[p.3]`

Two office-based options, both described as *reducing* the cord rather than removing it:

| Option | What happens | Recovery | Recurrence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Needle fasciotomy (needle aponeurotomy)** | Local numbing, then a needle cuts the cord in several places below the skin; the hand is then slowly stretched to break the cord | "Only a few days" | **"Roughly one third of patients will see the cord eventually come back after this procedure"** |
| **Collagenase injection** | Two visits: an injectable drug dissolves the cord at visit one; at visit two the numbed hand is stretched to break the cord | "Only a few days to a few weeks" | **"One third of patients will see the cord come back"** |

Both can cause small skin tears that heal over a few weeks, and both are explicitly stated to **not remove
the cord fully from below the skin** — which the source ties directly to the recurrence figure it gives for
each. Splinting and therapy may follow either, aimed at keeping the hand straight and rebuilding the ability
to make a fist.
sections.heading: Nonsurgical treatment

sections.body:
`[p.3]`

Two procedures, distinguished by how much tissue is removed:

- **Fasciotomy** — the tight cords are cut but not removed. "This is less invasive as only a small cut or
  cuts are used," but **"because all the tissue is not removed, there is possibly a higher chance the
  contracture could return."**
- **Fasciectomy** — cuts the cords *and* removes as much of the nodule, cords, and diseased skin as needed.
  "This often has longer wounds with more extensive dissection."

Surgery is outpatient/same-day, under a variety of anesthesia approaches, with either stitched or
intentionally-open wounds to reduce recurrence risk. **Fasciectomy recovery is about 6 weeks**, with hand use
continuing during that time, and the source frames post-surgical effort as directly determining outcome:
**"The more the patient does soon after surgery, the more successful the final result will be."** Waiting too
long to start therapy "may result in stiffness."
sections.heading: Surgical treatment

sections.body:
- **Firm lumps or nodules in the palm, stuck to the skin** `[p.1]`.
- **Thickened, puckered palm skin** ("speed bump" / "pothole" pattern) `[p.1]`.
- **A cord running from the palm into a finger, pulling it toward the palm** `[p.1]`.
- **Inability to lay the hand flat on a table, or open it fully** `[p.2]`.
- **Difficulty washing hands, wearing gloves, holding large objects, using pockets, or shaking hands** `[p.2]`.
- **Lumps on the soles of the feet, or thickening on the knuckles, alongside hand symptoms** `[p.2]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Cord** — thickened, non-contractile fascia; "not connected to a muscle... static and does not move" `[p.1]`.
- **Dupuytren's diathesis** — a pattern of disease appearing elsewhere in the body (feet, genitals, knuckles)
  alongside the hand, associated with more severe disease `[p.2]`.
- **Needle fasciotomy / needle aponeurotomy** — an in-office needle procedure that cuts the cord without
  removing it `[p.2]`.
- **Fasciectomy** — surgical removal of the cord, nodule, and affected skin, as distinct from a fasciotomy
  that only cuts the cord `[p.3]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: - **"Think of the Dupuytren's palm skin like a road... a speed bump... a pothole"** `[p.1]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
This is a patient-education handout from a professional hand-surgery society, not a study — its hedges are
plain-language limits on certainty rather than statistical caveats, and they are preserved here rather than
smoothed into confidence the source does not claim:

- **Cause: "unknown and very complex"** `[p.1]`.
- **Course: "It is difficult to predict how the disease will progress"** `[p.2]`.
- **Cure: "Even with treatment, the disease is not fully curable. The nodules and cords may come back in the
  same or a different location"** `[p.2]`.
- **Both nonsurgical options are stated with a specific, matching recurrence figure (roughly one third)**,
  and both are explicitly described as not removing the cord fully `[p.2]`–`[p.3]`.
- **Surgical improvement is stated as not guaranteed to last**: "this improvement may not maintained forever"
  [sic in source] `[p.3]`.
- **Splinting/stretching is explicitly stated as non-preventive**: "typically does not prevent worsening of
  the contracture but is safe to try" `[p.2]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges closely with `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`**, which independently states needle fasciotomy's
recurrence at "approximately 50% at 3 to 5 years" — consistent with this source's "roughly one third" for
both nonsurgical options, though NICE's figure runs somewhat higher; both agree recurrence, not cure, is the
realistic expectation. **Converges with `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review` and
`shaheen-2025-treatment-comparison-review`**, both of which independently rank needle-based treatment as
recurring more than collagenase, and collagenase more than surgical fasciectomy — the same ordering this
source's "roughly one third" figure for both nonsurgical options (without distinguishing between them) is
consistent with, once the sharper split is available. **Converges with `girft-bssh-dupuytrens-pathway`**,
whose surgical referral threshold (30° at the MCPJ or 20° at the PIPJ) gives the precise numeric version of
what this source states only qualitatively as "the contracture prevents the hand from lying flat on a
table."
sections.heading: Conflicts with other sources

concepts: central slip attenuation and its correlation with preoperative joint angle
falsifiability as a standard for surgical practice (Russell's teapot versus the Higgs boson)
the counterintuitive finding that gentler technique outperformed aggressive technique on severe cases
management: digital fasciectomy, followed stepwise by gentle passive manipulation, volar plate release, accessory collateral ligament release, and central slip treatment as needed

sections.body:
**Most PIP joint surgery in Dupuytren's is practiced like Bertrand Russell's unfalsifiable teapot rather
than like real science — and Smith proposes a stepwise algorithm instead, where each step has an
observable, testable consequence before moving to the next.** His framing: **"a lot of the clinical work in
Dupuytren's is up there with the teapots"** rather than being put to observable test like the search for the
Higgs boson `[01:05]`–`[02:06]`. His single most counterintuitive finding: **"if you start at the top with
manipulation alone... [that means] taking the most severe patients and getting the best results — and the
more aggressive we became, the less successful and effective we were"** `[11:27]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[03:07]`–`[10:24]` — Presented as a strict sequence, each step attempted only if the prior one fails to
achieve full extension:

1. **Digital fasciectomy** — limited fasciectomy via linear incision converted to multiple Z-plasties,
   combined with open palm technique; care taken around the **spiral cord's displacement of the nerve**;
   **lateral bands are freed from adhesions** (always present, both to the dorsum of the proximal phalanx
   and to dorsal skin) and tested by pulling to see if they extend the joint.
2. **Gentle passive manipulation** — flexing the MP joint, then gently leaning on the PIP joint for about
   two minutes. **Periarticular adhesions reliably respond to this alone.**
3. **Volar plate release** (± tendon sheath) — if a volar contracture remains, released through the
   posterior surface of the volar plate with a Beaver blade, turned 90 degrees, cut to bone; a
   low-exposure technique.
4. **Accessory collateral ligament release** — checked next by testing joint stability: a finger that
   "snaps" into flexion or extension rather than holding position mid-range indicates a tight accessory
   collateral ligament over the condyle, treated by releasing it.
5. **Central slip check and treatment** — via what Smith calls testing for central slip attenuation
   (flexing the wrist and MP joints together and checking for passive PIP extension) — if the digit still
   "lies in flexion" despite being otherwise fully correctable, this is the cause.
6. **Conjoined lateral band check** — full passive DIP flexion is confirmed last, to rule out tightness in
   the conjoined lateral bands (seen as DIP hyperextension), treated by Fowler's procedure or, occasionally,
   gentle manipulation alone.
sections.heading: The algorithm, step by step

sections.body:
`[07:14]`–`[09:18]` — Across **188 PIP joint contractures** studied: **113 resolved with digital fasciectomy
alone**; **75 required an additional PIP joint procedure**; and of those 75, **54 (72%) had central slip
attenuation.** Severity predicted this strongly: **if the preoperative joint angle exceeded 60 degrees, 80%
of those patients had central slip attenuation.** Smith is direct about the consequence of missing this:
**"if you ignore that, your patients will just immediately go into that position after operation."**
Treatment for an intact central slip allows immediate mobilization and standard night splinting; an
attenuated central slip instead requires **three weeks of static splinting followed by three weeks of
[dynamic/tapered] splinting.**
sections.heading: Central slip attenuation is far more common than expected

sections.body:
`[10:24]`–`[11:27]` — Outcome breakdown from their patient series: the **vast majority required no PIP
joint procedure at all**; **8% responded to gentle passive manipulation**; **5% required accessory
collateral ligament release**; **10% required volar plate tenotomy**; **9% required tendon sheath release**;
a small number required joint capsule release. Notably, **3% had extensor tendon repair and 2% had the PIP
joint K-wired** — procedures Smith now explicitly disavows: **"these are things I would never do now,"**
describing that period candidly as **"a reflection of early insanity."** Restated with current practice, the
manipulation-alone group grows to roughly **13%** once the abandoned procedures' former candidates are
redirected to gentler management. Reviewing outcomes by contracture severity confirmed the core finding: **the
gentlest technique (manipulation alone) produced the best results even on the most severe patients**, while
escalating aggressiveness correlated with worse outcomes.
sections.heading: What actually got used, and what they abandoned

sections.body:
- **A PIP joint that fails to fully extend despite apparently complete fasciectomy**, worked through via
  the staged algorithm rather than treated as a single undifferentiated problem `[05:10]`.
- **A "snapping" finger** — instability flicking between flexion and extension rather than holding
  mid-range position — as the specific sign of a tight accessory collateral ligament `[06:13]`.
- **A digit that passively straightens but persistently "lies in flexion"** — the specific sign of central
  slip attenuation, distinguished from other causes of incomplete correction `[07:14]`.
- **DIP joint hyperextension with tight conjoined lateral bands**, limiting full DIP flexion `[09:18]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Central slip attenuation** — stretching/weakening of the central extensor slip from prolonged PIP
  flexion, tested for by flexing the wrist and MP joints and checking passive PIP extension `[07:14]`.
- **Conjoined lateral bands (tightness)** — a cause of DIP extension limitation distinct from the cord
  itself, checked last in the algorithm and treated by Fowler's procedure `[09:18]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Bertrand Russell's orbiting teapot versus the search for the Higgs boson** — an extended, memorable
  framing for the difference between an unfalsifiable claim and a properly testable one, applied directly to
  surgical decision-making `[00:03]`–`[02:06]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Unusually candid about past mistakes: Smith names two abandoned procedures directly (extensor tendon repair,
K-wiring) and calls the period he used them **"early insanity,"** rather than omitting or softening this
history. The central slip attenuation figures (72% of PIP-procedure patients, 80% above 60 degrees) are
presented as measured findings from a defined patient series (188 joints), not estimates.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly corroborates and extends `iD3mYMmfN-Q`** (Eaton's anatomy talk), which separately identifies
central slip stretching and lateral band changes as causes of early lost correction — this talk supplies the
specific stepwise clinical algorithm and quantified attenuation rates (72%/80%) behind that anatomical
description. **Directly relevant to `1BURdqs3a4U`** (Pess's technique talk), whose dynamic splinting practice
for "an active extension lag... probably a stretched central slip" matches this talk's specific splinting
protocol (three weeks static, three weeks dynamic) for the same finding. **Complements `L3kjpUIwHIQ`**
(Leclercq's severe PIP contracture talk), which uses a similarly named "Tubiana disease test" for extensor
slackening — likely testing the same underlying central slip problem from a related angle, worth treating as
convergent evidence rather than two separate findings.

management: concurrent double-dose collagenase (CCH) injection, two joints treated 24-72 hours apart in the same hand

sections.body:
**In a 714-patient efficacy analysis across 1,448 joints, injecting two collagenase doses in the same hand
within 24–72 hours of each other reduced contracture by 74% overall, with efficacy and safety broadly similar
to single-dose historical data — except for a higher rate of skin laceration (22%) — and no evidence of
greater overall risk from treating two joints concurrently rather than one at a time.** Badalamente states the
conclusion directly: **"the concurrent administration of collagenase in the same hand decreased total
contracture and increased range of motion, and efficacy and safety were similar to prior studies, although the
skin lacerations at finger manipulation were higher... there doesn't appear to be a greater risk of using the
two doses concurrently as compared to one dose"** `[06:18]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:01]`–`[01:06]` — This talk reports the trial data underlying the double-dose approach discussed
clinically in a companion talk by Dr. Pess (see `1BURdqs3a4U` for his related percutaneous fasciotomy/
collagenase technique talk). **56 sites** enrolled patients with **two or more contractures of at least 20
degrees, affecting at least two joints in the same hand.** Patients received **up to 0.58mg collagenase per
injection**, with the second injection given **24–72 hours after the first**, followed by manipulation and a
**31-day follow-up.** Outcomes tracked: change in flexion contracture from baseline, range of motion, clinical
success (defined, per prior trial convention, as essentially a straight finger), clinical improvement (greater
than 50% contracture reduction), and adverse events.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[02:07]`–`[03:11]` — **714 patients analyzed for efficacy, across 1,448 joints (896 MP, 552 PIP)**. Overall
contracture reduction across all treated joints: **74%.** Broken down by joint-pair combination:

| Joint pairing | Mean contracture reduction |
|---|---|
| **Two MP joints, different fingers** | 84% |
| **Two PIP joints, different fingers** | 61% |
| **One MP + one PIP, different fingers** | 68% |
| **One MP + one PIP, same finger** (largest sample) | 72% |

Significant increases in total range of motion were seen across all joint-pair combinations. Overall clinical
**success** (straight finger) rates: **64% for MP joints, 28% for PIP joints** — notably lower for PIP than
the roughly 40% single-joint PIP success rate reported in the original CORD I trial (`OwSS6grbMAc`), a
comparison Badalamente does not explicitly draw but which is directly relevant. Clinical **improvement**
(>50% contracture reduction): **89% for MP joints, 71% for PIP joints.**
sections.heading: Results by joint pairing

sections.body:
`[04:12]`–`[05:15]` — Badalamente notes the FDA specifically requires surveying patients' own perception of
treatment, not just objective clinical measures — most patients in this study reported being **either very or
quite satisfied.** She frames this as important context for interpreting the strict >50%-reduction success
metric: a contracture reduction that falls short of that strict threshold can still leave a patient satisfied
if their hand feels functional to them in practice.
sections.heading: Patient satisfaction

sections.body:
`[05:15]`–`[06:18]` — Several case examples are shown, including a PIP-contracture case on the ring and small
fingers, a more complex case, and one patient with prior surgery. On safety: **skin laceration incidence was
somewhat higher (22%)** than typically reported for single-dose injections, echoing a point Badalamente notes
was also raised in Dr. Pess's companion talk — but this was the specific, isolated safety difference found;
no broader increase in risk was observed from treating two joints concurrently compared to treating one joint
at a time.
sections.heading: Case examples and safety

sections.body:
`[06:18]`–`[07:19]` — Badalamente notes this concurrent, double-dose approach was approved by the **US Food
and Drug Administration in 2014**, described as a very recent approval at the time of this talk, and frames
the practical benefit as allowing **more rapid treatment of two affected joints** rather than requiring
sequential, separately-scheduled single-joint treatment sessions.
sections.heading: Regulatory context

sections.body:
- **Skin laceration during finger manipulation**, specifically identified as elevated (22%) relative to
  single-dose historical safety data — the one clear safety trade-off of the concurrent approach `[06:18]`.
- **Patient-perceived hand functionality**, tracked separately from the strict clinical-success contracture
  threshold, per FDA-required patient-reported outcome surveying `[04:12]`.

against the more favorable patient satisfaction data, without claiming the two measures tell the same story.

`OwSS6grbMAc`** (Badalamente's own CORD I single-joint collagenase trial talk) — this double-dose study's

specifically. **Relevant to `-PUJvVwlJis`** (Dias's MCID talk) — this talk's own point about patient

the gap between statistically/clinically defined outcome measures and patient-perceived benefit that Dias's

concepts: propensity score matching as a technique for balancing observational study groups
separating vibration exposure from confounding hand trauma, and why that separation couldn't be fully achieved here
vibration measured continuously (hours per week times years) rather than as a simple yes/no exposure

sections.body:
**Studying elderly Dutch field hockey players — chosen specifically because their vibration exposure comes
from leisure sport rather than occupation — Broekstra's group found a statistically significant, dose-
dependent association between hand vibration exposure and Dupuytren's disease.** She states the core result
directly: **"based on these data, we can say that vibration is significantly associated with DD in this
sample, and we were able to show a dose-response relation, which is in line with some previous studies"**
`[03:03]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[01:01]` — Vibration is a frequently cited risk factor in the Dupuytren's literature, but Broekstra
notes nearly all prior studies focus on **occupational** vibration exposure — overlooking that hands are also
exposed to vibration during leisure and sports activities. **Elderly male field hockey players** (Dutch field
hockey, played on grass, not the ice hockey more familiar to American/Canadian audiences) were chosen as a
study population specifically to isolate non-occupational vibration exposure.
sections.heading: Why field hockey players

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[03:03]` — **170 elderly male field hockey players** and a control group drawn from a colleague's
(Lanting's) existing dataset were recruited; **manual workers and vibration-exposed controls were excluded**
from both groups. The resulting groups were substantially unbalanced on baseline characteristics, so
**propensity score matching** was used — balancing on age, diabetes, smoking, and alcohol use, with 1:1
matching without replacement — reducing the sample to **40 matched pairs (80 participants total)**. Vibration
exposure itself was measured **continuously, as hours per week multiplied by years of exposure**, rather than
the simple yes/no dichotomy used in most prior literature. Broekstra shows descriptive statistics before and
after matching: before matching, the two groups differed on **almost every variable**; after matching, **most
differences disappeared**, at the cost of losing a substantial number of cases — an expected trade-off of the
matching method, with any differences remaining after matching interpreted as likely related to the exposure
itself rather than confounding.
sections.heading: Study design and matching

sections.body:
`[03:03]`–`[04:04]` — Multiple logistic regression, controlling for the propensity score:

- **Vibration as a dichotomous factor**: odds ratio **3.95**, statistically significant.
- **Vibration as a continuous factor** (hours/week × years): odds ratio **1.006** per unit, still statistically
  significant — demonstrating a **dose-response relationship** consistent with prior studies.
sections.heading: Results

sections.body:
`[04:04]`–`[05:06]` — Broekstra is explicit that **the role of concomitant hand trauma remains unclear**: the
study did ask participants about hand trauma, but most had difficulty recalling exactly what happened or which
hand/finger was affected, making the variable **too unreliable to include in the analysis.** She also notes
the study lacks any **biomechanical data on what actually happens in the hand during field hockey play** —
meaning the observed effect might partly reflect **hand trauma from play, not vibration exposure alone.** Data
gathered by interview also carries a general **recall bias** risk.
sections.heading: Limitations acknowledged directly

sections.body:
`[04:04]` — Field hockey is described as an elitist sport in the Netherlands, meaning nearly every participant
was a **white-collar worker** — producing an unusually **homogeneous, non-occupational vibration exposure
group**, minimizing confounding from occupational vibration specifically. All participants were **physically
examined by experienced physicians**, and propensity score matching was used deliberately to balance otherwise
very unequal groups.
sections.heading: Strengths acknowledged directly

sections.body:
None beyond the presence and severity of Dupuytren's disease itself, tracked as the primary study outcome
rather than as individual symptoms `[01:01]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Propensity score matching** — a statistical technique for balancing two observational study groups on
  measured confounders, used here to compare hockey players and controls fairly `[01:01]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None stated — the talk presents epidemiological study design and results directly.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Broekstra is unusually direct about limitations that could undermine her own headline finding: she explicitly
flags that concomitant hand trauma during hockey play could confound the vibration-DD association, and states
outright the study cannot rule this out due to the lack of biomechanical data and unreliable trauma recall.
She frames the sample's homogeneity (white-collar, non-occupational) as a genuine strength while still
flagging recall bias as a real limitation of interview-gathered data, rather than presenting the study as
methodologically flawless.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Relevant to `HE6nBpteAAo`** (Rayan's risk factor talk) and any other note discussing vibration or trauma as
a Dupuytren's risk factor — this talk supplies a methodologically distinct (non-occupational, dose-quantified)
line of evidence for vibration specifically, while explicitly flagging that this evidence cannot yet fully
separate vibration's effect from concomitant hand trauma. **Relevant to `rNihCBbmTx8`** (Lanting's Dupuytren
disease clusters talk) — this study's control group is drawn from Lanting's existing dataset, making that talk
a natural companion for understanding the broader population this control group was sampled from.

management: candidate anti-fibrotic drugs tested in lab models (interferon alpha-2b, interferon gamma, TGF-beta 3, tamoxifen)

sections.body:
**Dupuytren's shares its underlying molecular biology with a whole family of fibrotic conditions — keloids,
hypertrophic burn scars, rhinophyma, breast implant capsular contracture — closely enough that Robson's lab
models built for one reliably reproduce the same findings across all of them, and TGF-beta remains the
central shared target.** His framing: **"if we've taken tissue from all those conditions [and] put them in
the laboratory models... we get very similar results, and that allows us... to come up with some potential
molecular treatments for each of these conditions"** `[01:06]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:07]`–`[04:09]` — Robson cites a decades-old transplant experiment (attributed to "Ashley"): fibroblasts
taken from **keloid-forming patients and transplanted into non-keloid-formers did not produce keloids**;
fibroblasts taken from **non-keloid-formers and transplanted into keloid-formers did produce keloids.** His
interpretation: the fibroblast itself may not be the disease's root cause — **"it's an end organ... many
things are telling that fibroblast what to do"** — meaning effective molecular targets may lie in whatever
is signaling the fibroblast, not in the cell type itself. Across every fibrotic condition his lab has
studied, one shared finding stands out: **"an overexpression or dysregulated activation of TGF-beta appears
to be directly related"** to the fibrotic outcome, a point he traces to Mark Ferguson's original 1989
observation, which he says has only accumulated more supporting data since.
sections.heading: The fibroblast may be an "end organ," not the culprit

sections.body:
`[04:09]`–`[05:12]` — Of the three TGF-beta isoforms, **1 and 2 are fibrogenic; 3 is not** (Ferguson has
since built a company around TGF-beta 3 as a therapeutic direction). Comparing Dupuytren's cord tissue
against palmar aponeurosis from carpal tunnel patients (as a non-diseased control), Robson reports **TGF-beta
2 was "dramatically increased"** — more so, in his lab's data, than TGF-beta 1, though **both fibrogenic
isoforms were elevated.**
sections.heading: TGF-beta 2, specifically, in Dupuytren's tissue

sections.body:
`[05:12]`–`[10:22]` — **Fibroblast-populated collagen lattices (FPCLs)**: fibroblasts from Dupuytren's
tissue versus matched carpal-tunnel-derived control fibroblasts, embedded in a collagen gel and tracked for
contraction over 5 days. Dupuytren's-derived fibroblasts showed **markedly increased contraction** — and
Robson notes the same bar-graph pattern appears for keloids, burn hypertrophic scars, and capsular
contracture, **"and I cannot tell you which one is due to Dupuytren's versus which ones [are] due to the
others."**

The more novel contribution is an **in vivo nude rat explant model**, developed because no satisfactory
animal model exists for these human-only fibrotic conditions (a Duroc pig model was tried and abandoned; a
newer "red Duroc pig" model from a Seattle group is noted but not corroborated by his own experience).
Human Dupuytren's tissue is transplanted into a nude rat on a **surgically isolated flap with a single
artery and single vein**, deliberately severed from local lymphatics — allowing the explanted human tissue
to be perfused directly and pharmacologically manipulated while remaining alive. Robson reports this tissue
**persists for at least a year**, confirmed still human via **factor VIII monoclonal antibody staining of
the endothelial cells** at the one-year mark, and can be serially biopsied and cultured throughout.
sections.heading: Two lab models, applied identically across conditions

sections.body:
`[11:25]`–`[13:27]` — Perfusing the explanted tissue with **TGF-beta 2 alone** for 10 days produced clear
increases in fibroblast proliferation kinetics, DNA production, and collagen I/III content at a 30-day
biopsy — **reversed back to control levels when a TGF-beta 2 antibody was co-administered.** The effect had
mostly worn off by 60 days, consistent with the 10-day perfusion window rather than a permanent change.
sections.heading: What perfusion experiments in that model showed

sections.body:
`[13:27]` — Investigating *why* TGF-beta exposure increases fibroblast numbers, Robson's group found
**TGF-beta-treated tissue showed decreased apoptotic protein markers and increased anti-apoptotic nuclear
markers** compared to controls — proposing that **TGF-beta doesn't just stimulate fibroblast proliferation,
it also suppresses fibroblast programmed cell death**, allowing an already-larger fibroblast population to
persist and keep producing scar tissue.
sections.heading: Why: a proposed apoptosis mechanism

sections.body:
`[14:29]`–`[15:29]` — Among several candidate anti-fibrotic treatments tested across these models
(interferon alpha-2b, interferon gamma, TGF-beta 3), Robson specifically tested **tamoxifen** in the
Dupuytren's FPCL system: adding tamoxifen **inhibited the increased contraction** seen in Dupuytren's-derived
fibroblast lattices, and **directly decreased the amount of TGF-beta 1 and 2 measured in the culture
supernatant.** This supplies a specific proposed mechanism for a clinical finding reported elsewhere in this
symposium.
sections.heading: Testing tamoxifen directly in the model

sections.body:
None directly — this is laboratory mechanism and model-validation science, not a discussion of patient
symptoms.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Fibroblast as "end organ"** — Robson's framing that the fibroblast may be responding to disease
  signals rather than generating them independently, based on the classic keloid transplant experiment
  `[02:07]`.
- **Nude rat explant model** — the isolated single-artery/single-vein flap technique keeping live human
  fibrotic tissue viable and perfusable for pharmacological study over roughly a year `[08:16]`.
- **TGF-beta isoform specificity** — the distinction between fibrogenic isoforms (1, 2) and the
  non-fibrogenic isoform (3) `[04:09]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None stated — the talk presents experimental design and results directly.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Robson is explicit that Dupuytren's own cause remains unknown despite the shared-mechanism findings:
**"the etiology obviously is still not totally known"** `[15:29]`. He also flags a specific disagreement
with a competing animal model in the literature (the "red Duroc pig," reported successful by a Seattle
group) without dismissing it outright — **"that's not been our experience"** — rather than asserting his
own model is uniquely correct. The TGF-beta 1-versus-2 relative importance is stated as his own
interpretation ("I happen to think it's more important [than] beta 1") rather than a settled conclusion.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly supplies the mechanism behind `-OKFB6sX_64`** (Degreef's tamoxifen trial) — Degreef's clinical
trial found tamoxifen reduced post-surgical recurrence but didn't explain why; this talk shows tamoxifen
inhibiting Dupuytren's fibroblast contraction and lowering TGF-beta levels directly in a lab model, a
plausible mechanistic account for that clinical result. **Extends `dsPwSUDrz1Y`** (Phan's mechanism talk)
and **`Fj5WfRonTOg`** (Hart's collagen biology primer) — both describe TGF-beta's role in myofibroblast
differentiation from other tissue models; this talk adds a proposed **apoptosis-suppression** mechanism not
covered in either, plus a genuinely novel in vivo model neither talk uses. **Relevant to `x_vecaIme58`** and
**`oXR_NOAaSa0`** (the radiotherapy talks), which describe radiation's mechanism as also TGF-beta-mediated —
consistent with this talk's broader claim that TGF-beta sits at the center of most viable Dupuytren's
treatment strategies, whatever the delivery method.

sections.body:
**In a randomized trial of 302 patients, surgery produced significantly less progression in the treated
finger than either needle fasciotomy or collagenase injection over 2 years — but none of the treatments
changed how likely progression was in fingers that weren't treated** `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶5]`

This is a **finger-level analysis from the DETECT (Dupuytren Treatment Effectiveness Trial) dataset**,
covering **302 participants and 423 initially treated fingers**. Progression was defined precisely, not left
to judgment: **"an increase in contracture angle between 3 months and 2 years after treatment."** The
analysis deliberately separates three finger categories — the treated finger itself, an adjacent untreated
finger, and all untreated fingers — to see whether treating one finger has any spillover effect on others.
sections.heading: The trial design

sections.body:
`[¶6]`

Follow-up was strong: **279 of 302 participants (92%) completed 3-month measurements, and 274 (91%) completed
2-year measurements.** In treated fingers, **surgery resulted in significantly less progression than needle
fasciotomy** (mean difference 9.7°, 95% CI 3.7 to 16°) **and less than collagenase injection** (mean
difference 6.0°, 95% CI 0.1 to 12°), with fewer retreatments needed after surgery. Critically, **"no
between-group differences were observed in adjacent untreated or all untreated fingers"** — treating one
finger surgically doesn't appear to protect, or otherwise affect, the fingers left alone. Risk factors
identified for progression or retreatment, regardless of which treatment was used: **younger age at
treatment, smoking, a dominantly-affected proximal interphalangeal joint, and involvement of the little
finger.**
sections.heading: What it found

sections.body:
- **Increase in contracture angle over time**, defined as the trial's specific progression measure, tracked
  separately in treated versus untreated fingers `[¶5]`.
- **Retreatment need**, tracked as a downstream consequence of progression `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **DETECT (Dupuytren Treatment Effectiveness Trial)** — the source trial this finger-level analysis draws
  its data from `[¶5]`.
- **Finger-level analysis** — analysing outcomes per finger rather than per patient, which is what lets this
  study separate treated-finger effects from any effect on untreated fingers in the same hand `[¶5]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None — outcomes are reported as measured angles and confidence intervals.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The authors are explicit about which claim their data does and doesn't support: **"Surgery offers more
durable results in treated fingers compared with percutaneous methods, although progression and retreatment
rates in untreated fingers are similar across all treatment groups"** — i.e., don't extend the treated-finger
finding to imply any protective effect elsewhere in the hand `[¶7]`. They translate the risk-factor findings
into a specific counseling recommendation: **"Patients at higher risk for progression (ie, young smokers with
affected little fingers) may benefit most from surgery"** `[¶7]`. A funding and conflict-of-interest
disclosure is stated directly: **"The authors have no financial relationships or conflicts of interest to
declare. This study has been funded by the Research Council of Finland"** `[¶7]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Converges with both `shaheen-2025-treatment-comparison-review` and `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`**
on the same directional finding — surgery/fasciectomy holds its result better than needle- or
injection-based treatment — reached here from a single randomized trial rather than pooled study data, which
is a stronger form of the same evidence. **Extends `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review`'s finding that
PIP-joint contractures recur more than MCP-joint ones**: this trial identifies "dominantly affected proximal
interphalangeal joint" as an independent risk factor for progression specifically, naming the same joint as a
risk marker through a different outcome measure (progression angle, not binary recurrence).

concepts: keratinocyte-to-dermis signaling as a driver of fibrotic thickening
myofibroblasts as active participants in angiogenesis, not just matrix contraction
self-assembly tissue engineering as an in-vitro model that behaves like in vivo tissue

sections.body:
**Using a tissue-engineered skin model, Moulin's lab found that keratinocytes from hypertrophic scar tissue
secrete a factor — identified as tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (TIMP-1) — that by itself is enough
to make the underlying dermis grow thicker, and separately, that myofibroblasts (more than ordinary
fibroblasts) actively promote new capillary network formation, a role not previously appreciated for this
cell type.** Her closing summary states the throughline directly: **"interactions between numerous cell
populations contribute to normal and pathological tissue formation, and these parameters have to be thought
[of] when we study this different pathology"** `[09:18]`.

Note: this talk is framed throughout around **hypertrophic scarring**, not Dupuytren's disease by name — its
relevance to this library is that myofibroblasts are the shared pathological cell type central to both
conditions, and the talk was presented at this symposium on that basis.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:06]`–`[02:09]` — Moulin's lab uses a **self-assembly tissue engineering model**: dermal fibroblasts are
cultured with ascorbate so they build their own extracellular matrix into a sheet; keratinocytes are then
added on top, and once confluent, the skin/dermis interface is raised to air to mature the epidermis. The
stated advantage over standard cell culture: **cells experience conditions closer to those found in vivo**
`[00:06]`.
sections.heading: The tissue-engineering method

sections.body:
`[02:09]`–`[06:15]` — Two myofibroblast populations were compared (isolated from hypertrophic scar versus
normal wound), each paired with either hypertrophic-scar-derived or normal keratinocytes. Trichrome staining
showed: **regardless of which dermal (myofibroblast) population was used, adding hypertrophic-scar
keratinocytes produced a measurably thicker dermis than adding normal keratinocytes** `[03:10]`. Screening
keratinocyte culture supernatants by two-dimensional electrophoresis identified a protein spot present
strongly in hypertrophic-scar keratinocyte secretions and weak or absent in normal keratinocyte secretions;
sequencing identified it as **tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 (TIMP1)** — a protein that inhibits
matrix metalloproteinases/collagenase and has separately been shown to stimulate cell growth and inhibit
apoptosis `[04:12]`. ELISA confirmed **elevated TIMP1 in hypertrophic-scar keratinocyte supernatant**, both in
monolayer culture and in the full skin-equivalent model. Adding TIMP1 directly to a normal-keratinocyte skin
equivalent **reproduced the thickened-dermis effect seen with hypertrophic-scar keratinocytes**, and biopsy
findings from actual hypertrophic scar versus normal skin confirmed **higher keratinocyte-secreted TIMP1
in vivo** as well. Moulin's stated takeaway: hypertrophic scarring is usually thought of as primarily a dermal
pathology, but this shows **keratinocytes play a significant role in driving fibrosis formation** `[06:15]`.
sections.heading: Keratinocyte-driven dermal thickening

sections.body:
`[06:15]`–`[09:18]` — A second model used a **fibrin gel** (representing the earliest wound-healing
provisional matrix), combining endothelial cells with either normal fibroblasts or myofibroblasts (normal- or
hypertrophic-scar-derived), assessed at 40 days for capillary-like network formation and quantified as an
**angiogenic index**. Results: endothelial cells alone formed only a weak capillary-like network; adding
mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts or myofibroblasts) increased the angiogenic index; **adding myofibroblasts —
and especially hypertrophic-scar-derived myofibroblasts — produced a significantly stronger increase than
plain fibroblasts.** Moulin frames the novelty explicitly: it was already known fibroblasts could support
capillary formation, but **"it's very new that myofibroblasts can have a role during the angiogenesis"**
`[08:17]` — myofibroblasts had previously been understood mainly for their role in matrix contraction, not
in promoting new vessel growth.

management: post-surgical night splinting, tested against hand therapy alone across three randomized trials

sections.body:
**Arguing the "no benefit" side of a formal debate, Chojnowski presents three randomized trials — his own
SCoRD study, a similarly designed Collis study, and a stricter Dutch study with no crossover allowed — that
together found no statistically significant benefit to adding night splinting to routine hand therapy after
surgery, though one single non-operative paper suggested modest benefit for motivated, non-surgical
patients.** He states the conclusion directly: **"there is no evidence to support the addition of night
splinting to routine hand therapy practice"** post-surgery, closing with a deliberately blunt framing:
**"this is head over heart — the science says no"** `[05:06]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]` — Chojnowski opens with a laboratory finding offered as a conceptual, not clinical, argument:
**pulling on fibroblasts/myofibroblasts in culture causes them to pull back harder** — a tensile-stress
response he explicitly flags as "only a laboratory model" that "may not apply so much clinically," but offers
as an interesting reason to question whether increasing tensile load (as splinting does) is actually
beneficial to this specific cell biology.
sections.heading: A laboratory rationale against splinting tension

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[01:00]` — For patients **not undergoing surgery**, Chojnowski identifies only one relevant paper —
a study from the London, Ontario unit — using **nighttime splinting combined with exercises and friction
massage** in **13 patients with PIP joint contractures**, followed over roughly a year, showing about **15
degrees of improvement** and some qualitative changes. He notes this aligns with patient-reported benefit
described in the symposium's own patient survey (`LVxj5lEVnz0`). His caveats: this applies specifically to a
**motivated, compliant patient with mild-to-moderate contracture**; the splint was **combined with other hand
therapies**, making its independent contribution unclear; and the study didn't examine what happens after
the splint is discontinued.
sections.heading: The one paper on non-operative splinting

sections.body:
`[02:01]`–`[05:06]` — Three RCTs are presented in sequence, each testing whether adding a **night splint** to
standard post-surgical hand therapy improves outcomes:

1. **SCoRD (Chojnowski's own study, East Anglia)**: 154 patients randomized preoperatively to night splint
   (worn 6 months) or no splint, both receiving standard hand therapy, with one-year follow-up. **13 patients
   crossed over** (8 due to surgeon concern despite no actual evidence of recontracture) — about 17% crossover
   — analyzed under **intention-to-treat**. Results: no meaningful difference in DASH scores; **active
   extension showed no statistically significant difference** between splint and no-splint groups; patient
   satisfaction was high in both, and adherence to the splint (when prescribed) was good. Chojnowski's stated
   conclusion from this trial: routine night splinting for every patient isn't necessary — a **wait-and-see**
   approach is safe, with splinting reserved for a small subgroup if needed.
2. **Collis study**: same core methodology, a somewhat smaller sample, splint worn for **three months**, with
   3 patients crossing over. Result: the **hand-therapy-only group did numerically better** (33 degrees better
   active extension than the splint group), though **not statistically significant**; patient satisfaction
   trended **higher in the hand-therapy-only group**, with patients trending toward preferring not to wear a
   splint at all. Roughly 10% required late "wait-and-see" splinting.
3. **A Dutch study** (referred to in the transcript by a name likely garbled by auto-captions — described as
   from a Dutch institution): a stricter design with **no crossover permitted**. Splint options tested: full-
   time wear for weeks followed by nights for three months, versus hand therapy alone. Result: hand therapy
   alone performed numerically better, but again **no statistically significant difference**, including
   specifically at the **PIP joints of the little finger** — a site Chojnowski flags as particularly
   treatment-resistant ("the feared territory"). Conclusion from this study: **no difference at all** between
   splinting and no splinting, both groups receiving hand therapy.
sections.heading: Three randomized trials of post-surgical splinting

sections.body:
`[05:06]` — Chojnowski closes by naming what remains unanswered: **roughly 10–17% of patients do
"recontract"** after surgery across these trials, and **who will, why, and what specifically would help them**
all remain unknown — even though splinting has traditionally been applied by default to this group.
sections.heading: The unresolved question

sections.body:
- **Recontracture following surgery, in roughly 10–17% of patients across trials**, explicitly named as an
  unresolved problem regardless of the splinting conclusion `[05:06]`.

- **"Head over heart"** — Chojnowski's framing for choosing the evidence-based conclusion over the intuitive,
  emotionally appealing preference for a low-risk adjunctive therapy `[00:00]`, `[05:06]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Chojnowski is explicit this is a formal **debate** talk arguing one assigned side, not a neutral review — he
opens by asking listeners to "leave your prejudices aside" and closes by directly naming the tension between
intuitive appeal and trial evidence. He is careful to distinguish the one favorable non-operative-splinting
study's real limitations (small sample, splint combined with other therapies, no post-discontinuation data)
from the three larger, more rigorous post-surgical RCTs, and does not claim the debate resolves what causes
recontracture or how to identify at-risk patients — he states plainly this remains unknown.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `rNihCBbmTx8`** (Lanting's disease clusters talk) — that talk finds Dupuytren's disease
course fluctuates substantially even without treatment, meaning any apparent splinting benefit in a study
without a no-treatment comparison arm could partly reflect natural disease-course variation rather than a true
splinting effect; this strengthens the case for the randomized-trial evidence this talk relies on over
anecdotal or uncontrolled reports. **Directly paired with `2-Ad4vp1EOA`** (Wach's "Debate: Splinting is Beneficial," the opposing side of this
same formal symposium debate) — Wach's anecdotal cases and small study more often describe splinting for
recurrence-prone joints or as a standalone preventive measure, distinct from the routine post-surgical
splinting these three RCTs specifically test; read together, the two talks may be more reconcilable than
opposed. **Directly relevant to `qoktkyD8P_o`** (Degreef & Brauns's tension-versus-compression splinting RCT) — that
trial found both splint types produced significant extension-deficit improvement over three months in a
non-surgical population, a result that sits somewhat in tension with this talk's more skeptical framing;
the two are reconcilable since Chojnowski's most skeptical conclusions are specifically about **post-surgical**
splinting, while Degreef & Brauns study splinting as a **primary, non-operative** treatment — closer to the
one favorable paper Chojnowski himself cites. **Relevant to `LVxj5lEVnz0`** (Wach's patient survey talk) —
Chojnowski explicitly references that survey's patient-reported splinting benefit as part of his discussion of
the non-operative splinting literature, directly linking self-reported patient perception to the single
supporting study he could find. **Relevant to any note discussing post-surgical recurrence prediction** — the
open question Chojnowski names (who recontracts, and why) remains genuinely unresolved across the notes in
this library, worth flagging wherever a note discusses recurrence risk factors.

sections.body:
**This talk is basic molecular biology from pulmonary, renal, and hepatic fibrosis research, presented at
the symposium as mechanism science likely to generalize to myofibroblast differentiation in Dupuytren's —
not as Dupuytren-specific findings.** The speaker states this framing himself at the outset: **"it's
clearly impossible to talk about mechanisms of differentiation in 15 minutes, so I'll just highlight some
recent exciting events in this area"** `[00:09]`, working entirely from lung/kidney/liver fibrosis models.
The single explicit point of connection to Dupuytren's disease itself is a passing remark about a signaling
molecule, Fizz1, **"which is also called resistin-like molecule alpha... considered to be an adipokine
initially... and potentially may be relevant even in Dupuytren's, where there are fatty or fat deposits
around this fascia"** `[12:26]` — offered as a hypothesis, not a finding.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:09]`–`[08:19]` — Phan reviews competing origin hypotheses for myofibroblasts in fibrosis, using
lineage-tracing evidence (not from Dupuytren's tissue) to rule two of them down:

- **Circulating/bone-marrow origin**: using a bone-marrow transplant model with GFP-tagged donor cells, his
  group found the tagged cells expressed collagen but **did not become myofibroblasts, even when treated
  with TGF-beta** — "the classical signal for inducing differentiation" `[02:11]`–`[04:16]`. His conclusion:
  this is "probably an unlikely contribution," though these cells may still act indirectly, in a paracrine
  role, by releasing TGF-beta that induces differentiation locally.
- **Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT)**: described as "rather controversial." The most definitive
  cited study used genetic lineage-tracking to tag kidney epithelial cells directly and found **"no evidence
  of colocalization... they concluded from this study that there's no evidence for epithelial-mesenchymal
  transition in vivo"** (in vitro evidence existed, but not in vivo) `[05:16]`–`[07:18]`.
- **What's left**: the working model — attributed to a review by his department chair — is that
  myofibroblasts **"predominantly arise from... the perivascular adventitial fibroblast, and primarily due
  to stimulation by TGF-beta"** `[07:18]`.
sections.heading: Where myofibroblasts come from

sections.body:
`[08:19]` — Phan states his own group's earlier finding that TGF-beta does two jobs, not one: **"in addition
to inducing differentiation, they can also inhibit apoptosis in the myofibroblast"** (shown against nitric
oxide-induced death), making it **"a potent signal for both the differentiation as well as the persistence,
or survival, of the myofibroblast."** He then locates this at the promoter level: two SMAD binding elements
were identified on the alpha-smooth-muscle-actin gene promoter, and mutating the upstream element (SBE1)
disrupted TGF-beta responsiveness, while mutating the downstream element (SBE2) had no effect — **direct
evidence for SMAD-mediated transcriptional control at a specific site** `[10:23]`–`[11:24]`.
sections.heading: TGF-beta drives both differentiation and survival

sections.body:
`[12:26]`–`[15:32]` — presented as a TGF-beta-*independent* route to the same endpoint. Fizz1/RELMα, induced
in a lung fibrosis model, activates Notch signaling through the ligand Jagged1; overexpressing Jagged1
enhanced alpha-actin expression beyond Fizz1 alone, and blocking Jagged1 suppressed it — **"indicating that
Fizz1 induction of alpha-actin expression, or myofibroblast differentiation, is dependent on Jagged1."** A
CSL-complex binding element was located on the alpha-actin promoter close to the SMAD site described above.
sections.heading: The Fizz1 → Jagged1 → Notch pathway

sections.body:
`[16:34]`–`[19:35]` — beyond induction, Phan describes active suppression keeping fibroblasts undifferentiated
at rest: Krüppel-like Factor 4 (KLF4) competes for promoter binding sites and inhibits SMAD3 binding to the
SMAD element; a short-form CBP/beta-catenin also inhibits. These are described as **induced** repressors,
not present at baseline. Separately, his lab identified **NKX2.5** — normally a cardiomyocyte marker — as a
baseline repressor specific to fibroblasts (opposite its role in vascular smooth muscle): mutating an
upstream NKX2.5 binding site increased promoter activity, suppressing NKX2.5 was sufficient to promote
differentiation, and **fibrotic tissue in vivo showed reduced NKX2.5 expression** — consistent with a
repressor being switched off as fibrosis proceeds `[18:34]`–`[19:35]`.
sections.heading: Active repression as a second, independent layer

sections.body:
`[20:36]`–`[26:44]` — Two mechanisms, both shown to matter more than expected: **histone deacetylase
inhibition unexpectedly blocked differentiation** (counterintuitive, since deacetylation normally silences
genes — Phan attributes this to an indirect route through another suppressor molecule). **DNA methylation**
at three CpG islands on the alpha-actin promoter was found to differ sharply between fibroblasts (low
methylation downstream, permissive) and alveolar epithelial cells that never express alpha-actin (high
methylation) — and a demethylating agent produced a dose-dependent increase in alpha-actin expression,
**"confirming that methylation is an important mechanism by which these cells are being kept
undifferentiated."** A separate liver-fibrosis study (Mann's group, UK) is cited converging on a related
pathway through MeCP2 and microRNA-132, ultimately suppressing PPAR-gamma to permit alpha-actin expression.
sections.heading: Epigenetic gatekeeping

sections.body:
None directly — this is cell-signaling and gene-regulation science from non-Dupuytren tissue models, with
no patient-facing symptoms discussed.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Myofibroblast differentiation** — the process by which fibroblasts acquire contractile,
  alpha-smooth-muscle-actin-expressing phenotype `[00:09]`.
- **Perivascular adventitial fibroblast** — the cell type identified as the likely local precursor to
  myofibroblasts `[07:18]`.
- **SMAD binding element (SBE)** — a specific promoter DNA sequence through which TGF-beta signaling
  activates alpha-actin gene expression `[10:23]`.
- **Fizz1 (RELMα)** — an adipokine-derived signal shown here to activate Notch/Jagged1 signaling and
  induce differentiation, with a stated (unconfirmed) hypothesis of relevance to fat deposits near
  Dupuytren's-affected fascia `[12:26]`.
- **NKX2.5** — a transcription factor identified here as a fibroblast-specific repressor of
  differentiation, distinct from its known role in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle `[17:34]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
None — the talk is delivered as a direct review of molecular findings rather than through illustrative
comparison.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The speaker is explicit that this is a partial, fast-moving review rather than a settled account: **"it may
sound a little bit disjointed... that's the limitation of the time"** `[00:09]`. He separately flags EMT's
contribution as **"rather controversial"** with the level of contribution "not entirely clear," notes the
cited lineage-tracing study is **"not the final word,"** and explicitly labels the Dupuytren's connection
to fat deposits as a stated possibility ("potentially may be relevant"), not a tested finding `[05:16]`,
`[12:26]`. The histone-deacetylase result is flagged by the speaker himself as "somewhat counterintuitive"
and only partially explained.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**No Dupuytren-specific claim to converge or conflict with yet** — this is background mechanism science
from other fibrotic diseases (lung, kidney, liver), offered by the symposium as plausibly relevant
molecular biology rather than direct evidence about Dupuytren's tissue. Any later note that discusses
TGF-beta signaling, myofibroblast biology, or fat/fascia involvement specifically **in Dupuytren's tissue**
should be checked against this talk's mechanisms as a candidate shared pathway, not treated as independent
confirmation — the speaker's own data here comes from other organs entirely.

the Jacobsen flap (H-shaped skin flap, open-palm healing by secondary intention)

sections.body:
**For advanced-stage (Tubiana III/IV) little finger Dupuytren's, the Jacobsen flap — an H-shaped open-palm
flap technique — produced staging improvement in roughly half of patients with a manageable complication
profile, and Tripoli argues it compares favorably to both needle fasciotomy and dermofasciectomy with
full-thickness grafting for this specific presentation.** His stated conclusion: **"because of the rapid
surgical technique [and] the minor risk of complications... the Jacobsen flap is a better option [than]
fasciectomy and percutaneous needle fasciotomy in treatment of stage three [and] four disease at the little
finger"** `[09:22]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:08]`–`[04:13]` — Tripoli frames early-stage disease as suitable for standard incisional approaches
(Bruner incision, selective aponeurectomy), but describes three distinct options once skin is contracted at
**Tubiana stage III or IV**:

- **Percutaneous needle fasciotomy** — indicated for advanced stage with contracted skin, elderly patients,
  and a clinically evident cord. Advantages: immediate digital movement restoration, rapid and minimally
  traumatic. Disadvantages (per the literature): neurovascular injury risk and a high recurrence rate.
- **Dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin graft** — indicated for frequent recurrence or high-diathesis
  patients. Advantages: essentially no recurrence *within* the graft margin (occasional recurrence at the
  graft's own edge). Disadvantages: donor-site scarring, graft failure risk, and stiffness from the
  immobilization the graft requires.
- **The McCash technique** — indicated for fibromatosis in the palmar/metacarpal region with contracted
  skin, requiring additional digital incisions and sometimes skin grafting at the interdigital creases.
sections.heading: Comparing three surgical options for advanced disease

sections.body:
`[04:13]`–`[07:19]` — First published by Jacobsen in 1977 (Scandinavian Journal of Plastic and Reconstructive
Surgery), a modification of the McCash approach using **two or three incisions**, specifically for **little
finger disease at Tubiana stage III/IV with contracted skin.** Technique: a first incision at the distal
palmar crease, a second perpendicular incision along the midlateral line of the little finger extending to
the level of contracture; the flap is elevated to **immediately identify the neurovascular bundles**, then a
**selective aponeurectomy** is performed. The resulting **H-shaped flap is advanced distally, leaving the
palm open to heal by secondary intention over about three to four weeks.**
sections.heading: The Jacobsen flap technique itself

sections.body:
`[07:19]`–`[08:22]` — Across two institutions over 8 years: **133 patients operated (88 at stage IV, 45 at
stage III)**, none with prior Jacobsen flap surgery; all completed physical therapy; **123 patients had
adequate follow-up data.** Staging results: of **86 stage IV patients, 38 reached stage 0** postoperatively;
of **37 stage III patients, 25 reached stage 0** at 18 months — combined, **roughly 49% of operated patients
reached stage 0** after surgery.

**Complications**: two nerve injuries, one arterial injury (attributed to a spiral cord), one case of
marginal flap necrosis (managed with escharotomy). **Recurrence occurred in 14 cases**; 10 of these underwent
repeat Jacobsen flap surgery, though some ultimately required amputation due to compromised ("ectopic")
blood supply. **Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD) occurred in 11 patients**, all of whom achieved **complete
symptom remission with analgesics and about three months of physical therapy.**

**Stated advantages**: rapid procedure, open palm reduces hematoma risk, no skin graft required, rapid
movement restoration. **Stated disadvantages**: frequent dressing changes (2–3 times weekly), patient
psychological discomfort from the visible open wound in the first two to three weeks, infection risk, and
delayed healing specifically in patients with metabolic disorders (e.g. diabetes), requiring careful wound
monitoring in that group.
sections.heading: Outcomes from an 8-year, 133-patient series

sections.body:
`[10:23]`–`[12:24]` — Tripoli closes by naming specific inconsistencies he sees in current risk-factor
explanations, without resolving them:

1. **Diabetes**: cited elsewhere as a major risk factor, yet **Asia has the world's highest diabetes
   burden while having comparatively low Dupuytren's prevalence** — "diabetes is [not] so determinant."
2. **Chronic microtrauma**: proposed to break longitudinal fibers and drive fibroblast collagen deposition,
   yet **children performing daily repetitive manual labor in Tanzania, Pakistan, and India** don't develop
   the disease, while it appears mainly in older patients elsewhere — and separately, **onset commonly
   differs in timing between a person's two hands**, hard to explain by uniform mechanical exposure alone.
3. **Race/genetics**: Caucasians carry the highest risk, with only isolated cases in Asian and Black African
   populations — yet the **TGF-beta polymorphism linked to keloid scarring** (itself common in African
   populations) is plausibly related to Dupuytren's biology, raising the question of why the disease itself
   remains rare in that same population.

His conclusion: **"Dupuytren's disease remains, for now, an idiopathic disease"** and, until better
understood, **surgery remains the necessary treatment.** He closes wryly noting a hoped-for future
anti-TGF-beta topical cream, while admitting he'd rather keep operating on patients a while longer.
sections.heading: Three unresolved epidemiological puzzles

sections.body:
- **Reflex sympathetic dystrophy after surgery**, reported in 11 of 123 followed patients, fully resolving
  with conservative management (analgesics, ~3 months physical therapy) `[08:22]`.
- **Compromised digital blood supply after recurrence surgery**, in some cases severe enough to require
  amputation `[08:22]`.
- **Psychological distress from viewing an open, healing surgical wound** in the weeks after Jacobsen flap
  surgery, named explicitly as a real disadvantage of the technique, not just a physical one `[09:22]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Jacobsen flap** — the H-shaped, open-palm-healing flap technique for advanced little-finger disease,
  described in full above `[04:13]`.
- **Tubiana staging (0 through IV)** — used throughout as the outcome measure for pre- and post-operative
  comparison `[02:08]`.

Tripoli separates established literature-reported risks (neurovascular injury and recurrence rates for
needle fasciotomy) from his own series' outcomes, and closes by explicitly naming his own explanatory
puzzles as unresolved rather than offering a false resolution — repeating "why" without supplying an answer
for each of the three epidemiological inconsistencies he raises.

sections.body:
**Complements `1BURdqs3a4U`** (Pess's technique talk) and **`L3kjpUIwHIQ`** (Leclercq's severe PIP
contracture talk) — all three address technique choice for advanced disease, though this talk is the only
one specifically focused on little-finger disease and the Jacobsen-flap open-palm approach as a distinct
third option alongside needle fasciotomy and grafting. **Extends the risk-factor discussion in `g40N2M2C6qM`**
and **`-0JtjUrrU4o`** (the genetics talks) and **`HE6nBpteAAo`** (Rayan's ectopic-disease talk) — this talk's
diabetes/geography and race/TGF-beta puzzles are concrete counterexamples worth weighing against any single-
factor risk explanation offered elsewhere in this library.

a four-point necrosis grading scale (0 to 3)
