contrasted against standard open-palm (McCash) and larger Z-plasty/Bruner closed techniques

sections.body:
**A short-zigzag incision design with thick, tangentially elevated flaps produced very low rates of skin
necrosis across 55 consecutive cases, offering an alternative to both open-palm technique and the larger
flap elevations of standard Z-plasty and Bruner incisions.** Papaloïzos's summary of the tradeoff he was
trying to solve: standard closed techniques **"usually [require] large skin flaps... elevated, [which] leads
to skin loss and delayed healing"** `[03:12]`, while open-palm technique is **"very demanding
post-operatively for the patient"** and its effect on recurrence **"has been questioned recently in
different papers"** `[02:10]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:05]`–`[04:13]` — Both major closure strategies carry real costs: **open-palm (McCash) technique**
applies only in the palm (fingers still need skin flaps), and requires **daily or every-other-day dressing
changes over a long period.** **Closed-skin techniques** (his general preference for primary cases) — Z-
plasty, V-Y plasty, zigzag, or Bruner incisions — typically require **large skin flap elevation**, causing
skin loss, delayed healing, and a bothersome, repeatedly-redressed wound that can **impair early
rehabilitation and lead to edema, infection, or algodystrophy (reflex sympathetic dystrophy).**
sections.heading: The problem with existing approaches

sections.body:
`[04:13]`–`[05:15]` — Papaloïzos describes the idea's origin directly: **"I was sailing on the Geneva
lake... when you are against the wind, you have to tack from one side to the other... maybe I could do
small tacks"** — instead of the large flap-elevation "tacks" standard techniques require, use **many short
zigzag increments.** The resulting technique: short-armed zigzag incisions with **flaps elevated tangentially
and kept as thick as possible** (minimizing devascularization), stitched with single sutures at each flap
tip.
sections.heading: A sailing-inspired solution

sections.body:
`[07:16]`–`[08:16]` — Short incision arms of **4–5mm**, with the elevation kept tangential and thick at the
base rather than broad and thin. One "way" (ray) typically corresponds to one incision, and up to **five**
have been used in a single case; the technique combines readily with **transverse or T-incisions in the
palm** for broad, thick aponeurosis, and with **V-Y plasty** when more skin coverage is needed. He notes he
suspects the arms could be made **even shorter**, but hasn't yet confirmed this is technically manageable.
sections.heading: Technique specifics

sections.body:
`[05:15]`–`[08:16]` — A **prospective, consecutive series, November 2007 to November 2009: 55 unoperated
cases**, mean age 63 (range 29–94), only **3 recurrent** (the rest primary). Deliberately short **mean
follow-up of seven weeks**, since the study's specific objective was skin healing, not recurrence. Staging:
roughly a third early-stage (Tubiana stage 1), about half stage 2, and about a quarter stage 3–4; joint
involvement spanned **20 MCP, 23 PIP, and 12 DIP** joints. Skin outcome was graded on a **four-point scale**
(0 = no skin loss; 1 = one limited point of superficial necrosis; 2 = two to three points of superficial
necrosis or one point of deeper, full-thickness necrosis; 3 = multiple, extended, or deep subdermal
necrosis), assessed at **day 5 (first dressing), day 12 (stitch removal), and four weeks.**
sections.heading: The series and its necrosis-grading system

sections.body:
`[10:17]`–`[11:17]` — **Very few necrosis cases at 5 days**; slightly more at one week but still limited in
extent; by one month, the picture had **settled back to no necrosis or only limited superficial necrosis.**
Total complications: **three small hematomas**, all resolving without further surgery or intervention.
sections.heading: Results

sections.body:
`[11:17]`–`[12:18]` — Advantages: a **simple design** not requiring large flaps, easily combined with other
local flaps (V-Y specifically), **versatile and usable anywhere on the hand**, and — notably — **"very easy
to learn and very easy to teach,"** promoting primary skin healing. Disadvantages he names directly: flap
elevation still requires care, closure is **relatively time-consuming**, and — importantly — **"I do not
pretend that this technique can be used in every case"**: dermofasciectomy with grafting remains necessary
for genuinely difficult cases. On recurrence specifically, he's blunt: **"with my seven-week follow-up, I
have no idea"** — explicitly promising to investigate that separately in the future rather than claiming any
recurrence benefit from a study never designed to measure it. He closes by quoting **Houston**: **"it is the
patient, not the surgeon, who determines the recurrence, by his inherited tendency to the disease"** — a
direct restatement of the diathesis concept discussed throughout this library.
sections.heading: Stated advantages and honest limits

sections.body:
- **Skin necrosis at incision flap tips**, graded systematically (0–3) rather than described impressionistically, at three specific follow-up points `[08:16]`.
- **Delayed wound healing requiring prolonged, repeated dressing changes**, named as a specific source of
  patient burden with standard flap techniques `[02:10]`.
- **Small hematomas as the only complications observed**, all self-resolving `[11:17]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Necrosis grading scale (0–3)** — the four-point skin-outcome scale defined and applied throughout this
  study `[08:16]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Sailing "tacks" against the wind, applied to incision design** — many small directional changes instead
  of a few large ones, the direct inspiration for this technique's short zigzag arms `[04:13]`.
- **Houston's dictum**: **"it is the patient, not the surgeon, who determines the recurrence, by his
  inherited tendency to the disease"** `[12:18]`.

sections.body:
Notably candid about the study's scope: Papaloïzos states outright that the seven-week follow-up means **he
has no data on recurrence at all**, rather than implying a benefit the study wasn't designed to detect. He
also explicitly limits the technique's claimed applicability — **"difficult cases remain difficult
cases"** — rather than presenting it as a universal replacement for dermofasciectomy and grafting.

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `klWbjOcG3Kk`** (Ketchum's dermofasciectomy talk) — both address skin-related surgical
technique, though aimed at different problems: Ketchum's squared-graft-margin technique targets long-term
recurrence specifically, while this technique targets short-term wound-healing complications; Papaloïzos is
explicit his own technique doesn't replace dermofasciectomy for genuinely difficult cases. **Consistent with
`MO1w1Ed-Yqc`** (Skirven's hand therapy talk) and **`1BURdqs3a4U`** (Pess's technique talk) — all describe
skin tears, dressing burden, and delayed healing as real costs of Dupuytren's surgery worth actively
minimizing through technique choice. **Directly echoes the diathesis framing in `-jLfWXX3YUM`** (Seven
Questions) and **`klWbjOcG3Kk`** — the closing Houston quotation restates the same patient-biology-determines-
recurrence principle found throughout this library.

concepts: IC50/LC50 testing for differential drug effect
selective versus non-specific antiproliferative activity
topoisomerase inhibition and tubulin interference as a drug mechanism

sections.body:
**Of four newly synthesized compounds tested against cells cultured directly from patients' own diseased
tissue, one — "compound 4" — showed genuine selectivity, suppressing diseased cells specifically while
sparing healthy tissue, unlike the most potent compound tested, which killed cells indiscriminately.**
Jurisic's framing of that distinction: **"the strongest compound... has no differential activity on those...
cell cultures, so it was highly cytotoxic. The one being mostly interesting for us is compound 4, because...
it has shown to be highly specific for the [diseased] cell lines... preserving the [near-diseased] and the
control cells"** `[05:10]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:06]`–`[04:09]` — Eight male patients (six primary cases, two recurrences), with tissue samples marked
**D** (microscopically diseased tissue), **ND** (tissue taken near the primary incision, without visible
phenotypic disease expression), and true healthy controls from **carpal tunnel release patients.** Four
compounds tested: **5-fluorouracil (5-FU)** as the reference control (chosen for its known antiproliferative
effect in ophthalmologic surgery), plus three newly synthesized compounds (numbered 1–3, with 3 and 4 already
patented at the time of the talk — compound 4 being tested alongside, not among, the patented pair as best
understood from the transcript). A practical technical note: for **advanced (Tubiana stage 3–4) disease**,
excessive tissue manipulation and exposure during a long dissection degraded cell culture quality — solved
by **removing and handling palm tissue first, before continuing the dissection into the finger**, to keep the
sample viable.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[04:09]`–`[06:10]` — Tested at day 3, 6, and 13 of culture. **Compound 3 was the most potent
antiproliferative agent overall, but showed no selectivity** — equally toxic to diseased, near-diseased, and
healthy control cells, making it clinically unsuitable. **Compound 4, by contrast, was highly specific to
diseased (D) cell lines at tested concentrations, while preserving ND and control cells.** IC50/LC50 values
were determined specifically to identify this kind of differential effect between diseased and healthy
tissue. Immunofluorescence tracking alpha-smooth-muscle-actin expression alongside a fluorescent signal
confirmed the pattern; for compounds 1–3, treated cells showed **enlargement interpreted as cell-cycle
arrest.**
sections.heading: Results

sections.body:
`[07:11]`–`[08:13]` — Belongs to a class of compounds that **specifically inhibit mammalian topoisomerase
activity**, binding DNA and causing DNA damage, and additionally **interferes with tubulin polymerization**
— a described, real mechanism class (topoisomerase inhibition plus microtubule disruption). Given its
selectivity for diseased cells and **low toxicity across all tested cell cultures**, Jurisic proposes two
potential applications: **selective treatment during the early, highly proliferative disease phase**
specifically, and **postoperative use aimed at the wound-healing process**, given its low toxicity profile.
sections.heading: What compound 4 actually is

sections.body:
`[08:13]` — Jurisic notes candidly that his own surgical case selection likely captured tissue in a
**residual or evolutional phase** of disease rather than the truly early, highly proliferative phase this
compound would be best suited to target — **"I didn't catch the patients with the proliferative phase"** —
flagging this as something to actively consider when designing future treatment-timing studies, rather than
glossing over the mismatch between his sample and his own proposed application.
sections.heading: An honest self-critique about disease phase

sections.body:
None directly — this is laboratory drug-screening science using patient-derived cell cultures, not a
description of clinical presentation.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Differential (selective) antiproliferative activity** — a drug's ability to suppress diseased cells
  specifically while sparing healthy cells, the key criterion distinguishing compound 4 from the more potent
  but non-selective compound 3 `[04:09]`.
- **Topoisomerase inhibition / tubulin interference** — compound 4's described mechanism class `[07:11]`.

sections.body:
Jurisic is direct about which compound failed and why (compound 3's lack of selectivity, despite its raw
potency, disqualifying it), and explicitly names a mismatch between his own patient sample (residual/
evolutional-phase disease) and the disease phase his proposed treatment application would actually target —
flagging a real limitation of his own study design rather than glossing past it. He also states outright that
this is preclinical work: compound 4 is proposed for **"further preclinical studies and optimization,"** not
presented as ready for clinical testing yet.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Complements `2Yi43NqnvfM`** (Samuel's relaxin talk) and **`6YYYYh8aoJE`** (Gabbiani's N-terminal peptide
talk) as a third, mechanistically distinct candidate anti-fibrotic/antiproliferative approach under
development at the same symposium — relaxin works through TGF-beta/SMAD signaling, Gabbiani's peptide acts
directly on assembled actin filaments, and this compound acts through DNA topoisomerase inhibition and
tubulin disruption, each targeting the disease process at a different molecular level. **Relevant to
`XMQEyF-Gtv0`** (O'Gorman's cell biology talk) and **`ic6Wd3sT62Q`** (Kathju's animal model talk) — all three
studies rely on the same core methodology of comparing patient-derived diseased cells against matched
healthy-tissue controls from the same patients, a recurring experimental design choice across multiple
independent labs represented in this symposium.

concepts: a literature-derived minimum clinically important difference used to plan sample size
alternating (quasi-randomized) group assignment across scheduled treatment sessions
distinguishing pain at the injection itself from pain during the later manipulation/extension procedure
management: collagenase injection, with or without local anesthesia given 20 minutes beforehand

sections.body:
**In a randomized comparison, giving local anesthesia 20 minutes before the collagenase injection itself
significantly reduced patient-reported injection pain — mean VAS 2.3 versus 4.3, a difference of 2.1 points —
though pain experienced at home in the following one to two days before manipulation was the same in both
groups, and the department has since adopted local anesthesia as routine practice as a direct result.**
Nordenskjold states the finding directly: **"we can see significantly lower VAS mean scores for the group
that got local anesthesia 20 minutes before the collagenase injection — 2.3, in contrast to a mean of 4.3 for
the no-LA group, with a mean difference of minus 2.1"** `[04:03]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[01:01]` — At Nordenskjold's department (a hospital in southern Sweden), collagenase is the
**first-line treatment** for Dupuytren's contracture, with **475 patients treated since 2011.** It was already
standard practice to give local anesthesia before the **finger manipulation/extension** step, since that
procedure is known to be painful. The open question this study addresses: is the **collagenase injection
itself** — separate from the later manipulation — also painful enough to warrant local anesthesia
beforehand? Clinical observation suggested patients experienced substantial pain specifically at the time of
injection, motivating this trial.
sections.heading: The question behind the study

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[03:03]` — **162 consecutive patients** meeting standard inclusion criteria (extension deficit of
at least 20 degrees at the MCP or PIP joint, palpable cord) were **alternately assigned** (quasi-randomized) to
a **local anesthesia (LA) group**, receiving anesthetic **20 minutes before the collagenase injection**, or a
**no-LA group.** A single surgeon performed all injections using a modified technique, delivering collagenase
into multiple spots along the cord. **Mepivacaine, diluted with sodium bicarbonate** (to reduce the pain of
the local anesthetic itself, per prior literature), was the anesthetic used. Pain was measured via the
**visual analog scale (VAS, 0–10)** at the time of the first injection (whichever came first, LA or
collagenase), and again when patients returned **one to two days later** for the manipulation procedure, at
which point they also rated the pain experienced **at home** in the interim.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[03:03]`–`[04:03]` — The team reviewed the literature and identified **a 1.3-point difference in VAS score as
the established minimum clinically important difference**, drawn from two large prior studies, and used this
to calculate a required sample size of **50 patients per group.** Analysis used mean VAS scores and standard
deviation, with a covariance-adjusted (ANCOVA) approach.
sections.heading: Sample size planning

sections.body:
`[04:03]`–`[05:05]` — **Injection-time pain**: LA group mean VAS **2.3** versus no-LA group mean **4.3** — a
**statistically significant** difference of 2.1 points, comfortably exceeding the pre-specified 1.3-point
MCID. **Pain at home between visits** (before the manipulation step): **essentially identical between groups,
2.9 for both** — the anesthesia given before injection had no detectable carryover effect on pain experienced
in the following days.
sections.heading: Results

sections.body:
- **Pain specifically at the moment of collagenase injection**, quantified and distinguished from
  manipulation-related pain and from pain experienced at home in the days between visits `[04:03]`.

sections.body:
Nordenskjold, presenting as a new PhD student and incoming resident, discloses he personally has no conflicts
but is transparent that his co-author does (shown directly on the slide). He is candid that the study used
**alternating rather than true randomization** across scheduled treatment sessions, and reports a clean null
result for the home-pain comparison rather than selectively emphasizing only the positive injection-pain
finding. The department's resulting practice change (adopting routine local anesthesia before collagenase
injection) is presented as a direct, stated consequence of this specific study's result.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `bKXguv2CscM`** (Badalamente's concurrent collagenase injections talk) and `OwSS6grbMAc`
(Badalamente's CORD I trial talk) — both report collagenase-related pain and adverse events at a general level;
this talk supplies a specific, randomized, quantified answer to a narrower question (injection-specific pain,
and how to reduce it) not addressed in those broader trial-outcome talks. **Relevant to any note discussing
collagenase technique or patient tolerability** — this study's finding, that pre-injection local anesthesia
meaningfully reduces injection pain without needing to alter dosing or technique, is a low-cost, generalizable
practice recommendation worth surfacing wherever collagenase administration technique is discussed.

concepts: Kaplan-Meier and log-rank analysis applied to time-to-retreatment as the outcome
a patient-driven retreatment design, where the outcome event is the patient's own decision to seek further treatment
total extension deficit (TED) tracked over multiple years, not just a single postoperative timepoint
management: needle aponeurotomy (NA) alone
needle aponeurotomy combined with a steroid (triamcinolone) injection series

sections.body:
**In a long-term follow-up (7–53 months) of a randomized trial, adding a steroid injection series to needle
aponeurotomy produced significantly better total extension deficit than needle aponeurotomy alone through 24
months — but that advantage disappeared beyond 24 months, and while overall retreatment rates did not
significantly differ between groups, the non-steroid group sought retreatment measurably sooner.** Binhammer
states the conclusion directly: **"our null hypothesis was rejected, and for the short term — at least up to
24 months — there was a statistical difference with steroid-treated NA patients versus non-steroid-treated"**
`[05:14]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:00]`–`[01:01]` — This talk reports long-term follow-up of a previously published randomized controlled
trial comparing **needle aponeurotomy (NA) combined with a triamcinolone (steroid) injection series** against
**NA alone.** Binhammer is candid that the original trial, while randomized, was **not blinded** — he
performed the measurements himself and knew each patient's group assignment — and used **no stratification**,
enrolling all comers. The original 6-month result: **steroid + NA produced significantly greater improvement
in motion than NA alone.** This follow-up study's hypothesis: steroid + NA patients would show **less joint
contracture and a longer delay to retreatment** than NA alone; the stated null hypothesis was that retreatment
rate and contracture severity **would not differ** between groups.
sections.heading: Background: the original trial

sections.body:
`[01:01]`–`[02:03]` — Unlike the original trial's fixed follow-up schedule, this study allowed patients to
return **up to 18 months** on their own initiative; those who hadn't returned by then were contacted directly
and had their extension deficit measured. **Retreatment itself was patient-driven** — patients could choose
fasciotomy or repeat needle aponeurotomy (collagenase was not yet available at the time of this study), and
study participation ended once a patient underwent a second treatment. Primary outcomes: retreatment and
**total active extension deficit (TED).** **44 of the original 47 patients** were followed, over a range of
**7 to 53 months** (the short end reflecting one patient who proceeded to secondary treatment at 7 months).
sections.heading: Follow-up design

sections.body:
`[03:07]` — Consistent with the original 6-month report, **mean TED remained significantly higher in the
NA-alone group than the steroid group through 24 months.** **Beyond 24 months, this difference was no longer
statistically significant** — the steroid-added benefit, real in the short-to-medium term, did not persist
indefinitely.
sections.heading: TED results over time

sections.body:
`[03:07]`–`[05:14]` — Comparing overall retreatment rates: **no statistically significant difference** was
found between groups, though the p-value was **0.07** — close to, but not crossing, the conventional
significance threshold. A **Kaplan-Meier analysis** of retreatment as a percentage of subjects over time
showed the two curves converging by around **48 months.** However, a **log-rank test** found the **non-steroid
(NA-alone) group sought retreatment sooner** over the observed time period — a difference in *timing* not
fully captured by the simple overall-rate comparison. Additional predictors of retreatment, independent of
steroid use: patients whose **initial treatment involved two or more joints** were more likely to need
retreatment, and **younger patients** were more likely to need retreatment. A **Cox proportional hazards
regression** confirmed **baseline age and number of joints treated** as significant predictors.
sections.heading: Retreatment results

sections.body:
None beyond total extension deficit and retreatment as the tracked clinical outcomes — this talk does not
discuss individual patient-reported symptoms beyond these measures.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Binhammer is unusually direct about the original trial's methodological weaknesses — explicitly acknowledging
it was **unblinded, with the same investigator performing measurements while aware of group assignment**, and
**not stratified.** He is candid that this follow-up study's design (patient-driven return and retreatment
timing) is itself a limitation, since sample size naturally erodes over a long observation period as in any
longitudinal study, and patients self-select when to report back. He reports the borderline p=0.07 retreatment
result plainly rather than rounding it into either a positive or negative finding, and lets the more nuanced
Kaplan-Meier/log-rank timing result stand alongside it rather than picking one number to lead with.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `-32nd2vQexQ`** (Gan's needle aponeurotomy talk), `wSZhfP1r1OY` (Eaton's IFSSH needle
fasciotomy talk), and `vOSY4FZEJGM` (Erne's needle fasciotomy outcome talk) — this talk adds a distinct,
adjunctive-treatment angle (steroid co-injection) and, notably, the longest follow-up period (up to 53 months)
of any needle-technique outcome talk in this library. **Relevant to `rNihCBbmTx8`** (Lanting's disease clusters
talk) — that talk's finding that Dupuytren's disease course fluctuates naturally over time is relevant context
for interpreting why a real short-term treatment difference (through 24 months) might narrow by 48 months,
independent of any change in the treatments themselves. **Relevant to `R4WPhcOpAMo`** (Selles's consensus
recurrence definition talk) — this study's own outcome design (patient-driven retreatment as the event, TED as
a separate outcome) is a useful comparison point for how differently "recurrence" or treatment failure can be
operationalized across the studies in this library.

concepts: RSD (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) risk as a patient-selection factor
fat graft revascularization through a micro-porous trellis defect
meshing a contracted cord like a skin graft, via multiple superficial nicks
the "violin string" cutting principle
management: extensive percutaneous aponeurotomy (EPA)
fat grafting combined with percutaneous release

sections.body:
**Standard percutaneous release alone gives "very good but... limited relief," and open fasciectomy gives
better release at the cost of "high morbidity and long recovery" — Khouri's answer is to combine an
extensive, multi-nick percutaneous release with fat grafting into the space it creates**, arguing this adds
back tissue the disease itself has depleted: **"fat atrophy is really intrinsic to the pathology of
Dupuytren's"** `[00:04]`. He is explicit the fat-grafting idea is not novel in principle: **"fat grafted
Dupuytren's [was described] in the German literature... in the 1600s. We're not reinventing anything
new"** `[01:05]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:05]`–`[05:08]` — Khouri distinguishes his **extensive percutaneous aponeurotomy (EPA)** from standard
needle release by intent: rather than a few limited cuts, **"why don't we shred this cord?"** — many small,
superficial nicks rather than fewer larger ones. Three stated principles:

1. **The "violin string" effect**: a small nick under strong tension will cut cleanly, but the same nick
   in slack tissue will not — and **"the nerves are not under as much tension as the cord itself,"** making
   the technique selective for the taut cord over adjacent structures `[02:05]`.
2. **Stay superficial**: treating the cord like a woven material, **"if you just cause attrition cuts at
   multiple levels, it's going to fall apart"** without needing to cut deep — including near the spiral
   cord, where staying superficial matters most for safety `[03:06]`.
3. **Create space for the graft**: the multiple nicks also separate the cord from the dermis, creating
   vascularized "finger-like extensions" that increase the surface area available for the fat graft to
   revascularize and be incorporated `[03:06]`.

Instruments: an 18-gauge needle ("Dupuytome 1"), used bevel-up so **"the bevel is your depth gauge... never
completely buried,"** and a second bent needle ("Dupuytome 2") used with a "windshield-wiper" motion to
separate the cord from the dermis before fat is injected through a 14-gauge cannula `[04:07]`–`[05:08]`.
Post-procedure care: a splint incorporated into the dressing for a week, then a night splint from his hand
therapist.
sections.heading: The technique and its three principles

sections.body:
`[09:11]`–`[11:12]` — Run jointly with Steve Hovius, with **up to 42 months of follow-up, mean about 1.5
years**. Twenty patients had prior open surgery on the contralateral hand, giving an internal comparison
group; some patients had severe diabetes. **Overall satisfaction was high**, with essentially all patients
back to normal hand use, including golf, within two to four weeks. **Of 13 patients with recurrent disease
on the treated hand, all 13 preferred the new technique to their prior open surgery.** At a (short) 10-month
follow-up, looking at the worst-affected finger per patient: **96% improvement at the MP joint**, and
**PIP-joint residual contracture improved from 67% to 33%.** Compared informally against open-surgery
recurrence data (Khouri flags this comparison as not fully fair, given differing follow-up lengths), EPA
"seemed to be, if anything, slightly better," since open treatment showed more recurrence.
sections.heading: Outcomes from a 75-patient combined series

sections.body:
`[10:12]`–`[15:19]` — **One nerve injury**, occurring specifically in a recurrent-disease case where prior
surgical scar had bound the nerve to the cord, degrading Khouri's ability to differentiate them while
cutting. **His one serious complication**: a young woman he identifies as high RSD (reflex sympathetic
dystrophy) risk, whose hand turned red immediately post-op and whose fat graft **"completely melted
away."** A second attempt at grafting also failed. He also describes cases where old surgical scar tissue
tore open during release (new, unoperated skin did not tear, only prior scar did) — managed with a small
local flap plus fat grafting.
sections.heading: Complications and one detailed failure case

sections.body:
`[17:21]`–`[20:28]` — Khouri extends the same mesh-and-fat-graft principle to **burn/scar contractures**
(shown on a child's MCP-joint scar contracture), to **radiation-damaged tissue after lumpectomy**, and to a
**post-mastectomy, post-radiation shoulder contracture** in a physician patient in her 60s who could not
raise her arm — released and grafted with a documented one-month recovery sufficient to return to work
within days. He separately mentions a small series of **rheumatoid arthritis hands** treated the same way,
stating explicitly he is **not confident the technique affects the underlying disease** in that context,
only that "the hand sure looks better."
sections.heading: Broader applications shown

sections.body:
- **Residual finger contracture at the MP and PIP joints after percutaneous or open treatment**, with
  specific improvement figures reported `[10:12]`.
- **Palpable hard nodules softening ("melting") after mechanical disruption**, described as visible during
  the procedure itself `[12:14]`.
- **Post-procedure erythema (redness) as an early warning sign of fat graft failure**, in his one flagged
  complication case `[13:16]`.
- **Recurrence after fat grafting**, in at least one documented case, attributed by Khouri to insufficient
  graft volume in that area rather than a technique failure generally `[13:16]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Extensive percutaneous aponeurotomy (EPA)** — Khouri's multi-nick percutaneous release technique,
  distinct from standard limited-cut needle aponeurotomy `[01:05]`.
- **The "violin string" cutting principle** — a small nick cuts cleanly only in tissue under tension,
  giving selectivity for the taut cord over slack adjacent structures `[02:05]`.
- **RSD (reflex sympathetic dystrophy)** — named as the risk factor behind Khouri's one serious
  complication and his stated patient-selection caution `[13:16]`, `[21:29]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Meshing a skin graft** — the cord is opened with many small superficial nicks the way a skin graft is
  meshed, rather than with one large cut `[07:09]`.
- **The violin string** — tension, not blade force, determines what gets cut `[02:05]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Khouri is candid about the technique's limits: operative time is **not** reduced compared to open surgery
("it really takes a while"); the rheumatoid arthritis application is explicitly not claimed to modify
disease; and he states a personal, unproven impression rather than a tested finding when he says the
technique **"seems to alter the course of disease... rejuvenates the hand."** He flags a formal prospective
randomized trial as in progress (Hovius, ~60 patients enrolled at the time of the talk) rather than citing
it as completed evidence. His closing recommendation — **avoid the technique in young, female, high-RSD-risk
patients** — is stated as personal bias drawn from his one complication, not a established contraindication.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Extends `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy`**, which reports standard needle fasciotomy's recurrence at
roughly 50% at 3–5 years — Khouri's EPA-plus-fat-grafting series reports outcomes he describes as
comparable or better, though over a shorter and less rigorously matched follow-up period, so this should be
read as a promising uncontrolled series rather than a head-to-head refutation of that recurrence figure.
**Relevant to any note drawn from Eaton's or Hurst's talks on percutaneous techniques** — Khouri explicitly
positions EPA as a deliberate technical departure from the more limited-cut needle release those talks
describe, developed "gradually over five years" specifically because he judged the standard technique's
release to be insufficient.

anatomy: other digits of the same hand
concepts: future intervention as a single umbrella outcome spanning three different locations
retrospective cohort design at a single institution
management: collagenase treatment
surgical fasciectomy

sections.body:
**Within about 5 years of an initial procedure, more than 4 in 10 patients needed some further treatment for
Dupuytren's — split roughly into recurrence in the same digit, spread to another digit in the same hand, or
new disease in the opposite hand, each with its own timeline and risk factors** `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[¶5]`

A **single-institution database review**, starting from 658 patients coded for collagenase treatment or
surgical fasciectomy, narrowed to **341 eligible patients** — 141 initially treated with fasciectomy and 200
with collagenase, treated between 2015 and 2019. The primary outcome was simply whether the patient needed
subsequent treatment, and where: the same digit, another digit in the same hand, or the contralateral hand.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[¶6]`, `[¶7]`

At a **mean follow-up of 5.3 years, 142 of 341 patients (42%) underwent additional treatment.** That 42%
splits unevenly by location and by timeline: **same-digit revision in 88 patients (26%) at a mean of 3.2
years; another digit in the same hand in 35 patients (10%) at a mean of 3.6 years; and the contralateral hand
in 79 patients (23%) at a mean of 2.3 years** — meaning the opposite hand was, on average, the *fastest* site
to need treatment, even though same-digit recurrence was the single most common outcome. Different factors
predicted each location: **procedure type, multiple digits treated, and initial nontreated contracture**
predicted same-digit retreatment; **younger age, active smoking, and initial nontreated contracture**
predicted spread to another digit in the same hand; and **the dominant hand being the one initially treated,
plus initial nontreated contracture,** predicted treatment later being needed in the other hand.
sections.heading: What it found

sections.body:
- **Recurrence of contracture in the originally treated digit** `[¶6]`.
- **New Dupuytren's intervention needed in a digit that was not initially treated**, whether in the same hand
  or the opposite one `[¶6]`.
- **Pre-existing, untreated contracture in a digit other than the one initially addressed**, named repeatedly
  as a risk factor for further treatment regardless of location `[¶6]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Contralateral hand** — the hand not initially treated; this study tracks it as a distinct outcome
  location from the treated hand's other digits `[¶4]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body: None — outcomes are reported as percentages and follow-up years.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
The authors translate their findings directly into a counseling recommendation rather than leaving the reader
to infer it: **"Within 5 years of initial treatment for Dupuytren contracture in one digit, patients have
over 40% likelihood of future intervention for contracture... Key risk factors include age, multiple digits
treated, smoking, and the presence of initially nontreated fingers, which should be incorporated into patient
counseling"** `[¶7]`. The study labels its own evidence tier explicitly: **"3-Retrospective cohort study,
prognostic"** — a lower evidence tier than a randomized trial, stated as such rather than implied `[¶8]`. A
conflict of interest is disclosed directly: **"Dr Blazar is a consultant for Endo Pharmaceuticals"** (a
collagenase manufacturer), with the other authors reporting no related benefits `[¶8]`.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Relevant to, but not the same measurement as, `nocek-2026-recurrence-systematic-review` and
`detect-2026-progression-rct`**: those sources measure recurrence or progression within the treated joint;
this cohort is the only source in the library so far that tracks the disease appearing or needing treatment
somewhere *else* — another digit, or the other hand entirely — after an initial procedure. **No conflict in
direction**: all three sources agree that further treatment after an initial procedure is common, not rare.

concepts: matrix remodeling via cyclical slack creation and take-up
myofibroblast as phenotype rather than cell type (Gabbiani's functional definition)
periodic versus isometric contraction
the Rho-kinase pathway
the calcium/calmodulin/myosin light chain kinase pathway

sections.body:
**Myofibroblast contraction runs on two separable pathways with different jobs — one creates brief,
localized events; the other holds sustained tension — and Dupuytren's contracture likely emerges from their
repeated interaction over time, not from either one alone.** Hinz's own synthesis: **"you have two cycles —
one is a long-lasting, low-frequency cycle over probably days, where the cell is contracting strongly and
then remodeling on a local level... and over time would lead to these contractures that you observe in a
clinical situation"** `[15:18]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[02:06]` — Hinz opens by qualifying the field's usual shorthand: **"Professor Gabbiani, when he discovered
the myofibroblast, uses a functional definition of this cell — a contractile phenotype, and not necessarily
a molecular definition by alpha-smooth-muscle-actin expression — but it's so convenient to have this marker
that most people use it as a defining feature."** As a phenotype rather than a distinct cell type,
myofibroblasts appear across a wide range of conditions beyond Dupuytren's — hypertrophic scarring, burn
wounds, skin fibrosis, scleroderma, fibrotic responses to implants, lung fibrosis, heart failure, and, more
recently studied, atherosclerotic plaque evolution, chronic asthma, and the tumor stroma, where they are
described as actively promoting tumor growth `[02:06]`–`[03:07]`.
sections.heading: What a myofibroblast actually is

sections.body:
`[06:11]`–`[15:18]` — Working with cardiac myofibroblasts cultured on soft silicone substrates (chosen to
match scar stiffness, since **"the sheer fact that you put fibroblasts on a plastic dish transforms a good
part of them into myofibroblasts"**), Hinz's group tracked two readouts simultaneously: substrate wrinkling
(a proxy for sustained isometric tension) and bead movement on the cell surface (a proxy for small,
localized contractile events).

| Pathway | Mechanism | Speed/character | Drug used to isolate it | Effect of blocking it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Calcium pathway** | Calcium binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates myosin | Short-lived, high-frequency (**roughly every minute**) | Thapsigargin / 2-APB | Bead movement stops; **wrinkles (isometric tension) persist** |
| **Rho-kinase pathway** | Inactivates the enzyme that removes the phosphate from myosin, keeping myosin constitutively active | Long-lasting, sustained | Y-27632 | Wrinkles disassemble, isometric tension lost; **bead movement is unaffected** |

Blocking both simultaneously with blebbistatin abolished all cell tension within about ten minutes: **"the
beads don't move anymore, and the cells would lose completely this wrinkling behavior."** The two pathways'
effects are cleanly dissociable — each drug knocked out one readout while leaving the other intact — which
Hinz takes as evidence the two pathways genuinely do different jobs rather than being redundant routes to
the same output `[13:17]`–`[15:18]`.
sections.heading: Two contraction pathways, cleanly separated by drug experiments

sections.body:
`[15:18]`–`[16:18]` — Hinz's synthesis, offered explicitly as a working model rather than a proven
mechanism: **"imagine you're trying to contract a rubber band — what you have to do is pull it in, and then
you create a kind of slack... the rubber band for the cell is actually the extracellular matrix, the
collagen."** The Rho-kinase pathway produces a **strong, long-lasting contraction of the stress fibers,
which creates slack in individual collagen fibers**; the faster calcium-driven contractile events then
**"work on these stress-released fibers and pull them in, remodel them"** while the fiber is slack; the
matrix **takes over the load again**, and the cell re-spreads to repeat the cycle. Repeated over **days**,
this cumulative local remodeling is proposed as the route from small, reversible single-cell contractions to
the irreversible clinical contracture.
sections.heading: The rubber-band model

sections.body:
None specific to Dupuytren's presentation — this is in vitro cell mechanics, offered as background for
interpreting clinical contracture rather than a description of patient-facing symptoms.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Myofibroblast (functional definition)** — a contractile cell phenotype, defined by Gabbiani by function
  rather than strictly by alpha-smooth-muscle-actin expression `[02:06]`.
- **Calcium/calmodulin/MLCK pathway** — the fast, short-duration contraction route, shared with smooth
  muscle cell biology `[06:11]`.
- **Rho-kinase pathway** — the pathway sustaining long-lasting, isometric myofibroblast tension by keeping
  myosin dephosphorylated-inhibition removed `[06:11]`–`[07:11]`.
- **Isometric versus periodic-scale contraction** — Hinz's own terms for the two readouts (wrinkling versus
  bead movement) his assay separates `[14:17]`–`[15:18]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **The rubber band being pulled taut, creating slack that a second, faster process then takes up and
  remodels** — Hinz's own synthesis model for how brief and sustained contraction combine `[15:18]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Hinz is explicit that this is a working model built from in vitro cardiac myofibroblast data, not confirmed
Dupuytren's tissue biology: **"outside of the body, in a three-dimensional gel... we think that's what's
happening in the Dupuytren's contracture as well"** `[05:10]` — stated as an inference by extension, not a
direct finding. He also flags that the specific mechanism connecting calcium-pathway events to the
Rho-kinase pathway's role in creating the slack they act on is model-level reasoning: **"the idea that we
have... is the following"** `[15:18]`, not a demonstrated causal chain in Dupuytren's-affected tissue.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to the paired debate talks `QRUnLzXLyjE`** (Nanchahal, "active") **and `wsqTB5LAGYo`**
(Eaton, "passive"). Eaton's passive-contraction argument uses this exact same periodic-versus-isometric
framework and the same Rho-kinase/calcium pathway distinction — this talk is very likely the primary
science source underlying that argument, though Eaton's talk does not cite it directly. Notably, **Hinz's
own two-cycle model does not fully side with either debate position**: it requires both the strong,
Rho-kinase-driven contraction Nanchahal's "active" argument emphasizes (to create slack) and the
matrix-laxity-dependent remodeling Eaton's "passive" argument emphasizes (to lock the slack in) — read as a
synthesis rather than a vote for either side. This talk does not address the cell-to-cell adherens/gap
junction coupling central to Nanchahal's argument, so it neither confirms nor contradicts that part of his
case.

concepts: LOD score as a linkage-study significance threshold
copy number variation (CNV)
gene expression comparison across nodule, cord, and control tissue
personalized medicine / pharmacogenomics applied to treatment selection
sibling recurrence risk ratio as genetic evidence

sections.body:
Like `HE6nBpteAAo`, this video's auto-captions are considerably more degraded than most others in this
library, and the degradation is worst in the middle sections covering specific gene names and study
results. This note covers only what is confidently legible; where the transcript names a specific gene,
chromosome, or figure but the surrounding sentence is unrecoverable, that detail is omitted rather than
filled in from outside knowledge of Dupuytren's genetics.
sections.heading: A note on this source

sections.body:
**Multiple independent lines of evidence support a genetic component to Dupuytren's, but individual gene-
and variant-level findings have largely failed to replicate strongly across studies — the field has
evidence of heritability without yet having a clear molecular target.** Bayat states this directly about
his own field's candidate-gene work: after pooling several studies' findings, **"really nothing... sort of
[explains] disease pathology"** on its own `[09:21]`–`[10:22]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:09]`–`[02:13]` — Bayat lists the standard criteria applied: **presence in twins, a familial tendency,
ethnic-specific prevalence, and disease severity tracking with familial predisposition.** He cites a
**sibling recurrence risk ratio**, compared between UK and Icelandic cohorts, as showing a **"parallel
phenomena"** across populations — offered as evidence the genetic contribution is not a single population's
artifact. This sits alongside the geographic pattern noted at the start of the talk: **Dupuytren's clusters
in regions of Northern European descent worldwide**, consistent with other sources in this library.
sections.heading: Why Dupuytren's is considered genetic at all

sections.body:
`[02:13]`–`[03:14]` — Bayat flags a real methodological difficulty: genetic material can come from blood or
from tissue (fascia, skin, fat), but **disease latency means an apparently unaffected relative or control
patient may simply not yet have developed visible disease**, weakening family-history-based controls.
Historically, **carpal tunnel syndrome patients have been used as a tissue control group** for comparison.
He also flags that studies comparing **palm-only versus digit-involving disease** need to account for the
fact that a tissue sample is only a snapshot of whatever stage the disease had reached when it was removed.
sections.heading: The practical problem of studying it

sections.body:
`[05:16]`–`[13:27]`:

- **Linkage study** (English/Swedish families): reported a LOD score around 3 — Bayat notes genome-wide
  significance in family linkage studies conventionally requires a LOD score of at least 3, calling even a
  LOD of 3 "not very [high]" in practice, and flags that findings from a single family study carry limited
  weight `[07:17]`–`[08:18]`.
- **Candidate-gene association studies**, run by multiple groups comparing cases to controls: identified
  several genes of interest but, pooled together, **did not converge on a consistent account of disease
  pathology** `[09:21]`–`[10:22]`.
- **Copy number variation (CNV) studies**: an earlier 2008 study using a lower-density gene chip found no
  statistically significant result; Bayat's group repeated the analysis with a newer chip (**"about a
  million" markers**) and identified areas of interest on multiple chromosomes, flagged as needing further
  investigation rather than as a confirmed finding `[10:22]`–`[11:23]`.
- **Gene expression studies** comparing nodule, cord, and control tissue (published ~2008): found clear
  differential expression between nodule and control tissue, with affected gene-function categories
  including **cell proliferation and matrix deposition/organization**. One named candidate, **ADAM-12**,
  showed differing expression levels across fascia, cord, nodule, fat, and skin samples
  `[11:23]`–`[15:32]`.
sections.heading: What's been tried, and how far it got

sections.body:
`[16:34]`–`[18:37]` — presented explicitly as future direction, not current practice: Bayat frames genetic/
susceptibility testing as potentially useful for **prevention**, for **characterizing a patient's molecular
disease profile before choosing a therapy** ("a patient carrying a particular genotype... may not be
suitable" for a given treatment), and for **dosing decisions** — drawing an explicit analogy to
personalized-medicine pharmacogenomics in infection treatment, where patients on the same antibiotic
respond differently. He is clear this capability does not yet exist for Dupuytren's.
sections.heading: Where this could lead clinically

sections.body:
`[18:37]`–`[20:41]` — Bayat outlines an assessment sequence largely already standard: **detailed history**
(including diathesis and predisposing factors relevant to recurrence risk and treatment choice), **clinical
examination** to rule out other conditions and confirm the diagnosis, **Hueston's tabletop test**, and
**goniometry** for severity. He proposes genetic testing (**a buccal swab**) as a future addition to this
workflow, not a current one.
sections.heading: Proposed diagnostic workflow

sections.body: None specific — this is a study-methodology and genetics talk, not a discussion of patient-facing symptoms.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Sibling recurrence risk ratio** — a measure comparing disease risk in relatives of affected individuals
  against the general population, used as genetic evidence `[01:11]`.
- **LOD score** — the statistical measure of linkage significance in family genetic studies; ~3 is
  described as a conventional (if modest) significance threshold `[07:17]`.
- **Copy number variation (CNV)** — structural genetic variation examined as a possible susceptibility
  factor `[05:16]`.
- **ADAM-12** — a candidate gene shown here with differential expression across Dupuytren's-affected and
  unaffected tissue types `[14:31]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **Antibiotic response variability as an analogy for why genetic susceptibility testing might guide
  Dupuytren's treatment dosing** `[17:36]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Bayat is explicit that this field has not converged: candidate-gene findings are described as failing to
explain pathology when pooled, the CNV finding from his own repeated analysis is presented as requiring
further investigation rather than as confirmed, and the entire clinical-application section is framed
conditionally ("may become quite relevant") rather than as available now. Where this note's own coverage is
thin, that reflects transcript quality, not a hedge stated by the speaker — see the note above on source
quality.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Consistent with `AbY1KVhTVAo`** (Eaton's IDDB talk), which independently proposes a genetic/systemic
disease subset versus an exposure-driven subset — Bayat's talk supplies the underlying genetic-study
evidence (and its limits) behind that proposed split, without yet identifying the specific gene(s) that
would confirm it. **Consistent with the geographic/ethnic pattern** noted in `HE6nBpteAAo` (Rayan's talk),
which separately documents Dupuytren's occurring outside populations of Northern European descent —
relevant context for interpreting Bayat's genetic-clustering argument, which is about relative prevalence
rather than exclusivity to one ancestry.

concepts: a nerve branch pattern nicknamed "nerves to the disease"
describing location as a percentage of finger length for surgical reproducibility
nerve injury rates in Dupuytren's surgery

sections.body:
**A consistent, previously undescribed pair of nerve branches — found in every single finger examined —
arises from the proper digital nerve at a predictable location and could be mistaken for the proper digital
nerve itself during Dupuytren's surgery, especially once distorted by a spiral cord.** Choa's summary states
the safety stakes directly: **"there are constant pairs of nerve branches which could be mistaken for the
proper digital nerves... we found it's quite a predictable location — this hopefully will serve to aid
surgical dissection and facilitate protection of the proper digital nerve"** `[07:11]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:03]`–`[01:04]` — Nerve injury is a recognized complication of Dupuytren's surgery, with **reported
rates of 1.4–7.8%** varying across surgeons and units in the literature. The study originated from an
informal observation by Choa's consultant colleague, who noticed **large-caliber branches diverging from the
proper digital nerves**, colloquially nicknamed **"nerves to the disease."** The concern: these branches
could be **large enough to be mistaken for the proper digital nerve itself**, particularly once normal
anatomy is distorted by a spiral cord — and a literature search found **no prior formal description of these
specific branches.**
sections.heading: Why this mattered

sections.body:
`[01:04]`–`[02:04]` — **40 fingers** dissected from cadaveric hands (10 pairs from male specimens, plus
additional specimens from a female body), all **screened and confirmed free of hand pathology or
Dupuytren's disease** before dissection. Skin was removed from the proximal transverse palmar crease to the
distal joint crease, and each specimen was examined for the A1 pulley, the common and proper digital
nerves, and the branch pattern in question.
sections.heading: Study design

sections.body:
`[03:07]`–`[05:09]` — Photographic documentation showed **paired branches diverging from the proper digital
nerves and meeting at the finger's midline**, forming a shape the consultant colleague described as a
**"chevron."** Measuring from the **midpoint of the A1 pulley's proximal edge**, the branch origin distance
was recorded with calipers alongside total finger length, allowing the location to be expressed as **a
percentage of finger length** for generalizability across different-sized fingers. Result: **a constant
chevron pair was found in every finger from index through little finger**, occurring predictably at
**15–16mm from the A1 pulley**, which works out to **approximately 20% (roughly one-fifth) of the total
distance from the A1 pulley to the fingertip.** A **dense concentration of Pacinian corpuscles** was found
near these branch points, and the branches were confirmed **anatomically distinct from the dorsal digital
nerve branches** — ruling out that this was simply a case of dorsal branches being misidentified.
sections.heading: The "Chevron pair" finding

sections.body:
`[06:11]` — Since the A1 pulley isn't routinely dissected or directly identified during standard
Dupuytren's surgery, Choa's group combined their chevron-branch location data with **an existing published
surface-marking technique** (attributed to Wilhelmy) for locating the A1 pulley from external landmarks —
allowing surgeons to **predict roughly where these at-risk nerve branches will be**, without needing to
formally expose the pulley itself, as an aid to safer dissection.
sections.heading: Making the finding usable in surgery

sections.body:
- **Nerve injury as a recognized surgical complication**, with a specific cited rate range (1.4–7.8%) from
  the existing literature `[00:03]`.
- **Risk of mistaking a chevron-pair branch for the proper digital nerve itself**, specifically flagged as
  more likely once the anatomy is distorted by a spiral cord `[03:07]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Chevron pair** — the paired nerve branches from the proper digital nerve, meeting at the finger midline
  in a V-shaped pattern, found consistently across all examined fingers `[03:07]`.
- **"Nerves to the disease"** — the informal nickname the branches were given prior to formal study,
  reflecting their apparent association with the diseased tissue region `[01:04]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **The chevron (V) shape** — the visual/geometric description used throughout to describe how the paired
  branches meet at the finger midline `[03:07]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Choa is direct about the study's limitations: **only 40 specimens**, though he notes this is comparable to
other similarly scaled cadaveric nerve studies in the literature, and no directly comparable prior
description of this specific branch pattern could be found despite a search (distinguishing it from separate,
existing work on dorsal digital nerve branching patterns by other named authors). He also notes candidly that
he personally hadn't performed many Dupuytren's operations himself, relaying the clinical concern as reported
by his more experienced consultant colleague rather than from his own direct surgical experience.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Directly relevant to `1BURdqs3a4U`** (Pess's technique talk) and **`atbGE2kJ5_U`** (Smith's PIP joint
algorithm talk) — both describe careful attention to neurovascular structures during dissection and
manipulation; this talk supplies a specific, previously undescribed anatomical hazard neither of those
talks names directly. **Relevant to `iD3mYMmfN-Q`** (Eaton's anatomy talk) — that talk's detailed review of
cord and fascial anatomy doesn't cover this specific nerve branch pattern, making this note a useful
supplement to the anatomical reference elsewhere in this library. **Complements the spiral cord risk
discussed in `L3kjpUIwHIQ`** (Leclercq's severe PIP contracture talk) and **`fmWiC5V76YI`** (Khouri's EPA
talk) — both flag spiral cords as displacing the neurovascular bundle into surgical danger; this talk adds a
specific, previously unnamed additional structure at risk in that same anatomical region.

concepts: patient satisfaction as a distinct, separately tracked outcome from objective remission
progression defined precisely as new/enlarging nodules, new cords, or worsening symptoms
the cross-specialty communication gap between hand surgeons and podiatrists
management: contrasted against local/wide excision, subtotal and total plantar fasciectomy
radiotherapy (10x3Gy, two courses eight to twelve weeks apart) for Ledderhose disease

sections.body:
**Ledderhose disease is treated far worse by surgery than its hand counterpart — largely because so few
surgeons ever operate on it — and radiotherapy achieves durable, well-quantified benefit that Seegenschmiedt
argues deserves the same attention Dupuytren's already receives.** At a median follow-up of almost 6 years:
**"the primary endpoint, no progression, is achieved in 91% of the cases"** `[11:18]`, with **84% of
patients reporting satisfaction** with treatment `[13:22]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:03]`–`[02:04]` — Named for Georg Lederhose, the Munich surgeon who first described it. Seegenschmiedt's
own examined population: **about 20% of Dupuytren's patients have Ledderhose disease, and about 50% of
Ledderhose patients have Dupuytren's** — framed as evidence Ledderhose signals a **higher-penetrance
Dupuytren's diathesis**, worth actively checking for. He illustrates the blind spot directly: a colleague
"who knew his hands quite well" didn't know he had Ledderhose disease on his own feet — **"we are not aware
of palpating our own feet."** He notes the specialty divide bluntly: **"have you ever met a podiatrist on a
hand surgeons meeting? And vice versa? They don't communicate."**
sections.heading: Naming, prevalence, and a cross-specialty blind spot

sections.body:
`[02:04]`–`[04:08]` — Standard surgical options (local excision, wide excision, subtotal or total plantar
fasciectomy) are typically performed by podiatrists, not hand surgeons, and Seegenschmiedt states **results
are "even worse than... the hand,"** attributing this to the operation's rarity — **"it's done by lay
people in the periphery, and it's not accumulated in centers"** — and to the practical problem that a
healing foot still has to bear weight. He notes the largest historical surgical series before his own work
was only about 50 cases, reported by Lederhose himself in 1897 and 1902, with most published series since
still under 20–25 cases.
sections.heading: Why surgical outcomes on the foot are worse than the hand

sections.body:
`[05:09]`–`[06:12]` — Demographics differ notably from Dupuytren's hand disease: **roughly a 1:1 male:female
ratio** (versus hand disease's well-documented male skew), **median age 56**, and **substantial bilateral
involvement — 222 feet affected versus only 54 unaffected** among followed patients. Of those with at least
one year of follow-up (138 patients), **91 patients (126 feet) received radiotherapy**; 47 declined and
served as an unrandomized control group (dose concept not yet established at the time). Risk factors in the
treated cohort: **about a third were smokers**, with knuckle pads, keloids, diabetes, epilepsy medication,
and — notably — **seven patients with liver disorders (including prior hepatitis and cirrhosis)**; **about
11–12% reported a prior foot injury or trauma.**
sections.heading: His cohort and their risk profile

sections.body:
`[07:13]`–`[10:16]` — Outcomes were tracked via **photographic documentation with a ruler** (an initial
photocopy-machine approach was abandoned as impractical), a **visual analog scale for symptoms**, and MRI or
ultrasound where needed — noting plantar nodules sit **deeper than Dupuytren's palmar nodules**, requiring
radiation depth coverage up to **2cm**. Across the cohort: **324 total nodules counted (1–5 per patient,
median 2×2cm, up to 6.5cm)**, and **142 cords in 46 patients** (cords were less common overall, which
Seegenschmiedt reads as **a marker of less advanced disease** than extensive nodularity). Treatment protocol
mirrored the hand: **10 fractions of 3 Gray, given as two 5-day courses 8–12 weeks apart**, using
orthovoltage photons or a linear accelerator, with lead shielding customized to protect non-target tissue —
**each session lasting about 3 minutes (or as little as 15 seconds on a linear accelerator)**, with setup
being the most time-consuming part; patients were in and out of the department within about 15 minutes.
sections.heading: Measurement and treatment protocol

sections.body:
`[11:18]`–`[13:22]` — **91% achieved the primary endpoint of no progression**; of the **11 cases that did
progress, 50% ultimately required surgery.** Roughly half of stable cases held steady in nodule size/count,
and half showed **objective remission**: **nodule count reduced by 33% on average**, with the most dramatic
individual response in a child treated for a nodule that shrank from 6×7cm to 2×3cm over about 9 years.
Cords showed softening or reduction in **45% of cases**, with measurable shrinkage in length. **Symptom
improvement was the most dramatic outcome category, reported by 60–80% of patients** — Seegenschmiedt
attributes this to both direct symptom relief and the resulting restoration of normal foot arch shape as
nodules shrank. **Overall patient satisfaction: 84%**, closely tracking the stabilization/improvement rate.
Acute toxicity (dryness, erythema, itching) occurred in about 20% and was **more common in previously
operated (recurrent) lesions than untreated primary ones**; chronic skin changes (mild dryness,
discoloration) occurred in about 15%, manageable with moisturizing.
sections.heading: Results at ~6-year median follow-up

sections.body:
- **Pressure, tension, and pain while walking or at rest, plus itching sensation and walking difficulty**,
  the primary patient-reported complaints in plantar fibroma disease `[06:12]`.
- **Deep, harder-to-palpate nodules compared to Dupuytren's**, requiring imaging support (MRI/ultrasound) in
  unclear cases `[07:13]`.
- **Foot arch shape distortion from nodule bulk**, described as improving as nodules shrink under treatment
  `[12:21]`.
- **Worse acute skin reaction in previously operated (recurrent) sites** than in untreated primary disease
  `[10:16]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Progression (as a defined trial endpoint)** — explicitly specified as any nodule enlarging or newly
  appearing, any new cord, or any worsening symptom `[08:14]`.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- **"Most of us stand on our foot, and we don't make handstands"** — a wry closing note on why foot disease
  deserves attention proportionate to, not lesser than, hand disease `[13:22]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Seegenschmiedt is careful to distinguish stabilization from true objective remission ("about a one-to-one
ratio between stabilizing the disease... and... objective remission") rather than combining them into one
inflated success figure, and states the control group was **not randomized** because a dose concept had not
yet been established when the study began. He also explicitly limits his own scope relative to surgery:
**"I don't want to step in [on] a very complicated surgical situation because I probably have no means to
deal with that... scarring"** — positioning radiotherapy as complementary, particularly for recurrent
disease, not a wholesale surgical replacement.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Substantially extends the Ledderhose summary in `oXR_NOAaSa0`** (Seegenschmiedt's other 2010 talk) — the
patient counts there (138 with 1+ year follow-up, 222 involved feet, 54 uninvolved) describe the same
underlying cohort at an earlier, shorter (1-year) follow-up snapshot; this talk reports the same program's
results at a far longer ~6-year median follow-up, with substantially more granular outcome data (91%
no-progression, 84% satisfaction, specific nodule/cord reduction percentages) not given in the other note.
**Consistent with `nLR3nKuAufs`** (Hellstrom's Peyronie's talk) and **`5fqC-xS8WhM`** (Spilken's cryotherapy
talk) — both describe other non-surgical approaches to fibrotic conditions in adjacent anatomical territory,
reinforcing this talk's broader point that minimally invasive, non-excisional treatment options for
Dupuytren's-family fibrotic conditions are consistently outperforming traditional surgery across multiple
independent research groups and modalities.

sections.body:
**This is a single-page NHS clinical care pathway, not a narrative source — it specifies exactly which
patients should be referred for surgery, on what criteria, and what happens at every stage from a GP
appointment through to discharge.** `[p.1]`. It is co-branded GIRFT (Getting It Right First Time) and BSSH
(British Society for Surgery of the Hand), dated December 2023, with BAPRAS and the British Orthopaedic
Association also credited.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

The pathway runs Presentation → Referral → Surgical review → Operative procedure → Recovery and
rehabilitation. **Presentation in primary care leads to a specific history-and-examination protocol** (hand
dominance, occupation, interference with daily activities, duration of symptoms, trauma, previous surgery,
recurrence, co-morbidities including diabetes/smoking, and family history) **and a specific examination**
(loss of hand function; skin thickening or pitting in the palm; firm nodules fixed to skin or deep fascia;
fibrous tendon-like cords; flexion deformity of the MCPJs and IPJs; reduced thumb–index webspace; inability
to lay the palm and fingers flat on a table top; and ectopic lesions — nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles
of the feet, or penile tissue).

**The pathway names a specific differential diagnosis list to rule out first**: callus, ganglion cyst, giant
cell tumour, inclusion cyst, ulnar nerve palsy, trigger finger, post-trauma or infection, joint disease,
diabetic cheiroarthropathy, camptodactyly, Volkmann's contracture, and (rarely) epithelioid sarcoma.
sections.heading: The five stages

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

**The pathway sets an explicit numeric bar for surgical referral**: "flexion contracture of 30° or more at
the MCPJ or 20° at the PIPJ," or a thumb contracture that impairs function, or previously failed
non-operative management, or rapidly progressive disease. Below that threshold, the pathway branches
differently depending on whether there is diagnostic uncertainty or intolerably painful nodules the primary
clinician isn't trained to inject — either routed to a community MSK service for confirmation and possible
steroid injection, or (if neither applies) simply reassured that "tender nodules [are] likely to become less
tender over time," with cortisone injection offered for pain and radiotherapy noted only as something to
"consider... as part of local audit or research if available" — not a standard offer.
sections.heading: The referral threshold

sections.body:
`[p.1]`

Once referred, the pathway requires **assessment by, or supervised by, a surgeon with appropriate training
in Hand Surgery**, confirmation of diagnosis, and a formal informed-consent process, before choice of
procedure — **percutaneous fasciotomy in outpatients, or listing for daycase surgery** — based on surgeon
preference, patient factors, and disease characteristics.

Recovery is staged explicitly: **at 3–5 days post-surgery**, dressing changes, wound checks, range-of-motion
exercises and a night splint are considered; **at 10–14 days**, suture removal (if needed) and ongoing hand
therapy, splinting, and scar management, with one review by the surgeon or an Extended Scope Practitioner.
The pathway's endpoint is **"Discharge with Patient Initiated Follow-up (PIFU)"** — the patient, not a
scheduled appointment, triggers any further contact.
sections.heading: Surgical review, procedure, and recovery

sections.body:
- **Firm nodules fixed to the skin or deep fascia, with skin thickening or pitting in the palm** `[p.1]`.
- **Fibrous, tendon-like cords, and flexion deformity at the MCPJ and IPJ** `[p.1]`.
- **Reduced span between thumb and index finger webspace; inability to lay the palm flat on a table** `[p.1]`.
- **Ectopic nodules over the dorsal PIPJs, soles of the feet, or penile tissue** `[p.1]`.
- **Persistent painful nodules**, distinguished in the pathway from nodules that are simply present but not
  painful `[p.1]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **MCPJ / PIPJ** — metacarpophalangeal joint / proximal interphalangeal joint, the two joint locations the
  pathway's surgical threshold is defined against `[p.1]`.
- **Patient Initiated Follow-up (PIFU)** — a discharge model where the patient contacts the service if
  needed, rather than being given a routine follow-up appointment `[p.1]`.

sections.body: None — this source is a procedural flowchart, not explanatory prose, and doesn't use illustrative analogies.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
This is an operational care pathway, not a graded evidence review — it states what should happen clinically,
not how strong the evidence is for each step. Two things are worth preserving as-is: the pathway explicitly
demotes radiotherapy to something to "consider... as part of local audit or research if available" rather
than a standard-offer treatment `[p.1]`, and it explicitly tells clinicians to reassure patients below the
surgical threshold that their nodules are "likely to become less tender over time" rather than promising
resolution `[p.1]`.

`nice-htg427-radiotherapy` (NICE's own graded evidence for the radiotherapy option this pathway treats as
audit-only) and `nice-htg21-needle-fasciotomy` (NICE's guidance on the percutaneous fasciotomy option this
pathway lists as one of the two surgical-review outcomes).

sections.body:
This is primarily a ceremonial welcome address (conference logistics, host-city facts about Groningen,
hospital statistics) opening the 2015 symposium — most of it is not substantive Dupuytren's content and is
not covered in this note. Two specific, substantive pieces of research history are extracted below.
sections.heading: A note on this source

sections.body:
**A hospital CEO's own unusual, non-hereditary Dupuytren's case — combined with his hunch about a specific
recreational vibration exposure — led directly to a real research finding, illustrating how patient-driven
observation can start formal research.** Aartsen states his reasoning directly: **"I am the only person in
my family to be afflicted. I suggested... that there could be a link between developing Dupuytren's and
playing hockey with a stick — anyone who plays hockey will immediately recognize the vibration you feel
through the stick when you hit the ball"** `[09:20]`.
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[00:04]`–`[01:06]` — Werker describes learning needle fasciotomy (percutaneous needle aponeurotomy) directly
from its French popularizer in Paris (the name renders in auto-captions as "Lermusiaux," not confidently
recoverable) in the late 1990s, then bringing the technique back to his own hospital and beginning formal
research on it: **first a pilot study, then a randomized clinical trial that lasted five years.** Early in
the following decade, he began a genetics collaboration with **Professor Roel Ophoff**, which by **2010,
meeting in Miami, grew into an international collaboration** with Dominic Furniss and Hans Hennies —
**published, Werker notes with evident pride, in the New England Journal of Medicine.**
sections.heading: Werker's path to the international genetics collaboration

sections.body:
`[09:20]`–`[10:21]` — Aartsen, the hosting hospital's CEO, describes himself as **"a hands-on expert not only
as a patient but also as an instigator of research"** into Dupuytren's. Being the only affected member of his
family cast doubt, in his own mind, on the disease being purely hereditary, prompting his vibration-exposure
hypothesis to Werker. The resulting research reportedly found Dupuytren's disease **"significant among male
hockey players at the Dutch veterans tournament"** — a specific, occupational/recreational vibration-exposure
finding arising directly from one patient's informal observation reaching a receptive researcher.
sections.heading: The hockey-vibration finding

sections.body:
- **Dupuytren's occurring in a patient with no other affected family members**, used here as the prompt for
  questioning a purely hereditary explanation in that specific case `[09:20]`.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body: None beyond terms already established elsewhere in this library.
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:

  own tourism slogan, offered as a light audience send-off rather than a substantive point `[11:23]`.
sections.heading: Analogies worth reusing

sections.body:
Both accounts are told as personal history/anecdote rather than presented with data in this talk itself —
Werker references the NEJM publication as an external, verifiable outcome of the collaboration he describes,
while Aartsen's hockey-vibration finding is summarized without given sample size or statistical detail in
this excerpt, though it is described as a completed, findings-bearing study rather than mere speculation.
sections.heading: Source-stated confidence

sections.body:
**Very likely describes the origin of the same GWAS work covered directly in `-3a_yiOu_3I`** (Dolmans's 2010
talk, presenting the study in progress) and **`-0JtjUrrU4o`** (Ophoff's 2015 talk, citing the completed
9-locus finding) — Werker's account here supplies the human/institutional backstory (his own meeting with
Ophoff, the 2010 Miami symposium as the moment the collaboration became international) behind those two
notes' scientific content. **Relevant to `dxYwTKGRBgk`** (Tripoli's Jacobsen flap talk) and **`jk7w-i8PPrs`**
(Eaton's Severity talk) — both discuss chronic vibration/mechanical exposure as a proposed environmental risk
factor; Aartsen's hockey-stick finding is a specific, named example of exactly that mechanism being
investigated and reportedly confirmed in one population.
